## Everything at a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Sketches** | `px.QuickSketch()` places every element once, without a solver; `px.Sketch()` takes the same calls and adds constraints and dimensions; `px.Move((h, v))` starts a QuickSketch at a point. |
| **Draw** | `Line`, `Arc`, `Spline`, `Circle`, `Rectangle`, `RectangleC`, `Slot`, `ArcSlot`, `Keyhole`, `Polygon`, `Hexagon`, `Close`, `Finish` |
| **Move the pen** | `Move((h, v))`, `Move(id)`, `Move(dh, dv)`, `Move(l)`, `Turn(angle)`, `Direction((dh, dv))` |
| **Lines** | `Line(l)`, `Line(dh, dv)`, `Line(to)`, `Line(from, to)`; helpers `until=`, `parallel=`, `distance=`, `perpendicular=`, `angle=`, `congruent=`, `tangent=`, `through=`, `reverse=` |
| **Arcs** | `Arc(r, sweep)`, `Arc(to)`, `Arc(to, r)`, `Arc(from, to, r)`; helpers `sweep=`, `center=`, `concentric=`, `congruent=`, `tangent=`, `through=`, `until=`, `reverse=` |
| **Circles** | `Circle(r)`, `Circle(h, v, r)`, `Circle(r, center=, concentric=, congruent=, through=, tangent=, reverse=)`. A full circle is one exact edge with no vertices. |
| **Rectangles** | `Rectangle(l, w)` from the pen, `Rectangle(p0, p1)` from two corners, `Rectangle(p0, p1, p2)` from a side and a point on the opposite side, `RectangleC(l, w)` around the pen or a center |
| **Ready-made shapes** | `Slot(l, w)`, `ArcSlot(r, sweep, w)`, `Keyhole(l, w, r)`, `Polygon(r, n)`, `Hexagon(af)`; see [Slots, keyholes and polygons](slots-polygons.md). |
| **Targets** | Ids, `px.H`, `px.V`, edges, wires, faces, OpenCASCADE shapes, or `(target, point)`, where the point decides that target's choice; `until=px.first` / `px.last`. |
| **Ids** | Automatic ids such as `Line.1`, `Arc.2`, `Point.3` and `Chain.1` for every element, point and chain, or your own with `id=`. `"id.start"`, `"id.end"`, `"id.mid"` and `"id.center"` refer to an element's points, `Chain.-1` counts from the end, and selections accept globs such as `"w.**.corner"`. |
| **Construction** | `construction=True`, `Vertex(id, point)`, `points`, `Location(id)`, `Edge(id)`, `Construction()` |
| **Offsets** | `Offset(source, d, both_sides=)`, or `(d, point)` for one side; the two sides are `.left` and `.right`. In a constraint sketch, `"<id>.d"` is its distance. |
| **Edit** | `Trim(a, b, reverse=)`, `Split(a, b)`, `Fillet(at, r)`, `Chamfer(at, d, d2=, angle=)` (see [Fillets and chamfers](fillets-chamfers.md)), `SymmetryLine(a, b)`, `Mirror(axis)`, `Mirrored(ids, axis)`, `LinearPattern(ids, dir, count, spacing)`, `CircularPattern(ids, center, count)`, `Remove(id)` |
| **Motions** | `Translate`, `Rotate`, `Scale`, `Mirror` and their copies `Translated`, `Rotated`, `Scaled`, `Mirrored`, on the whole sketch or, for `Mirror`, on chosen elements; see [Moving, rotating, mirroring, scaling](../basics/motions.md). |
| **3D geometry** | `Project(shape)`, `Intersect3d(shape)`; see [Projecting 3D geometry](../../integrations/occ/projecting.md). |
| **Properties** | `name`, `col`, `maxh`, `minh`, `hpref`, `layer` and `partition` on every drawing call; `id_wire=` on `Close` and `Finish`. |
| **Plane** | `px.QuickSketch(face)` on a face of a solid, with the global origin and x axis projected onto it; also a `px.Plane`, netgen axes or another planex2d object as the first argument, `copy=True` to take over its geometry. `px.Plane(face, origin=, axis=)` projects another origin or axis; `SetOrigin(point)`, `Copy()`. See [The plane in 3D](../basics/plane.md). |
| **Results** | `Wire()`, `Wires()`, `Face()`, `Shape()`, `Edge(id)` (a wire), `ToOCCShape()`, `Plot()` |

---

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/sketch/quicksketch.md

# Sketch or QuickSketch

planex2d has two sketch types with the same drawing calls:

- `px.QuickSketch` places every element once, from the pen and the references it is given, and keeps the geometry as
  drawn. No solver runs, so it stays fast for thousands of elements.
- `px.Sketch` draws the same way and adds a constraint solver. Constraints, dimensions, expressions and `Update` keep
  the intent of the drawing when a value changes. With `auto_constraint=True`, the references of the drawing calls
  become constraints as well.

Both produce the same wires, faces and exports. A QuickSketch suits outlines that are drawn once, generated in a loop
or imported. A `px.Sketch` suits parts whose dimensions change later, and geometry that has to be solved, such as a
mechanism. One converts into the other (see [Converting sketches](../constraints/converting.md)). The pages of this
section use the QuickSketch, and [Constraint sketches](../constraints/index.md) adds the solver.

```python
import time
import numpy as np
import planex as px
```

## The same link in both

The example is the link from [Tangents](tangent.md): two bosses as construction circles, the lines tangent to both,
the end arcs on the bosses, and a hole in each. One function draws it into any sketch. In a QuickSketch and in a
plain `px.Sketch`, it has no constraints. With `auto_constraint=True`, the tangents and the joints become constraints
(Figure 1).

```python
def link(sk):
    sk.Circle(0, 0, 1.5, id="boss1", construction=True)
    sk.Circle(6, 0, 1.0, id="boss2", construction=True)
    sk.Line(tangent=("boss1", "boss2"), id="upper")
    sk.Line(tangent=("boss1", "boss2"), reverse=True, id="lower")
    sk.Arc("lower.end", "upper.end", congruent="boss2", id="end2")
    sk.Arc("upper.start", "lower.start", congruent="boss1", id="end1")
    sk.Circle(0.6, center="boss1.center", id="hole1")
    sk.Circle(0.4, center="boss2.center", id="hole2")
    return sk


quick = link(px.QuickSketch())
plain = link(px.Sketch())
tied = link(px.Sketch(auto_constraint=True))
for name, sk in (("Sketch()", plain), ("Sketch(auto_constraint=True)", tied)):
    counts = {kind: len(entries) for kind, entries in sk.constraints.items()}
    print(name, sk.dof, "degrees of freedom, constraints", counts)
print("the same face:", quick.Face().mass, tied.Face().mass)
```

```text
Sketch() 28 degrees of freedom, constraints {}
Sketch(auto_constraint=True) 8 degrees of freedom, constraints {'Tangent': 4, 'Coincident': 8}
the same face: 18.523573419356737 18.523573419356737
```

```python
Row((quick, "QuickSketch", {"fill": False}), (tied, "Sketch(auto_constraint=True)", {"constraints": True}),
    caption="The same link in a QuickSketch and in a constraint sketch")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The constraint sketch is not fully constrained yet, so it is drawn in black. With dimensions for the radii and the
distance of the bosses, it becomes a parametric part, and the tangents keep the link a link when a dimension changes.
See [Drawing with constraints](../constraints/drawing.md) for details.

## What a QuickSketch does not have

A QuickSketch has no constraint calls. `Constrain`, `Expression`, `Update`, `dof` and the other analysis functions
belong to `px.Sketch`. A constraint flag, or `auto_constraint=True`, raises an error that names the alternative. The
references of the drawing calls work as in any sketch:

```python
qs = px.QuickSketch().Line(10, 0, id="a").Line(0, 5, id="b")
print("Constrain in a QuickSketch:", hasattr(qs, "Constrain"))
try:
    qs.Line(-10, 0, px.Horizontal)
except ValueError as err:
    print(err)
try:
    px.QuickSketch(auto_constraint=True)
except ValueError as err:
    print(err)
qs.Move((0, 5)).Line("b", parallel="a", id="c")
c = qs.Geometry("c")
print('Line("b", parallel="a"):', c["start"], "to", c["end"])
```

```text
Constrain in a QuickSketch: False
px.Horizontal: a QuickSketch has no constraints; px.Sketch(...) has them
QuickSketch(auto_constraint=True): a QuickSketch has no constraints; px.Sketch(...) has them
Line("b", parallel="a"): (0.0, 5.0) to (10.0, 5.0)
```

`px.Move((h, v))` starts a QuickSketch with its pen at a point. `px.Sketch((h, v))` and `px.QuickSketch((h, v))` do
the same for the respective sketch type.

## Speed: generated outlines

The example is a heat sink comb generated in a loop, with 50 fins of 30 on a base of 5 and four lines per fin. A
QuickSketch draws it without solving. A `px.Sketch` with the flags `px.Horizontal` and `px.Vertical` on every line
keeps each line's direction as a constraint and solves as it draws, which takes time. Both give the same face. The
times are measured on the machine that built this page.

```python
def comb(kind, n, flags=False):
    pitch, fin, width, base = 2.0, 30.0, 1.2, 5.0
    h, v = ((px.Horizontal,), (px.Vertical,)) if flags else ((), ())
    sk = kind((0, 0), dir=(1, 0))
    for _ in range(n):
        sk.Line(pitch - width, 0, *h).Line(0, fin, *v)
        sk.Line(width, 0, *h).Line(0, -fin, *v)
    sk.Line(0, -base, *v).Line(-n * pitch, 0, *h).Close(*v)
    return sk.Face(), n * pitch * base + n * width * fin


times = {}
runs = (("QuickSketch", px.QuickSketch, False), ("Sketch, flags", px.Sketch, True))
for name, kind, flags in runs:
    start = time.perf_counter()
    face, exact = comb(kind, 50, flags)
    times[name] = time.perf_counter() - start
    print(f"{name}: {times[name]:.4f} s, area {face.mass}, exact {exact}")
```

```text
QuickSketch: 0.0010 s, area 2300.0000000000005, exact 2300.0
Sketch, flags: 0.0576 s, area 2300.0000000000005, exact 2300.0
```

```python
Row((comb(px.QuickSketch, 50)[0], "A heat sink comb with 50 fins, 200 lines"))
Times(times, title="Drawing the comb and its face")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

Points from a file or a computation need no sketch at all: `px.FromPolyline(points, closed=True)` creates the wire
directly. The example builds an outline of 20,000 measured points in three ways, with the times again measured on the
build machine:

```python
a = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 20000, endpoint=False)
rho = 10 * (1 + 0.05 * np.sin(20 * a))
points = np.column_stack([rho * np.cos(a), rho * np.sin(a)])


def by_sketch(kind):
    sk = kind(points[0])
    for p in points[1:]:
        sk.Line(p)
    return sk.Close().Face()


ways = {"QuickSketch": lambda: by_sketch(px.QuickSketch),
        "Sketch": lambda: by_sketch(px.Sketch),
        "px.FromPolyline": lambda: px.Face([px.FromPolyline(points, closed=True)])}
for name, way in ways.items():
    start = time.perf_counter()
    face = way()
    print(f"{name}: {time.perf_counter() - start:.3f} s, area {face.mass}")
```

```text
QuickSketch: 0.235 s, area 314.55195151496093
```

```text
Sketch: 0.240 s, area 314.55195151496093
px.FromPolyline: 0.167 s, area 314.55195151496093
```

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/sketch/lines-and-arcs.md

# Lines and arcs

A sketch has a pen with a position and a direction. Every line and arc starts at the pen and leaves the pen at its
end, pointing along the end of what it drew, so the next element continues from there. A line is given in one of
three ways:

- `Line(l)` draws a length l along the pen's direction;
- `Line(dh, dv)` draws by an offset from the pen;
- `Line((h, v))` draws to a point.

`Turn(angle)` turns the pen by an angle in degrees, counterclockwise for a positive angle. An arc either continues the
pen's direction, as in `Arc(r, sweep)`, or runs to a point and leaves the pen along a given direction, as in
`Arc(to, tangent=(dh, dv))`. `Close()` joins the outline to its start. The four parts below show these forms, each
checked against its area formula.

```python
import math
import planex as px
```

## By length, offset and point

The example is a plate of 40 × 25 with one corner chamfered by 5 (Figure 1). It starts with a length along the pen's
direction, continues with two offsets, up and then diagonally across the chamfer, and goes to a point. `Close` draws
the last side. The corners are marked.

```python
plate = px.QuickSketch().Line(40).Line(0, 20).Line(-5, 5).Line((0, 25)).Close().Face()
```

```python
Row((plate, "A chamfered plate", {"marks": Vertices(plate)}))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

```python
print("plate", plate.mass, "exact", 40 * 25 - 5**2 / 2)
```

```text
plate 987.5 exact 987.5
```

## With Turn

The example is an M10 hex nut, 16 across flats, with a tapped hole of 8.5 (Figure 2). Its side is 16/√3 long. Five
sides are drawn by length and a turn of 60°, and `Close` draws the sixth. `Hexagon(16)` draws the same nut in one call
(see [Slots, keyholes and polygons](slots-polygons.md)). Here it is drawn side by side to show the pen.

```python
side = 16 / math.sqrt(3)
nut = px.QuickSketch((-side / 2, -8))
for _ in range(5):
    nut.Line(side).Turn(60)
nut.Close().Circle(0, 0, 4.25)
hexagon = nut.Face()
```

```python
Row((hexagon, "A hex nut"))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

```python
print("nut", hexagon.mass, "exact", math.sqrt(3) / 2 * 16**2 - math.pi * 8.5**2 / 4)
```

```text
nut 164.9574860633507 exact 164.95748606335064
```

## Arcs that continue the pen

`Arc(r, sweep)` continues the pen's direction on a circle of radius r and turns left for a positive sweep. The
example is a slot of 30 × 10: a line of 30, a half turn on a radius of 5, the line back and the second half turn
(Figure 3). `Slot(30, 10)` draws it in one call.

```python
slot = px.QuickSketch((-15, -5)).Line(30).Arc(5, 180).Line(30).Arc(5, 180).Face()
```

```python
Row((slot, "A slot"))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

```python
print("slot", slot.mass, "exact", 30 * 10 + math.pi * 5**2)
```

```text
slot 378.53981633974485 exact 378.53981633974485
```

## Arcs to a point

`Arc(to, tangent=(dh, dv))` runs to a point, starting along the given direction. The example is an arched window,
12 wide and 10 high to the start of its arch (Figure 4). The arch starts straight up from the right side, which makes
it a half circle over the width.

```python
window = px.QuickSketch().Line(12).Line(0, 10).Arc((0, 10), tangent=(0, 1)).Close().Face()
```

```python
Row((window, "An arched window"))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

```python

```


See [To, from and until](until-from-to.md) for lines that end on other edges, and
[Arcs from references](arc-references.md) for arcs on other circles or touching other edges.

# Circles and rectangles

A circle is drawn around the pen or a given center, or placed by references to other elements. It is one exact edge,
a real circle with no vertices on it, so nothing splits it until another edge crosses or touches it. A rectangle is
drawn from the pen along its direction, from two corners, or around a center.

```python
import math
import planex as px
```

## A square flange with a keyed bore

The example is a plate of 60 × 60 with four bolt holes of 6.6 on a 44 square and a bore of 20 with a DIN 6885 hub
keyway, 6 wide and 2.8 deep (Figure 1). The plate and its bolt holes are one sketch: `RectangleC(60, 60)` centers the
plate on the origin, and a loop draws the holes. The keyed bore is a second face, the bore united with the keyway,
and it is subtracted from the plate. The keyway is a rectangle 6 wide from the pen at (−3, 0), up to 2.8 beyond the
bore.

```python
plate = px.QuickSketch().RectangleC(60, 60)
for x in (-22, 22):
    for y in (-22, 22):
        plate.Circle(x, y, 3.3)

keyed_bore = px.Circle((0, 0), 10).Face() + px.QuickSketch((-3, 0)).Rectangle(6, 12.8).Face()
flange = plate.Face() - keyed_bore
```

```python
Row((flange, "A square flange with a keyed bore"))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The keyway overlaps the bore in a circular segment, so the area of the cut-out is the bore plus the keyway minus that
segment:

```python
overlap = 3 * math.sqrt(10**2 - 3**2) + 10**2 * math.asin(6 / 20)
print("area", flange.mass, "exact", 60**2 - (math.pi * 10**2 + 6 * 12.8 - overlap) - math.pi * 6.6**2)
```

```text
area 3131.280400094698 exact 3131.2804000946976
```

## Circles from references

A circle needs a center and a radius, and both can come from references:

- the center from `center=` (a point or a point id) or from `concentric=` (the center of another circle or arc);
- the radius as a number, from `congruent=` (the radius of another circle), from `through=` (a point on the circle)
  or from `tangent=` (an edge the circle touches).

### A measuring pin in a V-block

The example is a 90° V-block, 60 wide and 40 high, with a groove 30 wide, so its apex lies 15 below the top. A
measuring pin of radius 8 lies in the groove and touches both flanks. `Circle(8, tangent=("left flank", "right
flank"))` finds its center, and the pin is drawn dashed, as a construction circle (Figure 2). The pin's center lies
r / sin 45° above the apex, and the height over the pin is how such a groove is inspected.

```python
v = px.QuickSketch((-30, 0))
v.Line((30, 0), id="base").Line((30, 40), id="right side")
v.Line((15, 40), id="right top").Line((0, 25), id="right flank")
v.Line((-15, 40), id="left flank").Line((-30, 40), id="left top")
v.Close(id="left side")
v.Circle(8, tangent=("left flank", "right flank"), id="pin", construction=True)
m = v.Measure("pin")
```

```python
Row((v, "The V-block and the pin", {"marks": [m["center"][:2]]}))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

```python
center = 25 + 8 / math.sin(math.radians(45))
print("pin center", m["center"][1], "exact", center)
print("over the pin", m["center"][1] + m["radius"], "exact", center + 8)
```

```text
pin center 36.31370849898476 exact 36.31370849898476
over the pin 44.31370849898476 exact 44.31370849898476
```

### Holes placed by references

The example is a bracket leg of 100 × 50 with two bolt holes of 9 at the points A and B, 25 from the ends (Figure 3).
Hole A gets its radius as a number, and hole B is congruent to it, so both change together. Around hole B, three
construction elements check the design: a washer circle concentric with the hole, the circle around B that touches
the right side, whose radius is the edge distance, and a nut pocket, a square of 13 centered on A.

```python
s = px.QuickSketch()
s.Line(100, id="bottom").Turn(90).Line(50, id="right")
s.Turn(90).Line(100, id="top").Close(id="left")
s.Vertex("A", (25, 25)).Vertex("B", (75, 25))
s.Circle(4.5, center="A", id="hole A")
s.Circle(center="B", congruent="hole A", id="hole B")
s.Circle(9, concentric="hole B", id="washer B", construction=True)
s.Circle(center="B", tangent="right", id="edge distance", construction=True)
s.RectangleC(s("A"), 13, 13, id="nut pocket", construction=True)
leg = s.Face()
```

```python
Row((s, "A bracket leg: holes placed by references, the construction dashed"))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The edge distance comes out as 25, the distance from B to the right side:

```python
for ref in ("hole B", "washer B", "edge distance"):
    m = s.Measure(ref)
    print(ref, "center", m["center"][:2], "radius", m["radius"])
print("area", leg.mass, "exact", 100 * 50 - 2 * math.pi * 4.5**2)
```

```text
hole B center (75.0, 25.0) radius 4.5
washer B center (75.0, 25.0) radius 9.0
edge distance center (75.0, 25.0) radius 25.0
area 4872.765497529614 exact 4872.765497529614
```

## Rectangles from corners and around a center

A rectangle has four forms:

- `Rectangle(l, w)` starts at the pen and runs along its direction;
- `Rectangle(p0, p1)` takes two opposite corners in any order, with its sides along h and v;
- `Rectangle(p0, p1, p2)` takes the side from p0 to p1 and a point p2 on the opposite side, so it may be turned;
- `RectangleC(l, w)` is centered at the pen, and `RectangleC(center, l, w)` at a point, with l along the drawing
  direction.

The pen stays where it is for the corner forms and moves to the center for `RectangleC`. The example is a lid of
60 × 40 with a window from two corners, a label recess of 20 × 8 around a point, and a tilted slot for a key, given by
one side and a point on the opposite side (Figure 4).

```python
lid = px.QuickSketch().Rectangle(60, 40, id="lid")
lid.Rectangle((8, 8), (30, 32), id="window")
lid.RectangleC((45, 30), 20, 8, id="label")
lid.Rectangle((38, 6), (52, 14), (50, 16), id="key")
cover = lid.Face()
```

```python
Row((lid, "A lid with a window, a label recess and a tilted key slot"),
    caption="Rectangles from two corners, around a center and from a side and a point")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The tilted slot's width is the distance of p2 from the line through p0 and p1:

```python
side = math.dist((38, 6), (52, 14))
width = abs((52 - 38) * (16 - 6) - (14 - 6) * (50 - 38)) / side
print("key slot", side, "×", width)
print("area", cover.mass, "exact", 60 * 40 - 22 * 24 - 20 * 8 - side * width)
```

```text
key slot 16.1245154965971 × 2.7287641609625863
area 1668.0 exact 1668.0
```

---

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/sketch/slots-polygons.md

# Slots, keyholes and polygons

Some outlines come up in almost every part: a slot for an adjustable screw, an arc slot for an angle adjustment, a
keyhole for hanging a part on a screw head, and a hexagon for a nut. Each of them is one call in a sketch:

| Call | Draws |
|---|---|
| `Slot(l, w)` | A straight slot of width w along a spine of length l, with round ends |
| `ArcSlot(r, sweep, w)` | A slot of width w along an arc of radius r and the angle sweep, in degrees |
| `Keyhole(l, w, r)` | A slot of width w that starts in a round hole of radius r |
| `Polygon(r, n)` | A regular polygon with n corners on a circle of radius r |
| `Hexagon(af)` | A regular hexagon with the width across flats af, as for a nut |

The spine of a slot or a keyhole is placed like a line, so `Slot` takes every form of `Line` and `ArcSlot` every form
of `Arc`, with the width as the last number. `Polygon` and `Hexagon` are placed like a circle. The spine and the
polygon's circle are construction elements.

```python
import math
import planex as px
```

## A motor mounting plate

The example is a mounting plate of 120 × 80 for a small motor, with every one of these shapes (Figure 1):

- a pivot hole of 8.5 at (30, 40), about which the motor turns;
- an arc slot 6.6 wide around the pivot, on a radius of 40, from −30° to 30°, for the screw that holds the motor;
- two slots 6.6 wide and 20 long for the screws of a belt tensioner;
- a keyhole, so that the plate can hang on a screw head;
- a hexagonal opening that holds an M6 nut, 10 across flats.

The spine of each straight slot and of the keyhole starts at the pen and runs along the direction given to `Move`.
The arc slot uses the keyword form of `Arc`: its start point, the width, and the center and sweep of its spine. The
hexagon takes its center as the first two numbers, like a circle.

```python
sk = px.QuickSketch().Rectangle(120, 80, id="plate")
sk.Circle(30, 40, 4.25, id="pivot")
a = math.radians(-30)
sk.ArcSlot((30 + 40 * math.cos(a), 40 + 40 * math.sin(a)), 6.6, center=(30, 40), sweep=60, id="tilt")
for k, y in enumerate((12, 68)):
    sk.Move((80, y), dir=(1, 0)).Slot(20, 6.6, id=f"tension {k + 1}")
sk.Move((100, 32), dir=(0, 1)).Keyhole(10, 5, 5, id="hanger")
sk.Hexagon(12, 68, 10, id="nut")
plate = sk.Face()
```

```python
Row((sk, "A motor mounting plate, the spines dashed"), caption="Slots, a keyhole and a hexagon in one sketch")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

Each opening has a closed form for its area. A slot is a rectangle with two half discs, and an arc slot the band
along its arc with two half discs. A keyhole is the hole and the slot with its end cap, less the strip of the slot
inside the hole. A hexagon with the width across flats af has the area √3/2 af².

```python
def slot(length, width):
    return length * width + math.pi * (width / 2) ** 2


def keyhole(length, width, radius):
    inside = width / 2 * math.sqrt(radius**2 - width**2 / 4) + radius**2 * math.asin(width / (2 * radius))
    return math.pi * radius**2 + length * width + math.pi * (width / 2) ** 2 / 2 - inside


openings = math.pi * 4.25**2 + slot(math.radians(60) * 40, 6.6) + 2 * slot(20, 6.6)
openings += keyhole(10, 5, 5) + math.sqrt(3) / 2 * 10**2
print("area", plate.mass, "exact", 120 * 80 - openings)
```

```text
area 8699.114450362462 exact 8699.11445036246
```

## The parts of a shape

Every opening is a wire of its own, `tilt`, `tension 1` and so on, and its parts have ids of their own: the sides
`left` and `right`, the caps `startcap` and `endcap`, and for a keyhole the `hole`. The spine is the construction line
`spine`. The parts can be measured, selected and referred to like any other element:

```python
for part in ("left", "right", "startcap", "endcap", "spine"):
    print("tension 1." + part, "length", sk.Measure("tension 1." + part)["length"])
```

```text
tension 1.left length 20.0
tension 1.right length 20.0
tension 1.startcap length 10.367255756846319
tension 1.endcap length 10.367255756846319
tension 1.spine length 20.0
```

In a constraint sketch, the width of a slot, the radius of a keyhole's hole and the size of a polygon are dimensions
that can change later. See [Offsets and profiles revisited](../constraints/offsets-profiles.md) for details. See
[Circles and rectangles](circles-and-rectangles.md) for rectangles from corners and around a center, and
[Fillets and chamfers](fillets-chamfers.md) for rounding the corners of a part.

---

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/sketch/splines.md

# Splines

In a sketch, `Spline(points)` runs from the pen through the given points, and lines and arcs join it like any other
edge. `periodic=True` closes it smoothly, and `tangents=` sets its direction at chosen points. A spline through points
interpolates the curve the points come from, so it is close to that curve but not exactly on it. The checks below show
how close. See [Splines](../basics/splines.md) for how planex2d handles splines in general, including the two
interpolation styles, closed splines and points.

```python
import math
import numpy as np
import planex as px
```

## A NACA 0012 airfoil

The airfoil has a chord of 100 and a thickness of 12 %, in the form with a closed trailing edge, with 40 points per
side and cosine spacing. The angle θ runs once around the profile, from the trailing edge over the upper side to the
leading edge and back along the lower side, so the spline starts and ends at the trailing edge. `px.FromNACA("0012")`
creates the same profile in one call. Here it is drawn point by point to show `Spline` in a sketch.

A construction line at 75 % chord runs from the lower to the upper surface. It is the hinge line of a flap and is as
long as the profile is thick there (Figure 1). Its ends are given as `(target, point)`, which selects the
intersection with the profile nearest to the point.

```python
def thickness(x):
    return 60 * (0.2969 * np.sqrt(x) - 0.1260 * x - 0.3516 * x**2 + 0.2843 * x**3 - 0.1036 * x**4)


theta = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 81)[1:]
x = (1 + np.cos(theta)) / 2
points = np.column_stack([100 * x, np.sign(np.sin(theta)) * thickness(x)])

wing = px.QuickSketch((100, 0)).Spline(points, id="profile")
wing.Move((75, -100), dir=(0, 1))
wing.Line(("profile", (75, -100)), parallel=px.V, until=("profile", (75, 100)), id="hinge", construction=True)
profile = wing.Face()
```

```python
Row((wing, "NACA 0012 from one spline, the hinge line at 75 % chord dashed"))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The area is checked against the integral of the thickness formula, and the hinge line against the thickness:

```python
exact = 12000 * (0.2969 * 2 / 3 - 0.1260 / 2 - 0.3516 / 3 + 0.2843 / 4 - 0.1036 / 5)
print("area", profile.mass, "exact", exact, "relative", (profile.mass - exact) / exact)
print("hinge", wing.Edge("hinge").mass, "thickness", 2 * thickness(0.75))
```

```text
area 817.0611516356596 exact 817.0599999999997 relative 1.4094872590512479e-06
hinge 6.240877677195613 thickness 6.240878086031979
```

## A closed cam

The cam is a periodic spline through the lift curve r = R + h (1 − cos a) / 2 with R = 20 and h = 8 at 36 points,
with a bore of 10 (Figure 2). The area of the exact lift curve is π (R + h/2)² + π h²/8, and the spline matches it
within the interpolation error:

```python
a = np.radians(np.arange(0, 360, 10))
r = 20 + 8 * (1 - np.cos(a)) / 2
lift = px.Spline(np.column_stack([r * np.cos(a), r * np.sin(a)]), periodic=True)
cam = px.Face([lift, px.Circle((0, 0), 5)])
```

```python
Row((cam, "A cam: one periodic spline through 36 points, and the bore"))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

```python
exact = math.pi * 24**2 + math.pi * 8**2 / 8 - math.pi * 10**2 / 4
print("area", cam.mass, "exact", exact, "relative", (cam.mass - exact) / exact)
```

```text
area 1756.1465567096234 exact 1756.1502933566942 relative -2.127749022930798e-06
```

# Several loops

`Move` lifts the pen, so one sketch can hold many loops. `Face()` takes all drawn edges together and decides what is
material by nesting: a loop inside another loop is a hole, and a loop inside a hole is material again. The same rule
applies where separately drawn loops overlap: a region inside two loops counts as a hole. Parts that overlap and
should become one region are therefore drawn as separate faces and united.

```python
import math
import planex as px
```

## A pipe flange gasket

The example is a gasket with an outer diameter of 150, an inner diameter of 90 and eight holes of 14 on a bolt circle
of 120 (Figure 1). The first hole is drawn at 22.5°, and `CircularPattern` repeats it eight times around the origin.
These are ten circles in one sketch, and the nesting makes nine of them holes.

```python
s = px.QuickSketch().Circle(75).Circle(45)
a = math.radians(22.5)
s.Circle(60 * math.cos(a), 60 * math.sin(a), 7, id="hole")
s.CircularPattern("hole", "origin", 8)
gasket = s.Face()
```

```python
Row((gasket, "A pipe flange gasket: ten circles, one face"))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

```python
print("area", gasket.mass, "exact", math.pi / 4 * (150**2 - 90**2 - 8 * 14**2))
```

```text
area 10078.229232716058 exact 10078.229232716056
```

## A dog bone

The example is a dog bone: two discs of radius 10, 40 apart, and a bar 8 wide between their centers (Figure 2a).
Drawn into one sketch, the parts of the bar inside the discs lie inside two loops and become holes. The outline then
falls apart into three regions, so `Face()` raises an error, and `Shape()` keeps all three (Figure 2b). As separate
faces, `px.Unify` joins the three parts into one dog bone (Figure 2c).

```python
one_sketch = px.QuickSketch().Circle(10).Circle(40, 0, 10).Move((0, -4)).Rectangle(40, 8)
try:
    one_sketch.Face()
except ValueError as err:
    print(err)

discs = [px.Circle((0, 0), 10).Face(), px.Circle((40, 0), 10).Face()]
bar = px.QuickSketch((0, -4)).Rectangle(40, 8).Face()
bone = px.Unify([*discs, bar])
```

```text
Face(): the edges bound 3 regions; Shape() keeps them all
```

```python
Row((px.Compound([*discs, bar]), "Two discs and a bar"), (one_sketch.Shape(), "In one sketch: the overlaps are holes"),
    (bone, "United"), caption="A dog bone from overlapping parts")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The united area is the two discs and the bar, less the two pieces of the bar inside the discs:

```python
inside = 4 * math.sqrt(10**2 - 4**2) + 10**2 * math.asin(8 / 20)
print("area", bone.mass, "exact", 2 * math.pi * 10**2 + 40 * 8 - 2 * inside)
```

```text
area 792.6939503851675 exact 792.6939503851676
```

See [Faces, shapes and compounds](../basics/faces-shapes-compounds.md) for faces of several regions, and
[Boolean operations](../booleans/index.md) for unions and differences.

# To, from and until

A line often has to end where it meets another edge. Instead of computing that intersection, you give the edge as the
line's end, and planex2d finds the point. The end can be a named target, as in `Line("web", angle=...)`, or the first
or last edge ahead of the pen, with `until=px.first` or `until=px.last`.

```python
import math
import planex as px
```

## To an edge

The example is a gusset plate welded between a flange and a web. It runs 60 along the flange, its free edge rises at
35° until it meets the web, and its inner corner is sniped by 8 to clear the weld (Figure 1). The web is a
construction line. `Line("web", angle=180 - 35)` draws the free edge: the angle sets its direction, and the web sets
its end.

```python
s = px.QuickSketch()
s.Move((0, -5)).Line((0, 60), id="web", construction=True)
s.Move((8, 0), dir=(1, 0)).Line(52, id="flange side")
s.Line("web", angle=180 - 35, id="free edge")
s.Line((0, 8), id="web side").Close(id="snipe")
gusset = s.Face()
```

```python
Row((s, "The sketch, the web dashed", {"fill": False}), (gusset, "The gusset plate"),
    caption="A gusset plate whose free edge ends on the web")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The area is the triangle between the flange and the free edge, less the snipe:

```python
print("area", gusset.mass, "exact", 60**2 * math.tan(math.radians(35)) / 2 - 8**2 / 2)
```

```text
area 1228.3735687774779 exact 1228.3735687774774
```

## From one edge to another

With two targets, a line runs from the first to the second, and a helper such as `parallel=` sets the line it runs
on. The example is a rib between a hub and a wall, parallel to the pen's direction (Figure 2a).

```python
rib = px.QuickSketch().Circle(0, 0, 1, id="hub")
rib.Move((4, -2)).Line((4, 2), id="wall")
rib.Move((0, 0.3), dir=(1, 0))
rib.Line("hub", "wall", parallel=rib.pen, id="rib");
```

## Until the first or last edge

`until=px.first` stops a line at the first edge it meets ahead of the pen, and `until=px.last` at the last one,
construction edges included. The example is the link from [Tangents](tangent.md), with rays every 15° from a point
inside it, each ending on the first edge it meets (Figure 2b).

```python
link = px.QuickSketch()
link.Circle(0, 0, 1.5, id="boss1", construction=True)
link.Circle(6, 0, 1.0, id="boss2", construction=True)
link.Line(tangent=("boss1", "boss2"), id="upper")
link.Line(tangent=("boss1", "boss2"), reverse=True, id="lower")
link.Arc("lower", "upper", congruent="boss2", id="end2")
link.Arc("upper", "lower", congruent="boss1", id="end1")
link.Circle(0, 0, 0.6, id="hole1").Circle(6, 0, 0.4, id="hole2")
rays = link.Copy()
for angle in range(0, 360, 15):
    rays.Move((3, 0.3)).Line(angle=angle, until=px.first, col=(0.85, 0.35, 0))
```

```python
Row((rib, "A rib from the hub to the wall", {"fill": False}),
    (rays, "Rays until the first edge", {"colors": True, "fill": False}),
    caption="Lines between two targets, and until the first edge")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The difference between the two shows on a line that crosses a circle twice. A line along x from the origin meets a
construction circle of radius 1 around (3, 0) at x = 2 and at x = 4, and the pen ends at the first or the second
point:

```python
s = px.QuickSketch().Circle(3, 0, 1, construction=True).Move((0, 0), dir=(1, 0))
print("until=px.first:", s.Copy().Line(until=px.first).pen.position)
print("until=px.last:", s.Copy().Line(until=px.last).pen.position)
```

```text
until=px.first: (2.0, 0.0)
until=px.last: (4.0, 0.0)
```

## To other objects

A target does not have to be part of the sketch. Faces, wires and single edges work as well. The example draws a line
from (−3, 0.5) along x until it meets a plate of 4 × 2 centered on the origin, at (−2, 0.5):

```python
plate = px.QuickSketch().RectangleC(4, 2).Face()
end = px.QuickSketch((-3, 0.5), dir=(1, 0)).Line(until=plate).pen.position
print("the line ends at", end)
```

```text
the line ends at (-2.0, 0.5)
```

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/sketch/parallel-perpendicular-angle.md

# Parallel, perpendicular, angle

A line can take its direction from another edge instead of from the pen. `parallel=` runs it parallel to the edge,
and with `distance=` it becomes a parallel copy at that distance. `perpendicular=` runs it at a right angle to the
edge, and `angle=(a, edge)` at the angle a to it. Together with an end on a target, this draws most machined profiles
without a single computed point.

```python
import math
import planex as px
```

## A dovetail slide

The example is a slide, a block of 60 × 30 with a dovetail groove that is 24 wide at the surface and 10 deep, with
flanks at 60° (Figure 1). The block is drawn in two steps.

First the construction lines. The bottom is the reference. The top and the floor of the groove are parallel copies of
it, 30 and 20 above. The line of the left flank runs at 60° to the bottom through the groove's left corner at the
surface, (−12, 30).

```python
s = px.QuickSketch((-30, 0))
s.Line(60, id="bottom")
s.Line(-60, parallel="bottom", distance=30, id="top", construction=True)
s.Line(-60, parallel="bottom", distance=20, id="floor", construction=True)
s.Line(20, angle=(180 + 60, "bottom"), through=(-12, 30), id="left flank line", construction=True);
```

Then the outline, counterclockwise from the end of the bottom. The right flank runs down at 60° until it meets the
floor, the groove floor runs back until it meets the left flank's line, and the left flank runs up on that line until
it meets the top.

```python
s.Turn(90).Line(30, id="right side")
s.Turn(90).Line(18, id="right shoulder")
s.Line("floor", angle=(-60, "bottom"), id="right flank")
s.Line("left flank line", parallel="bottom", id="groove floor")
s.Line("top", congruent="left flank line", id="left flank")
s.Line((-30, 30), id="left shoulder").Close(id="left side")
slide = s.Face()
```

```python
Row((s, "The sketch, its construction lines dashed", {"fill": False}), (slide, "The slide"),
    caption="A dovetail slide from parallel copies and angles")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The area is the block minus the groove, a trapezoid 24 wide at the top and 10 deep:

```python
print("area", slide.mass, "exact", 60 * 30 - 10 * (24 + 10 / math.tan(math.radians(60))))
```

```text
area 1502.2649730810376 exact 1502.2649730810374
```

## A bracket with a constant wall

The example is a triangular bracket, 10 long, with a wall 0.8 thick all around (Figure 2). Its outer contour is a
ramp at 35° from the corner to the wall, the wall down to the ground, and the ground back. The ground and the wall are
construction lines.

```python
t = 0.8
b = px.QuickSketch()
b.Move((-1, 0)).Line((12, 0), id="ground", construction=True)
b.Move((10, -1)).Line((10, 8), id="wall", construction=True)

b.Move((0, 0)).Line("wall", angle=35, id="ramp")
b.Line("ground", congruent="wall", id="back")
b.Close(id="base");
```

The inner contour is made of parallel copies of the three sides, each at the distance t inward, so the wall
thickness is a single number. Two more lines join the copies where they meet. Last, the axis of a drain hole runs
perpendicular to the ramp, from its midpoint down to the ground.

```python
b.Move((0, 0), dir=(1, 0)).Line(14, parallel="ramp", distance=-t, id="ramp in", construction=True)
b.Move((0, 0), dir=(1, 0)).Line(12, parallel="ground", distance=t, id="ground in", construction=True)
b.Move((0, 0), dir=(0, 1)).Line(9, parallel="wall", distance=t, id="wall in", construction=True)
b.Line("ground in", "wall in", congruent="ramp in")
b.Line("ground in", congruent="wall in")
b.Close()

b.Move("ramp.mid")
b.Line("ground", perpendicular="ramp", id="drain", construction=True)
bracket = b.Face()
```

```python
Row((b, "The sketch: offsets and the drain axis", {"fill": False}), (bracket, "The bracket"),
    caption="A bracket whose inner contour is three parallel copies")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The inner triangle is the outer one shrunk toward the center of its incircle, so the area follows from the inradius.
The drain axis, from the ramp's midpoint to the ground, is a/2 · tan β / cos β long, with a = 10 and β = 35°:

```python
beta = math.radians(35)
height = 10 * math.tan(beta)
outer = 10 * height / 2
inradius = outer / ((10 + height + math.hypot(10, height)) / 2)
print("area", bracket.mass, "exact", outer * (1 - ((inradius - t) / inradius) ** 2))
print("drain", b.Edge("drain").mass, "exact", 5 * math.tan(beta) / math.cos(beta))
```

```text
area 19.468607780995338 exact 19.46860778099532
drain 4.273977847528156 exact 4.273977847528149
```

For a wall of constant thickness around a closed outline, `Offset` does the same in one call. See
[Offsets](offsets.md) for details.

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/sketch/tangent.md

# Tangents

A line or an arc can be given what it touches instead of where it ends. `tangent=` names the circle, arc or spline,
and planex2d computes the touch point, so no point of a tangent has to be worked out by hand. With two targets, as in
`tangent=("a", "b")`, a line touches both.

```python
import math
import planex as px
```

## A link from two bosses

The example is a link, a flat lever with a boss of radius 1.5 at one end and a boss of radius 1 at the other, 6
apart (Figure 1). The bosses are drawn as construction circles. Two lines are tangent to both, the upper one and, with
`reverse=True`, the lower one. The ends of the link are arcs on the bosses' circles, from one line to the other, and
each boss has a hole. `Face()` then makes the face of the link from the drawn edges (b).

```python
link = px.QuickSketch()
link.Circle(0, 0, 1.5, id="boss1", construction=True)
link.Circle(6, 0, 1.0, id="boss2", construction=True)
link.Line(tangent=("boss1", "boss2"), id="upper")
link.Line(tangent=("boss1", "boss2"), reverse=True, id="lower")
link.Arc("lower", "upper", congruent="boss2", id="end2")
link.Arc("upper", "lower", congruent="boss1", id="end1")
link.Circle(0, 0, 0.6, id="hole1").Circle(6, 0, 0.4, id="hole2")
face = link.Face()
```

```python
Row((link, "The sketch", {"fill": False}), (face, "The face"), caption="A link from two bosses and two tangents")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The area of the link is the area of the belt around two circles, which has a closed form, minus the two holes:

```python
r1, r2, d = 1.5, 1.0, 6.0
alpha = math.asin((r1 - r2) / d)
belt = (r1 + r2) * math.sqrt(d * d - (r1 - r2) ** 2) + r1**2 * (math.pi / 2 + alpha) + r2**2 * (math.pi / 2 - alpha)
print("area", face.mass, "exact", belt - math.pi * (0.6**2 + 0.4**2))
```

```text
area 18.523573419356737 exact 18.523573419356737
```

## From a point, along a circle, to a spline

A tangent can start at a point, leave a circle, or touch a spline (Figure 2).

- From a point, `tangent="circle"` draws one of the two tangents to the circle, and `reverse=True` the other (a).
- From a point on a circle, `Line(3, tangent="c")` leaves the circle along its tangent there, 3 long (b).
- From a point outside a spline, `tangent="curve"` touches the spline (c).

Where a line could touch a target at several points, a point given with the target, as in `tangent=("curve", p)`,
selects the touch point nearest to p.

```python
point = px.QuickSketch().Circle(5, 0, 1.5, id="circle", construction=True)
point.Move((0, 0)).Line(tangent="circle")
point.Move((0, 0)).Line(tangent="circle", reverse=True)

leaving = px.QuickSketch().Circle(0, 0, 1, id="c")
leaving.Move((0, 1)).Line(3, tangent="c")

spline = px.QuickSketch((0, 2)).Spline([(1, 1), (2, 0.8), (3, 1.2), (4, 2)], id="curve")
spline.Move((2, -1)).Line(tangent="curve");
```

```python
Row((point, "From a point", {"fill": False}), (leaving, "Leaving a circle", {"fill": False}),
    (spline, "Touching a spline", {"fill": False}), caption="Tangents from a point, along a circle and to a spline")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

An arc can be tangent too. See [Arcs from references](arc-references.md) for arcs that touch two edges, and
[Choosing between solutions](choosing.md) for picking one of several tangents.

---

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/sketch/arc-references.md

# Arcs from references

An arc needs a circle and two ends. Each can come from the geometry that is already drawn. The circle can have a
given center (`center=`), share another arc's center (`concentric=`), lie on another arc's circle (`congruent=`), or
touch two edges (`tangent=`). The ends can be targets, so the arc runs from one edge to the next.

```python
import math
import planex as px
```

## An arc touching two edges: a root fillet

The example is an equal angle section of 40 × 40 × 5 with a root radius of 6 (Figure 1). The inner faces of the two
legs are construction lines, and the root is an arc of radius 6 tangent to both. Two lines meet in four corners, so
the point (40, 40) given with each face picks the corner the arc sits in. The outline then runs around the section
and ends on the root.

```python
s = px.QuickSketch()
s.Move((-1, 5)).Line((41, 5), id="leg face", construction=True)
s.Move((5, -1)).Line((5, 41), id="web face", construction=True)

s.Arc(6, tangent=(("leg face", (40, 40)), ("web face", (40, 40))), id="root")
s.Line((5, 40), id="web").Line((0, 40)).Line((0, 0)).Line((40, 0)).Line((40, 5))
s.Line("root", congruent="leg face", id="leg")
angle = s.Face()
```

```python
Row((s, "The sketch, the inner faces dashed", {"fill": False}), (angle, "The angle section"),
    caption="An angle section whose root fillet touches both legs")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The root adds (1 − π/4) r² to the two legs. On a finished corner, `Fillet` does the same in one call (see
[Fillets and chamfers](fillets-chamfers.md)).

```python
print("area", angle.mass, "exact", 2 * 40 * 5 - 5**2 + (1 - math.pi / 4) * 6**2)
```

```text
area 382.72566611769184 exact 382.72566611769184
```

## Arcs between targets: a curved slot

The example is an adjustment plate of 62 × 62 with a pivot hole of radius 5 and a curved slot around the pivot,
8 wide, on a radius of 40, from 20° to 70° (Figure 2). The slot is built from references in three steps.

First, two construction rays from the pivot at 20° and 70° bound the slot, and its center line is a construction
arc of radius 40 from ray to ray. `Arc("ray0", "ray1", 40, center="pivot")` is an arc of radius 40 around the pivot
that runs from where it meets the first ray to where it meets the second.

```python
s = px.QuickSketch().Vertex("pivot", (0, 0))
s.Move("pivot").Line(80, angle=20, id="ray0", construction=True)
s.Move("pivot").Line(80, angle=70, id="ray1", construction=True)
s.Arc("ray0", "ray1", 40, center="pivot", id="centerline", construction=True);
```

Then the outline of the slot: the outer arc of radius 44 from ray to ray, a half circle around the end of the center
line, the inner arc back to the first ray, concentric with the pivot, and a half circle around the start of the center
line. Last come the plate and the pivot hole.

```python
s.Arc("ray0", "ray1", 44, center="pivot", id="outer")
s.Arc(center="centerline.end", sweep=180, id="cap1")
s.Arc("ray0", concentric="pivot", id="inner")
s.Arc(center="centerline.start", sweep=180, id="cap0")

s.Move((-12, -12), dir=(1, 0)).Rectangle(62, 62, id="plate")
s.Circle(0, 0, 5, id="pivot hole")
plate = s.Face()
```

```python
Row((s, "The sketch, rays and center line dashed", {"fill": False}), (plate, "The adjustment plate"),
    caption="An adjustment plate with a curved slot")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The slot's area is the length of its center line times its width, plus the two half circles at its ends:

```python
slot = math.radians(70 - 20) * 40 * 8 + math.pi * 8**2 / 4
print("area", plate.mass, "exact", 62**2 - math.pi * 5**2 - slot)
```

```text
area 3435.9420208837255 exact 3435.9420208837255
```

`ArcSlot` draws the same slot in one call. See [Slots, keyholes and polygons](slots-polygons.md) for details. The
end arcs of the [link](tangent.md) are a third form, arcs on another circle with `Arc(from, to, congruent=...)`, and
[Choosing between solutions](choosing.md) shows the four corners in which an arc touching two lines can sit.

---

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/sketch/choosing.md

# Choosing between solutions

Geometry given by references often has more than one solution. An arc of radius 1 that touches two crossing lines can
sit in any of four corners, and a point outside a circle has two tangents to it. planex2d picks one by a fixed rule,
and two options choose another:

- By default, an arc touching two edges sits in the corner that the two edges face.
- `reverse=True` switches every free choice to the other side.
- A point given with a target, as in `("y", (5, 0))`, fixes the side of that target: the arc lies on the same side as
  the point.

```python
import planex as px
```

## Four corners and two tangents

The example has two construction lines, x and y, that cross at (3, 0), and four arcs of radius 1 that touch both
(Figure 1). The default arc is drawn in black and the one with `reverse=True` in red. The arc with the side of y fixed
by the point (5, 0) is green, and the arc with the side of x fixed by (0, −1) is blue. On the right are the two
tangents from (5, 0) to a circle around (10, 0): the default in black and the one with `reverse=True` in red. Every
element is named after its option, and the list of names shows that all six are drawn.

```python
red, green, blue = (0.8, 0, 0), (0, 0.5, 0), (0, 0, 0.8)
c = px.QuickSketch()
c.Move((-2, 0)).Line((8, 0), id="x", construction=True)
c.Move((3, -3)).Line((3, 3), id="y", construction=True)
c.Arc(1, tangent=("x", "y"), name="default")
c.Arc(1, tangent=("x", "y"), reverse=True, name="reverse=True", col=red)
c.Arc(1, tangent=("x", ("y", (5, 0))), name="y side fixed", col=green)
c.Arc(1, tangent=(("x", (0, -1)), "y"), name="x side fixed", col=blue)

c.Circle(10, 0, 1.5, id="circle", construction=True)
c.Move((5, 0)).Line(tangent="circle", name="tangent")
c.Move((5, 0)).Line(tangent="circle", reverse=True, name="tangent, reverse", col=red)
print(sorted(e.name for w in c.Wires() for e in w.edges))
```

```text
['default', 'reverse=True', 'tangent', 'tangent, reverse', 'x side fixed', 'y side fixed']
```

```python
Row((c, "Four arcs touching x and y, and two tangents to a circle", {"fill": False, "colors": True}))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## The touch point nearest to a point

For a circle, a point given with it selects the touch point nearest to that point. The example draws the tangent from
(4, 0) to the unit circle that touches it near (0, −1) (Figure 2). The exact touch point is (1/4, −√15/4).

```python
s = px.QuickSketch().Circle(0, 0, 1, id="c", construction=True)
s.Move((4, 0)).Line(tangent=("c", (0, -1)))
touch = s.pen.position
print("touch", touch, "exact", (0.25, -(15**0.5) / 4))
```

```text
touch (0.25, -0.9682458365518543) exact (0.25, -0.9682458365518543)
```

```python
Row((s, "The tangent from (4, 0) touching near (0, −1)", {"fill": False, "marks": [touch]}))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

# Construction elements and points

Construction elements and points are the helper geometry of a drawing: center lines, reference circles, the
positions of holes. They place what comes next but never become part of the part, so they never appear in `Wires()`,
faces or exports. Any element becomes construction with `construction=True`, and `Vertex(id, point)` adds a point
with an id. A construction element also leaves the pen where it is, so the outline continues as if it were not
there.

The points of every element can be referred to by id: `"id.start"`, `"id.end"`, `"id.mid"` and, for arcs and
circles, `"id.center"`.

```python
import math
import planex as px
```

## A pillow block from a construction circle

The example is a pillow block with a base of 80 × 12, an axis 45 high, a boss of radius 22 around the axis and a
bore of 25 (Figure 1). The boss is a construction circle around the point `axis`. Its outline is drawn in three
steps.

First the construction: the axis, the boss, and the left flank's tangent from the top of the left foot to the boss.
The point given with the boss, (0, 45), picks the touch point on the left side.

```python
s = px.QuickSketch()
s.Vertex("axis", (40, 45))
s.Circle(40, 45, 22, id="boss", construction=True)
s.Move((0, 12))
s.Line(tangent=("boss", (0, 45)), id="left tangent", construction=True);
```

Then the outline. The pen is still at (0, 12), so the outline runs down the left foot, along the base and up the
right foot, then tangent to the boss on the right. The crown follows the boss until it meets the left tangent, and
`Close` draws the left flank along it. Last, the bore goes around the axis, and a construction line from the middle of
the base up to the crown measures the overall height.

```python
s.Line((0, 0), id="left foot").Line((80, 0), id="base")
s.Line((80, 12), id="right foot")
s.Line(tangent=("boss", (80, 45)), id="right flank")
s.Arc("left tangent", congruent="boss", id="crown")
s.Close(id="left flank")
s.Move("axis").Circle(12.5, id="bore")
s.Move("base.mid", dir=(0, 1))
s.Line(until="crown", id="height", construction=True)
block = s.Face()
```

```python
Row((s, "The sketch, the boss and the height line dashed", {"fill": False}), (block, "The pillow block"),
    caption="A pillow block from a construction circle")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The flanks touch the boss, so their distance from the axis is the boss radius of 22. The center of the crown is the
axis, and the height line is 45 + 22 long:

```python
for ref in ("left flank", "right flank"):
    print(ref, "distance from the axis", s.Edge(ref).Distance((40, 45)))
print("crown center", s.Location("crown.center"), "axis", s.points["axis"])
print("height", s.Edge("height").mass, "exact", 45 + 22)
```

```text
left flank distance from the axis 22.0
right flank distance from the axis 22.0
crown center (40.0, 45.0) axis (40.0, 45.0)
height 67.0 exact 67
```

## A bolt circle from points

The example is a round flange with an outer diameter of 100, a bore of 40 and six holes of 9 on a bolt circle of 75
(Figure 2). The hole positions are construction points with the ids `bolt0` to `bolt5` (a). `sk.points` lists every
point of the sketch, and a loop draws a hole around each (b).

```python
f = px.QuickSketch().Circle(50).Circle(20)
for k in range(6):
    a = math.radians(60 * k)
    f.Vertex(f"bolt{k}", (37.5 * math.cos(a), 37.5 * math.sin(a)))
points = f.Copy()
for ref in f.points:
    f.Move(ref).Circle(4.5)
flange = f.Face()
```

```python
Row((points, "The points bolt0 to bolt5", {"fill": False}), (flange, "The flange"),
    caption="A bolt circle from points with ids")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

```python
print("area", flange.mass, "exact", math.pi / 4 * (100**2 - 40**2 - 6 * 9**2))
```

```text
area 6215.641065127406 exact 6215.641065127405
```

The same bolt circle can also be drawn as one hole and a `CircularPattern` of it. See
[Several loops](several-loops.md) for an example.

# Automatic ids

Every element drawn in a sketch gets an id made of its kind and a number, such as `Line.1`, `Arc.2`, `Circle.1` or
`Spline.1`, as in CAD sketchers. Every point gets an id like `Point.3`, and every chain drawn in one go an id like
`Chain.1`. `id=` gives an element an id of your own instead.

Ids are the references within the sketch, and they never leave it. Faces, wires and exports carry only the names given
with `name=`, which travel with the geometry through Boolean operations and into the mesh.

```python
import math
import planex as px
```

## An L bracket drawn quickly

The example is an L bracket with legs 40 and 30 long and 10 thick, drawn without a single `id=` (Figure 1). Its six
sides are therefore `Line.1` to `Line.6` in drawing order, and its corners `Point.1` to `Point.6`, from the start at
the origin. The re-entrant corner is `Point.4`.

```python
s = px.QuickSketch().Line(40).Turn(90).Line(10).Turn(90).Line(30)
s.Turn(-90).Line(20).Turn(90).Line(10).Close()
corner = s.Location("Point.4")
print("Point.1", s.Location("Point.1"), "Point.4", corner)
```

```text
Point.1 (0.0, 0.0) Point.4 (10.0, 10.0)
```

```python
sides = [(f"Line.{k}", s.Location(f"Line.{k}.mid")) for k in range(1, 7)]
Row((s, "An L bracket labeled with its automatic ids", {"labels": sides + [("Point.4", corner)], "marks": [corner]}))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## Referring to them

Later calls refer to the automatic ids like to any other (Figure 2):

- a bolt hole of 5 lies opposite the middle of `Line.2`, the end of the long leg, 8 in from it, and gets the name
  `bolt` for the export;
- the washer around it is a construction circle, concentric with `Circle.1`, the automatic id of the hole;
- a construction line from the re-entrant corner `Point.4` to the outer corner `Point.1` marks where a gusset would
  go.

```python
end = s.Location("Line.2.mid")
s.Circle(2.5, center=(end[0] - 8, end[1]), name="bolt")
s.Circle(5, concentric="Circle.1", construction=True)
s.Move("Point.4").Line("Point.1", id="gusset line", construction=True)
bracket = s.Face()
```

```python
Row((s, "The hole Circle.1, its washer and the gusset line, by their ids"))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

Only the name given with `name=` reaches the face, while the ids stay in the sketch:

```python
print("area", bracket.mass, "exact", 40 * 10 + 20 * 10 - math.pi * 2.5**2)
print({e.name for e in bracket.edges})
```

```text
area 580.3650459150638 exact 580.3650459150638
{None, 'bolt'}
```

Ids are also how the editing calls find their elements. `Fillet("Point.4", 5)`, for example, rounds the re-entrant
corner by the id of its point. See [Fillets and chamfers](fillets-chamfers.md) for details.

---

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/sketch/fillets-chamfers.md

# Fillets and chamfers

A fillet replaces a corner with an arc of a given radius, tangent to both edges, and a chamfer replaces it with a
straight cut. Both work in two places: on finished geometry, where `Fillet` and `Chamfer` take a corner of a wire,
face or shape, and in a sketch, where the corner is given by the id of its point. In a constraint sketch, the radius
and the lengths become dimensions that can be changed later.

```python
import math
import planex as px
```

## On faces

The example is the profile of an angle bracket, with legs 60 and 40 long and 8 thick (Figure 1). Its inner corner
gets a fillet of radius 6, which adds material, and the outer corner at the end of the long leg gets a chamfer of 3.
A corner is given as a vertex, as a point on a vertex, or as a vertex name, and a list gives several corners at once.
`Filleted` and `Chamfered` return a copy, while `Fillet` and `Chamfer` change the object in place.

```python
bracket = px.FromPolyline([(0, 0), (60, 0), (60, 8), (8, 8), (8, 40), (0, 40)], closed=True).Face()
rounded = bracket.Filleted((8, 8), 6)
cut = rounded.Chamfered((60, 8), 3)
```

```python
Row((bracket, "(a) The bracket"), (cut, "(b) Filleted and chamfered"),
    caption="An angle bracket with a fillet in its inner corner and a chamfer on its long leg")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

A fillet in a right-angled corner adds or removes r²(1 − π/4), and a chamfer of 3 on both edges removes 3²/2:

```python
print("fillet", rounded.mass - bracket.mass, "exact", 6**2 * (1 - math.pi / 4))
print("chamfer", rounded.mass - cut.mass, "exact", 3**2 / 2)
```

```text
fillet 7.725666117691844 exact 7.725666117691862
chamfer 4.5 exact 4.5
```

A chamfer can also have two different lengths, with `d2=`, or a length and an angle, with `angle=` in degrees from
the first edge. A chamfer of 3 at 30° removes a triangle with the legs 3 and 3 tan 30°:

```python
steep = bracket.Chamfered((60, 8), 3, angle=30)
print("chamfer at 30°", bracket.mass - steep.mass, "exact", 3 * 3 * math.tan(math.radians(30)) / 2)
```

```text
chamfer at 30° 2.598076211353373 exact 2.598076211353316
```

## In a sketch

In a sketch, `Fillet` and `Chamfer` take the corner as a point id, such as `"bottom.end"`, as a point, or as a list
of them. The new arc gets the id `Fillet.1` and the new line `Chamfer.1`. The two edges at the corner keep their ids.
The pieces they lose stay in the sketch as construction lines that meet at the sharp corner, so a dimension can still
refer to that corner. The example is a cover plate of 50 × 30 with two corners rounded to 5 and one chamfered by 4
(Figure 2).

```python
sk = px.QuickSketch()
sk.Line(50, id="bottom").Turn(90).Line(30, id="right")
sk.Turn(90).Line(50, id="top").Close(id="left")
sk.Fillet(["bottom.end", "right.end"], 5)
sk.Chamfer("top.end", 4);
```

```python
Row((sk, "A cover plate, the cut-off corners dashed"), caption="Fillets and a chamfer in a quick sketch")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

```python
plate = sk.Face()
print("area", plate.mass, "exact", 50 * 30 - 2 * 5**2 * (1 - math.pi / 4) - 4**2 / 2)
```

```text
area 1481.2699081698725 exact 1481.2699081698725
```

The new arc or line takes the properties of the drawing calls, `name=`, `maxh=`, `hpref=` and `col=`, as one value
for all corners or as a list with one value per corner, for example
`sk.Fillet(["a.end", "b.end"], 1, name=["r1", "r2"])`.

In a constraint sketch, the radius of a fillet and the lengths of a chamfer are dimensions that can change later.
See [Offsets and profiles revisited](../constraints/offsets-profiles.md) for details.

See [Trimming and splitting](trimming.md) for corners cut by hand.

---

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/sketch/extending.md

# Extending edges

`congruent=` draws a line on the carrier of another line, the infinite line it lies on. With a target as its end, the
new line continues the other one until that target. This is how an edge is extended, for example to a point that
exists only on the drawing.

```python
import math
import planex as px
```

## A dovetail's theoretical sharp

A dovetail is dimensioned to its theoretical sharp, the point where its two flanks would meet if they continued above
the surface. The example is the dovetail slide from [Parallel, perpendicular, angle](parallel-perpendicular-angle.md),
drawn there step by step:

```python
s = px.QuickSketch((-30, 0))
s.Line(60, id="bottom")
s.Line(-60, parallel="bottom", distance=30, id="top", construction=True)
s.Line(-60, parallel="bottom", distance=20, id="floor", construction=True)
s.Line(20, angle=(180 + 60, "bottom"), through=(-12, 30), id="left flank line", construction=True)
s.Turn(90).Line(30, id="right side").Turn(90).Line(18, id="right shoulder")
s.Line("floor", angle=(-60, "bottom"), id="right flank")
s.Line("left flank line", parallel="bottom", id="groove floor")
s.Line("top", congruent="left flank line", id="left flank")
s.Line((-30, 30), id="left shoulder").Close(id="left side");
```

The left flank is extended upward by a construction line on its carrier, at 60° through the groove's corner. The right
flank is extended from its start, on its own carrier, until it meets that line. The end of this second line is the
sharp, marked in Figure 1.

```python
s.Line(40, angle=(60, "bottom"), through=(-12, 30), id="left flank up", construction=True)
s.Move("right flank.start")
s.Line("left flank up", congruent="right flank", id="sharp", construction=True)
apex = s.Location("sharp.end")
```

```python
Row((s, "The dovetail's flanks extended to the theoretical sharp", {"fill": False, "marks": [apex]}))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The sharp lies a/2 · tan α above the surface, with the width a = 24 at the surface and the flank angle α = 60°:

```python
print("apex", apex[1], "exact", 30 + 12 * math.tan(math.radians(60)))
```

```text
apex 50.78460969082654 exact 50.78460969082652
```

---

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/sketch/offsets.md

# Offsets

An offset is the geometry at a constant distance from a path. planex2d has two kinds:

- `Wire().Offset(d)` grows a wire into a face of width 2d, with round ends. Like a union, it is a result.
- `sketch.Offset(source, d)` adds new elements to the sketch at the distance d from a line, an arc, a spline or a
  chain of them. They are sketch elements like any other, with ids that later calls can refer to.

A slot around its center line, a seal groove around its seal line, a sheet from its inner surface and a cam from the
path of its roller are all offsets. In a constraint sketch, the offset also stays tied to its source and its distance
becomes a dimension. See [Offsets and profiles revisited](../constraints/offsets-profiles.md) for details.

```python
import math
import planex as px
```

## A heater track and a ring

The first example is a meander heater track, a path of six runs of 40 joined by half circles of radius 3, grown into a
track 2 wide (Figure 1a). The second is a ring, the offset of a closed wire, a circle of radius 20, so it has no ends
(b).

```python
s = px.QuickSketch()
for k in range(5):
    s.Line(40).Arc(3, 180 if k % 2 == 0 else -180)
s.Line(40)
heater = s.Wire().Offset(1)

ring = px.Circle((0, 0), 20).Offset(1.5)
```

```python
Row((heater, "A meander heater track"), (ring, "A ring"), caption="Wire offsets: a heater track and a ring")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

Where the path is smooth and the band does not overlap itself, its area is exactly 2d times the length of the path,
plus the two round end caps:

```python
length = 6 * 40 + 5 * math.pi * 3
print("heater area", heater.mass, "exact", 2 * length + math.pi * 1**2)
print("ring area", ring.mass, "exact", 4 * math.pi * 20 * 1.5)
```

```text
heater area 577.3893722612839 exact 577.3893722612836
ring area 376.99111843077503 exact 376.99111843077515
```

## A slot around a line

In a sketch, the offset of a line is a band with one side on its left and one on its right, joined by round caps at
the ends. The example is a motor plate of 120 × 80 with two adjustment slots for M8 screws (Figure 2). Each slot is 9
wide, around a center line 20 long, 25 above or below the middle. Around it, a construction offset of 8 marks the
clearance for the washer, 16 across.

The offset takes its properties from its source. The center lines are construction, so the slots are switched to
drawn edges afterwards.

```python
plate = px.QuickSketch().RectangleC(120, 80, id="outline")
for k, y in enumerate((-25, 25)):
    plate.Move((-10, y)).Line(20, 0, id=f"center{k}", construction=True)
    plate.Offset(f"center{k}", 4.5, id=f"slot{k}", name="slot edge")
    plate.Offset(f"center{k}", 8, id=f"washer{k}", name="washer")
    plate(f"slot{k}").construction = False
part = plate.Face()
```

```python
Row((colored(plate, blue=["slot0", "slot1"]), "Slot edges (blue), center lines and washers dashed", SMOOTH),
    (part, "The motor plate"), caption="A motor plate with two adjustment slots")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

`Measure` takes the id of a whole offset. The plate's area and the length of the washer outlines follow from the slot
and washer sizes:

```python
washers = sum(plate.Measure(f"washer{k}")["length"] for k in range(2))
print("area", part.mass, "exact", 120 * 80 - 2 * (20 * 9 + math.pi * 9**2 / 4))
print("washers", washers, "exact", 2 * (2 * 20 + math.pi * 16))
```

```text

washers 180.53096491487338 exact 180.53096491487338
```

## A loop around a closed chain

The offset of a closed chain is one loop, outside for d > 0 and inside for d < 0. `both_sides=True` gives both
sides, `"<id>.left"` inside the loop and `"<id>.right"` outside it. The example is a cover of 120 × 80 with the groove
of an O-ring face seal, 4.8 wide, around a seal line of 100 × 60 with a corner radius of 10 (Figure 3a). The groove is
a closed band, so the cover consists of two regions, the frame and the island inside the groove, and `Shape()` keeps
both (Figure 3b).

```python
cover = px.QuickSketch().RectangleC(120, 80, id="outline")
cover.Move((-40, -30), dir=(1, 0))
for side in (100, 60, 100, 60):
    cover.Line(side - 20).Arc(10, 90)
cover.Finish(id_wire="seal")
cover("seal").construction = True
cover.Offset("seal", 2.4, both_sides=True, id="groove")
cover("groove").construction = False
covered = cover.Shape()
```

```python
Row((colored(cover, blue=["groove"]), "The groove (blue) around the seal line", SMOOTH),
    (covered, "The cover with its groove"), caption="An O-ring groove as a two-sided offset of the seal line")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

Around a smooth closed line, the band between the two sides has an area of exactly its width times the length of the
line, and each side is π times the width longer or shorter than the line:

```python
seal = 2 * (100 + 60) - 8 * 10 + 2 * math.pi * 10
band = px.Face([cover.Edge("groove.right")]) - px.Face([cover.Edge("groove.left")])
print("groove area", band.mass, "exact", 4.8 * seal)
print("outer", cover.Measure("groove.right")["length"], "exact", seal + math.pi * 4.8)
print("inner", cover.Measure("groove.left")["length"], "exact", seal - math.pi * 4.8)
```

```text
groove area 1453.592894744621 exact 1453.5928947446203
outer 317.91149780902686 exact 317.91149780902686
inner 287.75220833456484 exact 287.7522083345649
```

A chain with corners, such as a rectangle, is offset differently on the two sides. Outside, the offset goes around
each corner with an arc, named after the element whose end it goes around, such as `"wall.box.Line.1.corner"`.
Inside, the sides meet in sharp corners. The example is a box of 40 × 20 with a wall 2 outside (blue) and a lining 2
inside (amber) (Figure 4):

```python
box = px.QuickSketch().Rectangle(40, 20, id="box")
box.Offset("box", 2, id="wall").Offset("box", -2, id="lining")
print(box.elements["Arc"])
```

```text
['wall.box.Line.1.corner', 'wall.box.Line.2.corner', 'wall.box.Line.3.corner', 'wall.box.Line.4.corner']
```

```python
Row((colored(box, blue=["wall"], amber=["lining"]), "A box: its wall (blue) and lining (amber)", SMOOTH))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

```python
print("wall", box.Measure("wall")["length"], "exact", 2 * (40 + 20) + 2 * math.pi * 2)
print("lining", box.Measure("lining")["length"], "exact", 2 * (36 + 16))
```
