## One side of an open chain

`both_sides=False` keeps one side of an open chain, without caps: the left side for d > 0. Its elements are named
after their sources, such as `"outside.web"`, without a side word. The example is a bent sheet, 2 thick, drawn from
its inner surface: a flange 40 up, a bend of inner radius 4 and a web 30 to the right (Figure 5). The sheet lies to
the left of the chain, on the outside of the bend. Two short lines close its ends, drawn to the offset's end points,
such as `"outside.web.end"`.

```python
sheet = px.QuickSketch((0, 0), dir=(0, 1))
sheet.Line(36, id="flange").Arc(4, -90, id="bend").Line(26, id="web")
sheet.Offset(["flange", "bend", "web"], 2, both_sides=False, id="outside")
sheet.Line("outside.web.end", id="end")
sheet.Move("flange.start").Line("outside.flange.start", id="foot")
profile = sheet.Face()
```

```python
Row((colored(sheet, blue=["outside"]), "The inner surface and its offset (blue)", SMOOTH),
    (profile, "The bent sheet"), caption="A bent sheet from its inner surface")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The outer bend radius is r + t = 6, and the area is t times the inner length plus t²/2 per radian of bend. A distance
given as `(d, point)` selects the side the point is on instead. A point inside the bend gives the right side, with
the radius r − t = 2:

```python
inner = 36 + 26 + math.pi / 2 * 4
print("area", profile.mass, "exact", 2 * inner + 2**2 / 2 * math.pi / 2)
print("outer bend radius", sheet.Geometry("outside.bend")["r"], "exact", 6)

other = px.QuickSketch((0, 0), dir=(0, 1))
other.Line(36, id="flange").Arc(4, -90, id="bend").Line(26, id="web")
other.Offset(["flange", "bend", "web"], (2, (5, 5)), id="inside")
print("inner bend radius", other.Geometry("inside.bend")["r"], "exact", 2)
```

```text
area 139.70796326794903 exact 139.70796326794897
outer bend radius 6.0 exact 6
inner bend radius 2.0 exact 2
```

## Ids and selection

| Id | What it is |
|---|---|
| `"slot0"` | The whole offset, for `Measure`, `Remove` and `sk("slot0")` |
| `"slot0.left"`, `"slot0.right"` | The two sides of a two-sided offset, with their point elements; for a loop, `left` is inside and `right` outside |
| `"slot0.left.center0"` | The offset of the source element `center0` on that side |
| `"outside.web"` | The offset of `web` in a one-sided offset, without a side word |
| `"wall.box.Line.1.corner"` | The arc around the end of `box.Line.1` |
| `"slot0.startcap"`, `"slot0.endcap"` | The round caps |

A selection takes the whole offset or one side, and `kind=` narrows it down. Their properties can be set like those of
any element, for example `sk("slot0").col`, `.name`, `.maxh` and `.construction`.

```python
print(sorted(i.split(".", 2)[2] for i in plate("slot0.left").ids))
print(sorted(i.split(".", 2)[2] for i in plate("slot0", kind="arc").ids))
```

```text
['slot0.left.Point.1', 'slot0.left.Point.2', 'slot0.left.center0']
['slot0.endcap', 'slot0.startcap']
```

## A cam from the path of its roller

A disc cam for a roller follower is designed backwards. The motion law gives the path of the roller's center, the
pitch curve, and the cam is the pitch curve offset inward by the roller radius. The example has a base circle of 25,
a roller of 8, a harmonic rise of 10 over 120°, a dwell, the return over 120° and another dwell. The pitch curve is a
closed spline through 48 of its points.

The offset of a spline is a derived curve: each of its points is the spline's point moved by d along the normal, so
it keeps the distance d exactly, not within a fit. Figure 6a shows the pitch curve dashed, the roller at a few
positions and the cam in blue, and Figure 6b shows the cam.

```python
default = px.config.spline_tol
px.config.spline_tol = 1e-10


def rise(deg):
    if deg < 120:
        return 10 * (1 - math.cos(math.pi * deg / 120)) / 2
    if deg < 180:
        return 10
    if deg < 300:
        return 10 * (1 + math.cos(math.pi * (deg - 180) / 120)) / 2
    return 0.0


path = []
for k in range(48):
    deg = 360 * k / 48
    rho, a = 25 + 8 + rise(deg), math.radians(deg)
    path.append((rho * math.cos(a), rho * math.sin(a)))

cam = px.QuickSketch(path[0]).Spline(path[1:], periodic=True, id="pitch", construction=True)
cam.Offset("pitch", -8, id="profile")
cam("profile").construction = False
disc = cam.Face()
```

```python
rollers = px.QuickSketch()
for p in path[::6]:
    rollers.Circle(p[0], p[1], 8)
Row((colored(cam, blue=["profile"]), "Pitch curve and rollers dashed, the cam (blue)",
     {**SMOOTH, "dashed": [rollers]}), (disc, "The cam"), caption="A disc cam from the path of its roller")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The check measures, at points along the cam, how closely the cam keeps the roller radius from the pitch curve. It
also compares the cam's area with the area of the parallel curve, A − L·r + π·r², from the pitch curve's area A and
length L. Areas and `Distance` use the spline's arc approximation, made when the spline is drawn, so this section
draws with `px.config.spline_tol` at 10⁻¹⁰ (the default is 10⁻⁶ of the spline's size). What remains in the checks is
that approximation, not the offset.

Where only the result counts, `Offset(d)` of the region inside the pitch curve gives the cam as a face, on the exact
parallel curve. It works in place, so the region becomes the cam:

```python
pitch = cam.Edge("pitch")
gaps = pitch.Distance(cam.Edge("profile").Polylines(1e-3)[0])
exact = px.Face([pitch]).mass - cam.Measure("pitch")["length"] * 8 + math.pi * 8**2
print(f"distance from the pitch curve: {gaps.min():.12f} to {gaps.max():.12f}")
print("area", disc.mass, "parallel curve", exact)

result = px.Face([pitch]).Offset(-8)
gaps = pitch.Distance(result.Polylines(1e-3)[0])
print(f"Offset(d) of the face: {gaps.min():.12f} to {gaps.max():.12f}")
print("its area", result.mass, "parallel curve", exact)
```

```text
distance from the pitch curve: 7.999999985354 to 8.000000011528
area 2867.4271873236135 parallel curve 2867.427187208249
```

```text
Offset(d) of the face: 8.000000000000 to 8.000000000000
its area 2867.4271872082313 parallel curve 2867.427187208249
```

A roller larger than the tightest bend of the pitch curve would leave a cusp on the cam. The offset refuses it,
which serves as the designer's undercut check:

```python
try:
    cam.Offset("pitch", -36, id="big")
except ValueError as err:
    print(err)
px.config.spline_tol = default
```

```text
Offset('pitch'): the offset of pitch would have a cusp: d = 36 is not below 31.49724549514452, the radius of its tightest bend towards that side, at (20.089127157288363, -26.18066022961032)
```

---

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/sketch/trimming.md

# Trimming and splitting

A common way to sketch is to draw elements past each other and cut them back afterwards, as on a drawing board.
`Trim(a, b)` cuts the element `a` where it meets `b` and turns one piece of it into construction, shown dashed in the
pictures:

- by default, the piece nearest to the pen;
- with `a` given as `(id, point)`, the piece nearest to the point;
- with `reverse=True`, the next piece instead.

Without `b`, `a` is cut wherever it meets another line, arc or circle. A full circle has no vertices, so it is cut
only where other edges cross it. The part that stays keeps the id, and the cut-off piece gets the id `<id>.trimmed.1`.
`Split(a, b)` cuts in the same way but keeps every piece, numbered `<id>.1`, `<id>.2` and so on along the element.

```python
import math
import planex as px
```

## A keyhole slot

The example is a keyhole for hanging a part on a screw: a head hole of diameter 20 for the screw head and a slot 10
wide whose end lies 30 from the hole's center. The slot is drawn from the center of the hole, so its sides reach into
the hole (Figure 1a). Three trims cut it back:

1. the upper side at the head, which turns the piece nearest to the pen into construction;
2. the lower side at the head, at the piece nearest to its start;
3. the head wherever it meets the sides, at the piece between them.

The cut pieces remain as dashed construction (Figure 1b), and Figure 1c shows the face. `Keyhole(30, 10, 10)` draws
the same outline in one call (see [Slots, keyholes and polygons](slots-polygons.md)). Here it is cut by hand to show
the trims.

```python
s = px.QuickSketch()
s.Circle(10, id="head")
s.Move((0, -5)).Line(30, id="lower side")
s.Arc(5, 180, id="end").Line((0, 5), id="upper side")
drawn = s.Copy()

s.Trim("upper side", "head")
s.Trim(("lower side", (0, -5)), "head")
s.Trim(("head", (10, 0)))
keyhole = s.Face()
```

```python
Row((drawn, "Drawn past each other", {"fill": False}), (s, "Trimmed", {"fill": False}), (keyhole, "The keyhole"),
    caption="A keyhole slot: drawn past each other, trimmed, and the face")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The area is that of the disc, the slot and the half disc at its end, minus the part of the slot inside the disc:

```python
segment = 5 * math.sqrt(10**2 - 5**2) + 10**2 * math.asin(5 / 10)
print("area", keyhole.mass, "exact", math.pi * 10**2 + 30 * 10 - segment + math.pi * 5**2 / 2)
```

```text
area 557.7680257797999 exact 557.7680257798
```

## The other piece

`reverse=True` turns the other piece into construction, here the part of the upper side outside the head. The part
that stays drawn keeps the id `upper side`. The head circle meets the side √(10² − 5²) from its center, so the two
results have these lengths:

```python
meet = math.sqrt(10**2 - 5**2)
outside = drawn.Copy().Trim("upper side", "head")
inside = drawn.Copy().Trim("upper side", "head", reverse=True)
print("default:", outside.Measure("upper side")["length"], "exact", 30 - meet)
print("reverse=True:", inside.Measure("upper side")["length"], "exact", meet)
```

```text
default: 21.33974596215561 exact 21.33974596215561
reverse=True: 8.660254037844387 exact 8.660254037844387
```

## Split keeps every piece

`Split` cuts the upper side at the head into two lines, `upper side.1` and `upper side.2` along it. `upper side`
itself now names the wire of both, so references to it keep working. Together, the two lines are as long as the side
was before.

```python
split = drawn.Copy().Split("upper side", "head")
pieces = {ref: split.Measure(ref)["length"] for ref in ("upper side.1", "upper side.2")}
for ref, length in pieces.items():
    print(ref, length)
print("together", sum(pieces.values()), "the side was", 30)
```

```text
upper side.1 21.33974596215561
upper side.2 8.660254037844387
together 30.0 the side was 30
```

## A keyed bore in one sketch

On [Circles and rectangles](circles-and-rectangles.md), the keyed bore of the square flange was a second face,
united from the bore and the keyway and subtracted from the plate. With trimming, the whole flange is one sketch. The
bore is a circle, and the keyway is drawn as three lines up from the bore's center line. The two sides are trimmed back
to the bore, and then the bore is trimmed inside the keyway (Figure 2).

```python
flange = px.QuickSketch().RectangleC(60, 60)
for x in (-22, 22):
    for y in (-22, 22):
        flange.Circle(x, y, 3.3)
flange.Circle(10, id="bore")
flange.Move((-3, 0)).Line((-3, 12.8), id="left").Line((3, 12.8), id="top").Line((3, 0), id="right")
flange.Trim(("left", (-3, 1)), "bore")
flange.Trim(("right", (3, 1)), "bore")
flange.Trim(("bore", (0, 10)));
```

```python
Row((flange, "The flange in one sketch, the cut pieces dashed", {"fill": False}), (flange.Face(), "The flange"),
    caption="A keyed bore trimmed in one sketch")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The area is the same as on [Circles and rectangles](circles-and-rectangles.md):

```python
overlap = 3 * math.sqrt(10**2 - 3**2) + 10**2 * math.asin(6 / 20)
print("area", flange.Face().mass, "exact", 60**2 - (math.pi * 10**2 + 6 * 12.8 - overlap) - math.pi * 6.6**2)
```

```text
area 3131.280400094698 exact 3131.2804000946976
```

# Symmetry

A symmetric part can be drawn as one half and mirrored. `Mirrored(ids, axis)` adds mirrored copies of the given
elements under `Mirrored.1`, each named after its original, such as `Mirrored.1.base`, and with the original's
properties, including its name. Ends on the axis stay exactly on it, so the half and its mirror bound one face.
`Mirror(axis)` mirrors the whole sketch instead. `SymmetryLine(a, b)` adds the axis between two points, two lines, or
two circles or arcs, as an infinite construction line.

```python
import math
import planex as px
```

## A lifting lug

The example is a lifting lug cut from flat bar 80 wide, with an eye of radius 30 whose center lies 70 above the base,
and a pin hole of 26 (Figure 1). The lug is drawn as its right half in two steps.

First the construction. The two edges of the bar are construction lines, and `SymmetryLine` adds the center line
between them as the axis. The eye is a point with a construction circle around it.

```python
lug = px.QuickSketch()
lug.Move((-40, -10)).Line((-40, 110), id="left edge", construction=True)
lug.Move((40, -10)).Line((40, 110), id="right edge", construction=True)
lug.SymmetryLine("left edge", "right edge", id="axis")
lug.Vertex("eye", (0, 70))
lug.Circle(30, center="eye", id="eye circle", construction=True);
```

Then the right half, from the axis along the base until the right edge, tangent to the eye, and around the eye back
to the axis (Figure 1a). `Mirrored` adds its mirror image, and the pin hole completes the lug (Figure 1b).

```python
lug.Move((0, 0), dir=(1, 0))
lug.Line(until="right edge", id="base")
lug.Line(tangent=("eye circle", (30, 70)), id="flank", name="flank")
lug.Arc("axis", congruent="eye circle", id="crown")
half = lug.Copy()

lug.Mirrored(["base", "flank", "crown"], "axis")
lug.Circle(13, center="eye", id="pin hole")
face = lug.Face()
```

```python
axis = px.Line((0, -10), (0, 110))
Row((half, "The right half", {"fill": False, "dashed": [axis]}),
    (lug, "Mirrored, with the pin hole", {"dashed": [axis]}), caption="A lifting lug from its right half")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The mirrored flank also has the name `flank`, so `lug(name="flank")` selects both. Each flank is a tangent from a
base corner to the eye, with a length of √((B/2)² + He² − Re²), where B = 80 is the width, He = 70 the height of the
eye and Re = 30 its radius. The area is that of the polygon through the base corners, the touch points and the eye's
center, plus the sector over the top, minus the hole:

```python
B, He, Re = 80.0, 70.0, 30.0
L0 = math.hypot(B / 2, He)
for e in lug(name="flank"):
    print(e.id, e.Measure()["length"], "exact", math.sqrt(L0**2 - Re**2))

theta = math.atan2(-He, B / 2) + math.acos(Re / L0)
T = (Re * math.cos(theta), He + Re * math.sin(theta))
polygon = [(-B / 2, 0), (B / 2, 0), T, (0, He), (-T[0], T[1])]
pairs = zip(polygon, polygon[1:] + polygon[:1])
shoelace = 0.5 * sum(p[0] * q[1] - q[0] * p[1] for p, q in pairs)
print("area", face.mass, "exact", shoelace + 0.5 * Re**2 * (math.pi - 2 * theta) - math.pi * 13**2)
```

```text
Sketch.1.flank 74.83314773547883 exact 74.83314773547882
Sketch.1.Mirrored.1.flank 74.83314773547883 exact 74.83314773547882
area 5803.697953996632 exact 5803.697953996631
```

## What SymmetryLine accepts

| a, b | Symmetry line |
|---|---|
| Two points | The perpendicular bisector |
| Two parallel lines | The midline |
| Two crossing lines | The bisector that maps a onto b best; `reverse=True` selects the other |
| Two circles or arcs | The perpendicular bisector of their centers |

The symmetry line is an infinite construction line with the id given by `id=`. In a constraint sketch, it stays
symmetric to its references when they move. See [Symmetry and patterns](../constraints/symmetry.md) for details.

---

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/sketch/placement.md

# Placing a sketch

A sketch draws in two coordinates, h and v, on a plane that can be positioned anywhere in 3D. The plane is given
when the sketch starts: a coordinate plane, an origin with a normal and an axis, or a face of a solid. The edges of
any solid can serve as references. A drawing call projects an edge it is given as a target into the sketch's plane,
and `Project` brings edges in as construction elements first, so that dimensions can refer to them. The faces of the
sketch go back into a solid as cuts or bosses.

The solids on this page are OpenCASCADE shapes, which come from `netgen-mesher`, an optional dependency of planex2d
(`pip install netgen-mesher`).

```python
import netgen.occ as occ
from ngsolve_webgpu.jupyter import Draw
import planex as px
```

## On a plane

`px.QuickSketch(plane)` starts on `px.XY` (the default), `px.YZ`, `px.ZX`, or a
`px.Plane(origin=, normal=, axis=)` with its normal and its h direction. netgen's `occ.Axes` is accepted as well. v
completes them, so that h, v and the normal turn like x, y and z. Figure 1 shows the same rectangle on four planes,
with h in blue and v in amber:

```python
planes = {"XY": px.XY, "YZ": px.YZ, "ZX": px.ZX,
          "tilted": px.Plane(origin=(60, 0, 0), normal=(1, 0, 1), axis=(0, 1, 0))}
plates = {k: px.QuickSketch(p).Rectangle(30, 20) for k, p in planes.items()}
for k, s in plates.items():
    print(k, "normal", s.Normal(), "(30, 20) at", s.ToXYZ((30, 20)))
```

```text
XY normal (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) (30, 20) at (30.0, 20.0, 0.0)
YZ normal (1.0, 0.0, 0.0) (30, 20) at (0.0, 30.0, 20.0)
ZX normal (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) (30, 20) at (20.0, 0.0, 30.0)
tilted normal (0.7071067811865476, 0.0, 0.7071067811865476) (30, 20) at (45.85786437626905, 30.0, 14.142135623730951)
```

```python
shapes = []
for s in plates.values():
    shapes += [(s.Face().ToOCCFace(), "shade"), (s.Face().ToOCCFace(), "ink")] + axes(s, 40)
Views(("The rectangle 30 × 20 on XY, YZ, ZX and a tilted plane, h in blue and v in amber", shapes), angles=(-65, 0, 135))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## On a face of a solid

The example is a wedge block 100 long and 60 wide, 50 high at the back and 20 at the front. Its profile is drawn on
the xz plane, with the normal along −y, and `px.Pad` extrudes it by 60 along that normal. The solid's faces carry the
names of the profile edges they come from, so its sloped face is `block.faces["slope"]` (see
[Pad and Pocket](../basics/pad-pocket.md)):

```python
profile = px.QuickSketch(px.Plane(normal=(0, -1, 0), axis=(1, 0, 0)))
profile.Line((100, 0), name="bottom").Line((100, 20), name="front")
profile.Line((0, 50), name="slope").Close(name="back")
block = px.Pad(profile, 60)
slope = block.faces["slope"][0]
```

`px.QuickSketch(slope)` sketches on the plane of the face, with its normal pointing out of the solid. The global
origin and the global x axis are projected onto the face, so h runs down the slope and v across it (Figure 2). See
[The plane in 3D](../basics/plane.md) for the rule. The origin lies wherever the projection puts it, here on the edge
at y = 0, which does not matter: everything below is placed from the solid's own edges.

```python
top = px.QuickSketch(slope)
plane = px.Plane(top)
print("origin", plane.origin)
print("h", plane.h, "v", plane.v, "normal", plane.normal)
```


## Drawing against the solid

`Project` lays the edges of a solid's face flat onto the sketch as construction elements. Without `id=`, they are
named `Projection.N.Edge.X`; with `id="slope"`, they are `slope.Edge.0` to `slope.Edge.3`. The number is netgen's own
edge number, the one that netgen's 3D view shows as "Edge N" when an edge of the face is clicked (Figure 3). Here,
`slope.Edge.1` is the top edge and `slope.Edge.0` the lower one:

```python
Draw(slope)
top.Project(slope, id="slope")
for k in range(4):
    print(f"slope.Edge.{k}", top.Geometry(f"slope.Edge.{k}")["length"], "long, middle at",
          top.ToXYZ(top.Location(f"slope.Edge.{k}.mid")))
```

The points of every projected element place what comes next. `Move(point, dir=)` starts at a point of an element,
and `Move(l)` moves the pen along. Two holes of diameter 10 lie 20 below the top edge and 15 in from the sides, and a
slot 10 wide lies around a center line 30 long, 30 up the slope from the middle of the lower edge (Figure 4). The
drawing is a function, so that it can be placed onto another face later:

```python
def pattern(s, holes_from, slot_from, holes_at, slot_at):
    s.Move(f"{holes_from}.mid", dir=(1, 0)).Move(holes_at)
    s.Turn(90).Move(15).Circle(5, name="hole")
    s.Turn(180).Move(30).Circle(5, name="hole")
    s.Move(f"{slot_from}.mid", dir=(-1, 0)).Move(slot_at)
    s.Turn(90).Move(15).Turn(180).Line(30, id="midline", construction=True)
    s.Offset("midline", 5, id="slot", name="slot")
    s("slot").construction = False
    return s


pattern(top, "slope.Edge.1", "slope.Edge.0", 20, 30)
for e in top(name="hole"):
    print(e.id, "center in 3D", top.ToXYZ(top.Location(f"{e.id}.center")))
```

## The same drawing on another face

The back face is 50 high. The holes go 12 below its top edge and the slot 12 above its lower edge, and both are
pockets 10 deep. The pattern measures down the face along h, as on the slope. On the back face, the global x axis is
the normal itself, so by the rule h would run along y. `px.Plane(back, axis=(0, 0, -1))` gives h downward instead.
This is where the `axis=` of `px.Plane` is needed. After the projection, the top edge of the back face is
`back.Edge.0` and its lower edge is `back.Edge.1` (Figure 6):

```python
back = block.faces["back"][0]
```

# Parametric design

A part can be written as a Python function of its parameters. The function draws the part from references, so every
point follows from the parameters, and a parameter study simply calls the function again. This is parametric design
without a solver. A [constraint sketch](../constraints/index.md) offers the other kind, where the dimensions of one
sketch are changed and the sketch is solved again.

The example is the lamination of a permanent magnet motor, with the number of slots, the magnet arc and the magnet
thickness as parameters. The sizes that stay the same in every design are constants. See the
[motor example](../../examples/motor.md) for the full motor with its magnetic field.

```python
import math
import planex as px
```

```python
R_out, R_bore, slot_d, open_d = 50.0, 30.0, 12.0, 1.0
R_rotor, R_shaft, poles = 26.0, 8.0, 8


def disc(r):
    return px.Circle((0, 0), r).Face()
```

## One slot and one magnet

A slot has its sides parallel to the slot axis and runs from the bore, through the slot opening, to the slot bottom,
with its mouth and its bottom on their circles. The slot width is half the slot pitch at the bore. The sides are
construction lines at half the width from the axis, and the outline runs between the circles on them. A point in the
middle of the slot, given with every reference it decides (as in `("bore", middle)`), selects the intersections on the
correct side of the center. The slot bottom runs clockwise (`reverse=True`).

```python
def slot_face(slots):
    width = 0.5 * 2 * math.pi * R_bore / slots
    middle = (R_bore + (open_d + slot_d) / 2, 0)
    s = px.QuickSketch()
    s.Circle(R_bore, id="bore", construction=True)
    s.Circle(R_bore + open_d + slot_d, id="bottom", construction=True)
    s.Move((0, 0)).Line(R_out, id="axis", construction=True)
    s.Move((0, 0), dir=(1, 0)).Line(R_out, parallel="axis", distance=width / 2, id="left side", construction=True)
    s.Move((0, 0), dir=(1, 0)).Line(R_out, parallel="axis", distance=-width / 2, id="right side", construction=True)
    s.Line(("bore", middle), ("bottom", middle), congruent="left side")
    s.Arc(("left side", middle), ("right side", middle), congruent="bottom", reverse=True)
    s.Line(("bottom", middle), ("bore", middle), congruent="right side")
    s.Arc(("right side", middle), ("left side", middle), congruent="bore")
    slot = s.Face()
    slot.name = "coil"
    return slot
```

A magnet lies on the rotor between two rays, at half the magnet's angle on either side of the axis, and its top is
the circle at the magnet's thickness. The same kind of middle point picks the intersections.

```python
def magnet_face(magnet_arc, magnet_thickness):
    half = 180 / poles * magnet_arc
    center = (R_rotor + magnet_thickness / 2, 0)
    m = px.QuickSketch()
    m.Circle(R_rotor, id="rotor", construction=True)
    m.Circle(R_rotor + magnet_thickness, id="top", construction=True)
    m.Move((0, 0)).Line(R_out, angle=-half, id="start", construction=True)
    m.Move((0, 0)).Line(R_out, angle=half, id="end", construction=True)
    m.Arc(("start", center), ("end", center), congruent="rotor")
    m.Line(("rotor", center), ("top", center), congruent="end")
    m.Arc(("end", center), ("start", center), congruent="top", reverse=True)
    m.Line(("top", center), ("rotor", center), congruent="start")
    magnet = m.Face()
    magnet.name = "magnet"
    return magnet
```

## The lamination

The lamination turns copies of the slot and the magnet around the center and combines everything with `px.Glue` into
the regions of one shape: magnets, rotor, coils, stator, and the air that fills the gap and the shaft. Where parts
overlap, the first one listed wins, so the magnets, the rotor and the coils come before the stator and the air. Every
part has a name, and the names travel with the regions, so a solver or a measurement can find them again in every
design.

```python
def GetGeometry(slots, magnet_arc, magnet_thickness):
    slot, magnet = slot_face(slots), magnet_face(magnet_arc, magnet_thickness)
    coils = [slot.Rotated((0, 0), 360 * k / slots) for k in range(slots)]
    magnets = [magnet.Rotated((0, 0), 360 * k / poles) for k in range(poles)]
    stator = px.Subtract([disc(R_out), disc(R_bore), *coils])
    rotor = disc(R_rotor) - disc(R_shaft)
    air = disc(R_out)
    stator.name, rotor.name, air.name = "stator", "rotor", "air"
    return px.Glue([*magnets, rotor, *coils, stator, air])
```

## Three designs

Each design is one call (Figure 1). The first has 12 slots and magnets over 90 % of the pole, 3 thick (a). The
second has 24 slots and magnets over 80 %, 2.5 thick (b), and the third has 36 slots and magnets over 70 %, 2 thick
(c).

```python
designs = [(12, 0.9, 3.0), (24, 0.8, 2.5), (36, 0.7, 2.0)]
laminations = [GetGeometry(*design) for design in designs]
```

```python
Row(*[(lamination, f"{slots} slots, {arc:.0%} of the pole, {thickness} thick")
      for lamination, (slots, arc, thickness) in zip(laminations, designs)],
    caption="Three motor laminations from one function")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The glued regions fill the outer disc exactly. The magnets are selected by their name, and each is a ring sector
whose angle is the pole angle times the magnet arc:

```python
for lamination, (slots, arc, thickness) in zip(laminations, designs):
    sweep = 2 * math.pi / poles * arc
    sector = sweep / 2 * ((R_rotor + thickness) ** 2 - R_rotor**2)
    magnets = lamination.faces(name="magnet").faces
    print(slots, "slots:", len(lamination.faces), "regions, total", lamination.mass, "disc", math.pi * R_out**2)
    print(len(magnets), "magnets of", magnets[0].mass, "exact", sector)
```

```text
12 slots: 24 regions, total 7853.981633974483 disc 7853.981633974483
8 magnets of 58.315813632260614 exact 58.315813632260536
24 slots: 36 regions, total 7853.981633974478 disc 7853.981633974483
8 magnets of 42.804199905160544 exact 42.80419990516093
36 slots: 48 regions, total 7853.981633974487 disc 7853.981633974483
8 magnets of 29.688050576423624 exact 29.688050576423546
```

# Constraint sketches


[![Jansen&#x27;s walking leg solved by one constraint sketch, the crank angle updated frame by frame](index_files/index_1.gif)<span><em class="px-tag">Example</em> Jansen&#x27;s leg: one sketch, the crank angle updated</span>](../../examples/jansen-linkage.md)
[![A horizontal tank with its dipstick: every mark solved so that 10 % of the volume lies between two marks](index_files/index_2.svg)<span>A dipstick: every mark solved for 10 % of the volume</span>](../../core/constraints/formulas.md)
[![A plate with a fillet and a hole, fully constrained, every constraint shown by its sign](index_files/index_3.svg)<span>A plate, fully constrained, with every constraint shown</span>](../../core/constraints/kinds.md)


A constraint sketch, `px.Sketch`, supports every drawing call of `px.QuickSketch`: lines, arcs, circles and splines
from references, construction elements, offsets, trimming and mirroring (see [Quick sketch](../sketch/index.md)). In
addition, it keeps constraints that turn a rough drawing into an exact one, such as a line that must be horizontal, an
arc that must be tangent, or a hole 8 in diameter and 40 from the center. planex2d solves these constraints, moves
every element as little as they allow, and shows what is still free.

Every dimension has an id, and setting a dimension solves the sketch again, so the sketch becomes a parametric part.
Expressions tie dimensions together as design rules. The same solver also moves mechanisms: given a crank angle, it
returns the position of every joint. The solved sketch exports like any other, as faces, wires, OpenCASCADE shapes and
netgen geometries.

# Drawing with constraints

A constraint sketch draws with the same calls as a [quick sketch](../sketch/index.md): `Move`, `Turn`, `Line`, `Arc`,
`Circle`, `Spline`, the profile tools and `Close`. Three things are added once constraints are involved:

- flags such as `px.Horizontal` in a drawing call constrain the element while it is drawn;
- the references of the drawing calls, such as `tangent=` or `until=`, can become constraints, with
  `auto_constraint=True`;
- where a constraint has several solutions, the drawing decides which one is meant.

```python
import warnings
import planex as px
```

## Flags while drawing

A flag after the numbers of a drawing call adds that constraint to the new element at once, and the sketch is solved.
The example is a rectangle drawn roughly, with a fixed start, horizontal top and bottom and vertical sides (Figure 1).
The solver squares it up and moves every side as little as it can. Its width and height are still free, which leaves
two degrees of freedom.

```python
sk = px.Sketch((0, 0), px.Fix)
sk.Line(40, 1, px.Horizontal, id="bottom")
sk.Line(1, 20, px.Vertical, id="right")
sk.Line(-41, 2, px.Horizontal, id="top")
sk.Close(px.Vertical, id="left")
print(sk.status, sk.dof, "degrees of freedom")
print({i: round(sk.Geometry(i)["angle"], 9) for i in ("bottom", "right", "top", "left")})
```

```text
under 2 degrees of freedom
{'bottom': 0.0, 'right': 90.0, 'top': 180.0, 'left': -90.0}
```

```python
Row((sk, "Drawn roughly, squared up by its flags", {"constraints": True}))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## Helpers, with and without auto_constraint

The references of the drawing calls, such as `until=`, `tangent=`, `perpendicular=` and `center=`, place an element
exactly. By default, that is all they do, and the element is afterwards as free as one drawn by eye. With
`auto_constraint=True`, every reference also becomes the matching constraint.

The example draws the same sketch both ways: a line dropped perpendicular onto a base, a belt tangent to a hub, and a
pin at the end of the base. Then the hub grows from a radius of 1 to 1.8. Without `auto_constraint`, the belt keeps
its place and the grown hub swallows it (Figure 2a). With it, the belt stays tangent, so its distance from the hub's
center equals the new radius (Figure 2b).

```python
def drawing(auto):
    sk = px.Sketch(auto_constraint=auto)
    sk.Move((0, 0)).Line(4, 0, px.Fix, id="base")
    sk.Circle(6, 3, 1, id="hub")
    sk.Constrain("hub.center", px.Fix)
    sk.Constrain("hub", px.Radius, 1, id="r")
    sk.Move((1, 2)).Direction(0, -1).Line("base", perpendicular="base", id="drop")
    sk.Move((0, 3)).Line(tangent="hub", id="belt")
    sk.Circle(0.4, center="base.end", id="pin")
    return sk


plain, auto = drawing(False), drawing(True)
for kind, entries in auto.constraints.items():
    if kind not in ("Fix", "Radius"):
        print(kind, list(entries.values()))
plain["r"] = auto["r"] = 1.8
for name, sk in (("helpers only", plain), ("auto_constraint", auto)):
    print(name, "belt", sk.Measure("hub.center", to="belt")["distance"], "from the hub's center, radius", sk["r"])
```

```text
Coincident ["drop.end", "base", px.Coincident, "belt.end", "hub", px.Coincident, "pin.center", "base.end", px.Coincident]
Perpendicular ["base", "drop", px.Perpendicular]
Tangent ["belt", "hub", px.Tangent]
helpers only belt 1.0 from the hub's center, radius 1.8
auto_constraint belt 1.8000000000000003 from the hub's center, radius 1.8
```

```python
Row((plain, "Helpers only, hub radius 1.8", {"constraints": True}),
    (auto, "auto_constraint, hub radius 1.8", {"constraints": True}),
    caption="The same drawing with helpers only and with auto_constraint, after the hub grew")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

With `auto_constraint`, a constraint that a reference implies but that removes no degree of freedom, because it
already follows from the others, is left out with a warning. In the example, `top` is horizontal by its flag, so
`parallel="base"` adds nothing. A redundant constraint given on purpose stays. See [diagnosis](diagnosis.md) for how
redundant constraints are reported.

```python
sk = px.Sketch(auto_constraint=True)
sk.Move((0, 0)).Line(3, 0, px.Horizontal, id="base")
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    sk.Move((0, 1)).Line(2, px.Horizontal, parallel="base", id="top")
for w in caught:
    print(w.message)
```

```text
auto_constraint: left out "base", "top", px.Parallel, it follows from Horizontal.1, Horizontal.2
```

## Which tangent: the drawing decides

A line tangent to two circles has four solutions: above, below, and two that cross between the circles. The
constraint takes the side from the drawing when it is created and keeps it. In the example, three lines are drawn
roughly (Figure 3a), and each is made tangent to both circles (Figure 3b). When the left circle grows (Figure 3c), all
three lines follow on their sides. They can still slide along themselves, so they are not fully constrained and stay
black.

```python
sk = px.Sketch()
sk.Circle(0, 0, 1.0, id="left")
sk.Circle(4, 0.5, 0.6, px.Fix, id="right")
sk.Constrain("left.center", sk.origin, px.Coincident)
sk.Constrain("left", px.Radius, 1.0, id="r")
sk.Move((-0.3, 1.4)).Line((4.2, 1.3), id="upper")
sk.Move((0.2, -1.3)).Line((4.1, -0.3), id="lower")
sk.Move((0.1, 1.2)).Line((3.6, -0.2), id="cross")
drawn = sk.Copy()
for line in ("upper", "lower", "cross"):
    sk.Constrain(line, "left", px.Tangent)
    sk.Constrain(line, "right", px.Tangent)
tangent = sk.Copy()
sk["r"] = 1.6
for line in ("upper", "lower", "cross"):
    print(line, "distance from the left circle", sk.Measure(line, to="left")["distance"])
```

```text
upper distance from the left circle 0.0
lower distance from the left circle 0.0
cross distance from the left circle 0.0
```

```python
Row((drawn, "Drawn", {"constraints": True}),
    (tangent, "Tangent to both", {"constraints": True}),
    (sk, "Left radius 1.6: all three follow", {"constraints": True}),
    caption="Three tangents keep the side they were drawn on")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

See [Constraints and dimensions](kinds.md) for every kind of constraint, and [Changing dimensions](update.md) for how
the solver follows a change.

# Converting sketches

A part often starts as a quick sketch and needs dimensions later, or it comes from a solid whose face is the starting
point. `copy=True` makes a new sketch from another one or from a face:

- `px.Sketch(quick, copy=True)` turns a quick sketch into a constraint sketch;
- `px.QuickSketch(sketch, copy=True)` turns a constraint sketch into a quick sketch;
- `px.QuickSketch(face, copy=True)` takes over the outline of a face of a solid.

Without `copy=True`, the same calls give an empty sketch on the plane of the object.

```python
import math
import netgen.occ as occ
import planex as px
```

## From a quick sketch to a constraint sketch

The example is a lever 40 long between the centers of its round ends, 12 wide, with a bore of 6 in its right end. It
is drawn as a quick sketch, with each round end continuing the line before it (Figure 1a).

```python
quick = px.QuickSketch((0, -6))
quick.Line(40, id="lower").Arc(6, 180, id="end").Line(40, id="upper").Arc(6, 180, id="back")
quick.Circle(40, 0, 3, id="bore");
```

`px.Sketch(quick, copy=True)` copies the geometry with its ids, names, construction elements and the pen, but no
constraints, because a quick sketch has none. With `auto_constraint=True`, it adds the constraints the drawing shows:
an arc tangent where a chain runs on smoothly, and coincident points where separate elements meet. Here, it finds
the four tangent joints and the closing point of the outline:

```python
lever = px.Sketch(quick, copy=True, auto_constraint=True)
print(lever.status, lever.dof, {kind: list(ids) for kind, ids in lever.constraints.items()})
```

```text
under 7 {'Tangent': ['Tangent.1', 'Tangent.2', 'Tangent.3', 'Tangent.4'], 'Coincident': ['Coincident.1']}
```

The rest are the dimensions of the part: the length and the radius of the ends, the bore, and its place in the right
end. With them, the lever is fully constrained (Figure 1b).

```python
lever.Constrain("lower.start", px.Fix)
lever.Constrain("lower", px.Horizontal)
lever.Constrain("lower", px.Distance, 40, id="L")
lever.Constrain("end", px.Radius, 6, id="R")
lever.Constrain("back", "end", px.Equal)
lever.Constrain("bore", px.Radius, 3, id="r")
lever.Constrain("bore.center", "end.center", px.Coincident)
print(lever.status, lever.dof)
```

```text
full 0
```

```python
Row((quick, "(a) The quick sketch"), (lever, "(b) Converted and dimensioned", {"constraints": True}),
    caption="A lever drawn quickly, then converted into a constraint sketch")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

A new length is now one dimension. The lever 60 long has the area of a slot of 60 × 12 less the bore,
60 · 12 + π 6² − π 3²:

```python
lever["L"] = 60
lever.Update()
print("area", lever.Face().mass, "exact", 60 * 12 + math.pi * 6**2 - math.pi * 3**2)
```

```text
area 804.8230016469245 exact 804.8230016469244
```

Rectangles, polygons, slots, fillets, offsets, patterns and mirrors of the quick sketch arrive as their lines and
arcs, without the constraints that would keep them a rectangle or a slot.

## From a constraint sketch to a quick sketch

`px.QuickSketch(sketch, copy=True)` keeps the solved geometry and drops the constraints, dimensions and expressions.
A quick sketch is faster to draw into, for example for many copies in a study:

```python
frozen = px.QuickSketch(lever, copy=True)
print(type(frozen).__name__, "area", frozen.Face().mass)
```

```text
QuickSketch area 804.8230016469245
```

## From the face of a solid

`px.QuickSketch(face, copy=True)` with a planar OpenCASCADE face gives a sketch on the face's plane with the face's
outline in it, as normal geometry. The example is the top of a block 30 × 20 × 10 with a bore of 8. The sketch has
the block's outline and the circle of the bore, and more elements can be drawn on top of them.

```python
block = occ.Box(occ.Pnt(0, 0, 0), occ.Pnt(30, 20, 10)) - occ.Cylinder(occ.Pnt(15, 10, 0), occ.Z, 4, 10)
top = block.faces.Max(occ.Z)
on_top = px.QuickSketch(top, copy=True)
print("area", on_top.Face().mass, "exact", 30 * 20 - math.pi * 4**2)
```

```text
area 549.7345175425633 exact 549.7345175425633
```

A list of OpenCASCADE wires works the same way, and `px.Sketch(wires, copy=True)` gives a constraint sketch from
them. See [Placing a sketch](../sketch/placement.md) for sketches on the faces of solids and
[Pad and Pocket](../basics/pad-pocket.md) for turning a sketch into a solid.

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/constraints/kinds.md

# Constraints and dimensions

`sk.Constrain(a, b, kind, value, id=...)` adds a constraint between one or two references, read from a to b:
`Constrain("line", "circle", px.Tangent)` makes the line tangent to the circle. A reference can be

- an element by its id, such as `"bottom"`;
- a point of an element, such as `"bottom.start"`, `"bottom.end"`, `"bottom.mid"` or `"fillet.center"`;
- a point made with `Vertex`;
- the sketch's axes `px.H` and `px.V`, or its origin `sk.origin`.

The geometric kinds also work as flags of the drawing calls (see [Drawing with constraints](drawing.md)). The
dimensions take a value and usually an id, so that they can be changed later.

| Kind | Between | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Coincident` | A point and a point, line, circle or spline | The point lies on the other reference |
| `Horizontal`, `Vertical` | A line, or two points | Along `px.H` or `px.V` |
| `Parallel`, `Perpendicular` | Two lines | Parallel, or at a right angle |
| `Tangent` | Two of line, arc, circle and spline | Touching, on the side as drawn |
| `Equal` | Two lines, or two circles and arcs | Equal lengths or radii |
| `Symmetric` | Two points and a line | Mirror images of each other |
| `SymmetricCarriers` | Two elements and a line | The mirror image of one element's line or circle is the other's |
| `Concentric` | Two circles or arcs | One common center |
| `Fix` | A point or an element | Stays where it is |
| `Distance` | A line's length, or points and lines | A dimension |
| `Radius`, `Diameter` | A circle or arc | A dimension |
| `Angle` | Two lines, or a line and an axis | A dimension in degrees |
| `RigidGroup` | Elements | Keep their shape and move as one |

```python
import planex as px
```

## A plate with a hole, all constraints shown

The example is the plate from the [section overview](index.md), with a hole of diameter 10, 15 from the bottom and 20
from the left side. `show_constraints` places a sign next to every constraint: a circle at a coincidence, a square in
a perpendicular corner, `H` and `V`, two short strokes along a tangent, an anchor for a fixed point, and the value of
each dimension with its id (Figure 1a). `show_ends` marks the start of every line and arc in blue and its end in
orange, which is what `.start` and `.end` refer to, and `show_direction` adds arrows (Figure 1b).
`sk.Plot(show_constraints=True)` draws the same with matplotlib. With `backend="plotly"`, the picture is
interactive, and every sign is explained on hover.

```python
sk = px.Sketch(id="plate")
sk.Move(sk.origin, px.Coincident)
sk.Line(37, 2.5, px.Horizontal, id="bottom")
sk.Arc(9, 95, px.Tangent, id="fillet")
sk.Line(-1, 17, px.Vertical, px.Tangent, id="right")
sk.Line(-46, 3, px.Perpendicular, id="top")
sk.Close(px.Perpendicular, id="left")
sk.Constrain("fillet", px.Radius, 10, id="r")
sk.Constrain("bottom.start", "right", px.Distance, 50, id="width")
sk.Constrain("bottom", "top", px.Distance, 30, id="height")

sk.Circle(20, 15, 5, id="hole")
sk.Constrain("hole", px.Diameter, 10, id="d")
sk.Constrain("hole.center", "bottom", px.Distance, 15, id="y_hole")
sk.Constrain("hole.center", "left", px.Distance, 20, id="x_hole")
print(sk.status, sk.dof, sorted(sk.dimensions))
```

```text
full 0 ['d', 'height', 'r', 'width', 'x_hole', 'y_hole']
```

```python
Row((sk, "show_constraints", {"constraints": True}),
    (sk, "show_ends and show_direction",
     {"constraints": {"show_ends": True, "show_direction": True}}),
    caption="A plate with a hole and all its constraints")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## Reference dimensions

A dimension with `reference=True` and no value drives nothing; it only measures. `sk["diagonal"]` is the distance
from the plate's origin to the hole's center in the current solution, and it follows every change.

```python
sk.Constrain(sk.origin, "hole.center", px.Distance, id="diagonal", reference=True)
print("diagonal", sk["diagonal"], "exact", (20**2 + 15**2) ** 0.5)
sk.Update({"x_hole": 30, "y_hole": 10})
print("diagonal", sk["diagonal"], "exact", (30**2 + 10**2) ** 0.5, sk.status)
```

```text
diagonal 25.0 exact 25.0
diagonal 31.622776601683793 exact 31.622776601683793 full
```

## Removing a constraint

`Remove(id)` removes a constraint, and the element it held can move again. Without the hole's diameter, the sketch
has one degree of freedom left.

```python
sk.Remove("d")
print("without d:", sk.status, sk.dof, "degree of freedom")
sk.Constrain("hole", px.Radius, 5, id="d")
print("with d again:", sk.status, sk.dof, "degrees of freedom")
```

```text
without d: under 1 degree of freedom
with d again: full 0 degrees of freedom
```

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/constraints/diagnosis.md

# Fully, under- and over-constrained

A sketch reports how much it can still move. `sk.dof` counts the remaining degrees of freedom, and `sk.status` is
`"full"`, `"under"` or `"over"`. The pictures color each element by its state: green when nothing about it can move,
black when something can, and pink where constraints conflict or repeat. This page shows what each state looks like
and how a sketch is made fully constrained.

```python
import warnings
import numpy as np
import planex as px
```

## Under-constrained

The example is a rectangle drawn with flags only: horizontal, with three right angles, starting at the origin. Its
width and height are free, which leaves two degrees of freedom (Figure 1a). With both as dimensions, it is fully
constrained and green (Figure 1b).

```python
sk = px.Sketch()
sk.Move(sk.origin, px.Coincident).Line(40, 1, px.Horizontal, id="bottom")
sk.Line(1, 20, px.Perpendicular, id="right").Line(-40, 1, px.Perpendicular, id="top")
sk.Close(px.Perpendicular, id="left")
free = sk.Copy()
sk.Constrain("bottom", px.Distance, 40, id="w")
sk.Constrain("bottom", "top", px.Distance, 20, id="h")
print(free.status, free.dof, "->", sk.status, sk.dof)
```

```text
under 2 -> full 0
```

```python
Row((free, f"{free.status}: {free.dof} degrees of freedom", {"constraints": True}),
    (sk, f"{sk.status}: width and height", {"constraints": True}),
    caption="A rectangle under-constrained and fully constrained")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## Redundant constraints

The left and right sides are already parallel because of the right angles. A `Parallel` constraint between them
repeats that. It is consistent and the sketch still solves, so planex2d keeps it, warns, and lists it in
`sk.redundant` together with the constraints it repeats. Its sign turns pink (Figure 2). `status` counts only degrees
of freedom, so it stays `"full"`. `Remove` takes the repetition back.

```python
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    sk.Constrain("right", "left", px.Parallel)
print(caught[0].message)
print(sk.status, sk.redundant)
repeated = sk.Copy()
sk.Remove("Parallel.1")
print(sk.status, sk.redundant)
```

```text
Parallel.1 ("right", "left", px.Parallel) is redundant (consistent) with Perpendicular.2, Perpendicular.3
full ['Perpendicular.2', 'Perpendicular.3', 'Parallel.1']
full []
```

```python
Row((repeated, "Parallel repeats the right angles: pink", {"constraints": True}))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## Over-constrained

A constraint that contradicts the others cannot be enforced. In the example, a diagonal of 50 disagrees with a width
of 40 and a height of 20. planex2d keeps the constraint but suspends it: a `PlanexWarning` names the constraints it
contradicts, the status is `"over"`, and the geometry stays at its last solution. The suspended constraint and the
ones it contradicts are drawn in pink. `Face()` and the exports still work on the last solution, with a warning.

```python
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always", px.PlanexWarning)
    sk.Constrain("bottom.start", "top.start", px.Distance, 50, id="diagonal")
print(caught[0].message)
print(sk.status, sorted(sk.dimensions))
```

```text
"bottom.start", "top.start", px.Distance, 50: no solution, it contradicts the constraints there are (Perpendicular.1, Perpendicular.2, w, h); diagonal is kept but not solved, the sketch is over-constrained
over ['diagonal', 'h', 'w']
```

Every later `Update` tries the suspended constraint again. A rectangle 40 × 30 has a diagonal of exactly 50, so with
the height changed to 30, the diagonal fits and is enforced, and the sketch is fully constrained again. The diagonal
now repeats what the width and the height already fix, so it is redundant, and a warning says so. Removing the
suspended constraint, or one it contradicts, also ends the conflict.

```python
sk["h"] = 30
sk.Update()
print(sk.status, sk.Measure("bottom.start", "top.start")["distance"])
```

```text
full 50.0
```

```text
stderr:
/tmp/ipykernel_834917/2222836129.py:2: PlanexWarning: diagonal ("bottom.start", "top.start", px.Distance, 50) is redundant (consistent) with Perpendicular.1, Perpendicular.2, w, h
  sk.Update()
```

## Strict mode

Exporting an under-constrained sketch is usually a mistake, because the part then has whatever size the drawing
happened to have. `Sketch(mode="strict")` refuses every export while the sketch can still move, and the error states
what is free. Reading remains allowed, including positions, measurements and pictures. Strict mode also turns a
change of branch into an error (see [changing dimensions](update.md)), so an unattended loop never produces a silently
flipped part.

```python
sk = px.Sketch(mode="strict")
sk.Move(sk.origin, px.Coincident).Line(40, 0, px.Horizontal, id="bottom")
sk.Line(0, 20, px.Perpendicular).Line(-40, 0, px.Perpendicular, id="top")
sk.Close(px.Perpendicular)
try:
    sk.Face()
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)
sk.Constrain("bottom", px.Distance, 40, id="w")
sk.Constrain("bottom", "top", px.Distance, 20, id="h")
print(sk.status, sk.Face().mass)
```

```text
Face(): mode='strict' and the sketch is not fully constrained (2 degrees of freedom; free: bottom, Line.1, top, Line.2)
full 800.0
```

## Condition

`sk.condition` states how strongly a small change of the dimensions can move the geometry. A well-posed part, like
this rectangle, stays at a few units. A large value means that some point depends on nearly parallel lines or nearly
tangent circles, so a tiny change of a dimension moves it far. planex2d warns above
`px.config.sensitivity_warning`.

```python
print(f"condition {sk.condition:.3f}")
```

```text
condition 2.864
```

## The Jacobian

`sk.jacobian` is the matrix the solver works with. It has one row per equation and one column per unknown, and
each entry is the derivative of that equation with respect to that unknown at the solved geometry. Rows are labeled
by their source, `(constraint id, row)`, and columns by what they move, `(reference, coordinate)`. The matrix is a
scipy sparse array. `scale` holds the scaling of its columns, and the raw derivatives are `matrix[:, k] / scale[k]`.
The plate from the [section overview](index.md) has eleven unknowns and eleven equations, and every equation involves
only a few of the unknowns (Figure 3).

```python
from scipy.sparse.linalg import spsolve

plate = px.Sketch(id="plate")
plate.Move(plate.origin, px.Coincident)
plate.Line(37, 2.5, px.Horizontal, id="bottom").Arc(9, 95, px.Tangent, id="fillet")
plate.Line(-1, 17, px.Vertical, px.Tangent, id="right")
plate.Line(-46, 3, px.Perpendicular, id="top").Close(px.Perpendicular, id="left")
plate.Constrain("fillet", px.Radius, 10, id="r")
plate.Constrain("bottom.start", "right", px.Distance, 50, id="width")
plate.Constrain("bottom", "top", px.Distance, 30, id="height")

J = plate.jacobian
print(J["shape"], J["matrix"].nnz, "of", J["shape"][0] * J["shape"][1], "entries")
print(J["rows"][:3], "...")
print(J["columns"][:3], "...")
```

```text
(11, 11) 63 of 121 entries
[('Horizontal.1', 0), ('Tangent.1', 0), ('Vertical.1', 0)] ...
[('bottom.end', 'x'), ('bottom.end', 'y'), ('fillet.end', 'x')] ...
```

```python
import io
import html
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from IPython.display import HTML, display
from docs_figures import INK, PLANEX, RED, _figure, _source


def matrix_figure(J, caption):
    A = J["matrix"].toarray()
    count = {}
    for id, _ in J["rows"]:
        count[id] = count.get(id, 0) + 1
    rows = [id if count[id] == 1 else f"{id} {k}" for id, k in J["rows"]]
    columns = [f"{ref} {c}" for ref, c in J["columns"]]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(0.3 * len(columns) + 2.2, 0.3 * len(rows) + 1.6))
    big = np.abs(A).max()
    for i, j in zip(*np.nonzero(A)):
        ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((j - 0.42, i - 0.42), 0.84, 0.84, lw=0,
                                   color=PLANEX if A[i, j] > 0 else RED,
                                   alpha=0.25 + 0.75 * abs(A[i, j]) / big))
    ax.set_xlim(-0.6, A.shape[1] - 0.4)
    ax.set_ylim(A.shape[0] - 0.4, -0.6)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(columns)), columns, rotation=90, fontsize=8, color=INK)
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(rows)), rows, fontsize=8, color=INK)
    ax.set_xticks(np.arange(-0.5, A.shape[1]), minor=True)
    ax.set_yticks(np.arange(-0.5, A.shape[0]), minor=True)
    ax.grid(which="minor", color="#eef1f5", lw=0.6)
    ax.tick_params(which="both", length=0)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    for side in ax.spines.values():
        side.set_color("#e3e8ee")
    fig.tight_layout()
    buffer = io.BytesIO()
    fig.savefig(buffer, format="svg", transparent=True)
    plt.close(fig)
    src = _source(buffer.getvalue(), "svg")
    display(HTML(_figure(f'<div style="width: 46%; margin: 4px auto 8px; text-align: center">'
                         f'<img src="{src}" alt="{html.escape(caption)}" style="width: 100%"></div>', caption)))


matrix_figure(J, "The sk.jacobian of the plate, with positive entries in blue and negative ones in red")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

### What a dimension moves

The equation of a dimension states that the measured length equals the set value, so changing the dimension by one
puts a one on the right-hand side of its row. Solving J dx = e for that row gives how far every unknown moves per unit
of the dimension. For the fillet's radius `r`, the bottom line ends one unit earlier, the right side starts one unit
higher, and the arc's center moves one unit to the left and one up (Figure 4). A finite difference of two `Update`s
gives the same result.

```python
rows, columns = J["rows"], J["columns"]
unit = np.zeros(J["shape"][0])
unit[rows.index(("r", 0))] = 1
dr = J["scale"] * spsolve(J["matrix"].tocsc(), unit)
for (ref, c), d in zip(columns, dr):
    if abs(d) > 1e-12:
        print(f"d {ref}.{c} / dr = {d:+.12f}")

h = 1e-4
up, down = plate.Copy().Update({"r": 10 + h}), plate.Copy().Update({"r": 10 - h})
fd = (up.Location("fillet.center")[1] - down.Location("fillet.center")[1]) / (2 * h)
k = columns.index(("fillet.center", "y"))
print(f"fillet.center.y: Jacobian {dr[k]:.12f}, finite difference {fd:.12f}")
```

```text
d bottom.end.x / dr = -1.000000000000
d fillet.end.y / dr = +1.000000000000
d fillet.center.x / dr = -1.000000000000
d fillet.center.y / dr = +1.000000000000
d fillet.r / dr = +1.000000000000
fillet.center.y: Jacobian 1.000000000000, finite difference 0.999999999944
```

```python
import math
from docs_figures import INK, PLANEX


def arrow(p, d, s, w):
    x, y = p[0], p[1]
    u, v = d[0] * s, d[1] * s
    n = math.hypot(u, v)
    if n < 1e-9:
        return None
    ux, uy = u / n, v / n
    head = min(4 * w, 0.45 * n)
    bx, by = x + ux * (n - head), y + uy * (n - head)
    corners = [(x - uy * w / 2, y + ux * w / 2), (bx - uy * w / 2, by + ux * w / 2),
               (bx - uy * 1.6 * w, by + ux * 1.6 * w), (x + u, y + v),
               (bx + uy * 1.6 * w, by - ux * 1.6 * w), (bx + uy * w / 2, by - ux * w / 2),
               (x + uy * w / 2, y - ux * w / 2)]
    outline = px.QuickSketch().Move(tuple(corners[0]))
    for q in corners[1:]:
        outline.Line(q)
    return outline.Close().Face()


def motion(sk, columns, d, caption, view, s=10, w=0.9):
    moves = {}
    for (ref, c), v in zip(columns, d):
        if c in ("x", "y"):
            moves.setdefault(ref, [0.0, 0.0])["xy".index(c)] = v
    points = [sk.Location(ref) for ref in moves]
    arrows = [arrow(p, m, s, w) for p, m in zip(points, moves.values())]
    return (sk.Face(), caption, {"fills": [(a, PLANEX) for a in arrows if a is not None],
                                 "dots": [p[:2] for p in points], "dot": INK, "names": False,
                                 "view": view})


Row(motion(plate, columns, dr, "How the plate's points move with r, drawn ten times larger", ((-6, 62), (-6, 38))))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

### Free motions

An under-constrained sketch has fewer independent rows than columns. `sk.dof` is the number of columns minus the
rank of J, and the null space of J holds the motions that change no equation. For the rectangle drawn with flags only,
at the top of this page, these are its free width and its free height (Figure 5).

```python
from scipy.linalg import null_space

Jf = free.jacobian
raw = Jf["matrix"].toarray() / Jf["scale"]
print(free.dof, "=", raw.shape[1], "columns -", np.linalg.matrix_rank(raw), "rank")
motions = null_space(raw)
print(motions.shape[1], "free motions")
```

```text
2 = 6 columns - 4 rank
2 free motions
```

```python
cf = Jf["columns"]
pick = [cf.index(("bottom.end", "x")), cf.index(("top.end", "y"))]
basis = motions @ np.linalg.inv(motions[pick, :])
view = ((-6, 52), (-6, 30))
Row(motion(free, cf, basis[:, 0], "Free motion: the width", view, s=8, w=0.8),
    motion(free, cf, basis[:, 1], "Free motion: the height", view, s=8, w=0.8),
    caption="The two free motions of the rectangle drawn with flags only")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

A redundant constraint adds a row but no rank. With the `Parallel` that repeats the right angles, the plate's matrix
has twelve rows but a rank of eleven, and `sk.redundant` names the rows that depend on each other.

```python
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
    plate.Constrain("right", "left", px.Parallel)
Jr = plate.jacobian
print(Jr["shape"], "rank", np.linalg.matrix_rank(Jr["matrix"].toarray()))
print(plate.redundant)
```

```text
(12, 11) rank 11
['Perpendicular.1', 'Perpendicular.2', 'Parallel.1']
```

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/constraints/update.md

# Changing dimensions

`sk["id"] = value` sets one dimension and solves, while `sk.Update({"a": 1, "b": 2})` sets several dimensions and
solves once. The solver starts from the current geometry and moves it as little as it can, so a part keeps the shape
it was drawn in.

```python
import math
import warnings
import planex as px
```

## A parameter study

The example is a bottle in profile, drawn as one half from the axis around to the axis again, with the shoulder as
a spline tangent to the body and the neck (see [splines](splines.md)). Its volume as a solid of revolution follows from
Pappus's theorem as the area of the half times the path of its centroid, 2π x̄. `Update` changes the shoulder radius
in a loop, and the volume follows.

```python
def bottle():
    sk = px.Sketch(id="bottle")
    sk.Move(sk.origin, px.Coincident).Line(30, 2, px.Horizontal, id="bottom")
    sk.Line(1, 50, px.Vertical, id="body")
    sk.Spline([(24, 66), (11, 76)], px.Tangent, id="shoulder")
    sk.Line(0, 14, px.Vertical, px.Tangent, id="neck")
    sk.Line(-10, 0, px.Horizontal, id="lip")
    sk.Constrain("lip.end", px.V, px.Coincident)
    waist = "shoulder.p1"
    sk.Constrain("bottom", px.Distance, 30, id="r")
    sk.Constrain("body", px.Distance, 50, id="h")
    sk.Constrain("neck", px.V, px.Distance, 10, id="r_neck")
    sk.Constrain("neck", px.Distance, 14)
    sk.Constrain("neck.start", px.H, px.Distance, 76, id="z_neck")
    sk.Constrain(waist, px.V, px.Distance, 27, id="r_shoulder")
    sk.Constrain(waist, px.H, px.Distance, 64, id="z_shoulder")
    sk.Close(id="axis")
    return sk


def volume(sk):
    half = sk.Face()
    return half.mass * 2 * math.pi * half.center[0]


sk = bottle()
print(sk.status, f"volume {volume(sk) / 1000:.2f} cm³")
radii = [20, 22, 24, 26, 27, 28]
volumes = [volume(sk.Update({"r_shoulder": r})) / 1000 for r in radii]
print([f"{v:.2f}" for v in volumes])
```

```text
full volume 195.89 cm³
['184.60', '187.43', '190.50', '193.98', '195.89', '197.93']
```

```python
narrow = sk.Update({"r_shoulder": 20}).Copy()
wide = sk.Update({"r_shoulder": 28}).Copy()
Row((narrow, "r_shoulder 20", {"constraints": True}),
    (wide, "r_shoulder 28", {"constraints": True}), caption="The bottle at two shoulder radii")
Chart("Shoulder radius", "Volume [cm³]", dots={"Update, then Pappus": (radii, volumes)},
      title="The volume over the shoulder radius")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## Walking in steps

A large change can turn a part around: a link swings through, or an arc flips. `Update` therefore halves every step
that would turn a line or an arc by more than 30°, and follows the branch the sketch was drawn in. `steps=` requests
more steps from the start.

## Branch changes

If even the smallest step turns something around, the change is a branch change. For example, a line pulled back
through its fixed start points the other way afterwards. A branch change produces a warning. With
`error_on_branch_change=True`, which is on in [strict mode](diagnosis.md), it is an error, and nothing changes.

```python
def pulled(**options):
    sk = px.Sketch(**options)
    sk.Move((0.5, 0), px.Fix).Line(0.5, 0, id="l")
    sk.Constrain("l", px.Horizontal)
    sk.Constrain("l.end", px.V, px.Distance, 1, id="x")
    return sk


with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    pulled().Update({"x": 0.1})
print(caught[0].message)

strict = pulled(error_on_branch_change=True)
try:
    strict.Update({"x": 0.1})
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)
print("unchanged:", strict["x"], strict.Location("l.end"))
```

```text
Update(x = 0.1): l turned round (180 degrees in one smallest step): the sketch leaves the branch it was drawn in
Update(x = 0.1): l turned round (180 degrees in one smallest step): the sketch leaves the branch it was drawn in; nothing changed (error_on_branch_change)
unchanged: 1.0 (1.0, 0.0)
```

---

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/constraints/expressions.md

# Expressions: design rules

A drawing is a set of numbers, and a design is a set of rules between them. A plate is three fifths as tall as it is
wide, a connecting rod is three and a half cranks long, or a duct keeps its cross-section while its shape changes.
`sk.Expression("height = 0.6*width")` adds such a rule: an equation between dimensions and measures of the solved
geometry, solved together with every other constraint. When one number changes, everything that depends on it
follows, and when the rules ask for something impossible, the sketch says so.

```python
import math
import warnings
import numpy as np
import planex as px
```

## One number drives the family

The example is a mounting plate with two bolt holes. Only the width is a number, and every other size is a rule. The
height is 0.6 of the width, the bolt diameter is a twelfth of it, and the edge distance is one and a half bolt
diameters, the usual rule for bolted plates. The holes sit at the edge distance from the sides and the bottom.

```python
plate = px.Sketch(id="plate")
plate.Move(plate.origin, px.Coincident).Line(80, 0, px.Horizontal, id="bottom")
plate.Line(0, 50, px.Perpendicular, id="right").Line(-80, 0, px.Perpendicular, id="top")
plate.Close(px.Perpendicular, id="left")
plate.Constrain("bottom", px.Distance, 80, id="width")
plate.Constrain("left", px.Distance, 50, id="height")
plate.Circle(10, 10, 3, id="hole L").Circle(70, 10, 3, id="hole R")
plate.Constrain("hole L", px.Diameter, 6, id="d")
plate.Constrain("hole L", "hole R", px.Equal)
plate.Constrain("hole L.center", "left", px.Distance, 10, id="e")
plate.Constrain("hole R.center", "right", px.Distance, 10, id="e right")
plate.Constrain("hole L.center", "bottom", px.Distance, 10, id="e bottom")
plate.Constrain("hole L.center", "hole R.center", px.Horizontal)

for rule in ("height = 0.6*width", "d = width/12", "e = 1.5*d", "e right = e", "e bottom = e"):
    plate.Expression(rule)
print(plate.status, plate.dof)
for id, rule in plate.expressions.items():
    print(id, rule)
```

```text
full 0
Expression.1 height = 0.6*width
Expression.2 d = width/12
Expression.3 e = 1.5*d
Expression.4 e right = e
Expression.5 e bottom = e
```

A sweep of the width takes one `Update` per size, and the rules hold exactly at every step. A driven dimension can
no longer be set directly: setting it is refused, and the error names the rule that drives it.

```python
family = []
worst = 0.0
for width in (60, 80, 100, 120):
    plate.Update({"width": width})
    W, H, d, e = (plate[k] for k in ("width", "height", "d", "e"))
    worst = max(worst, abs(H - 0.6 * W), abs(d - W / 12), abs(e - 1.5 * d), abs(plate["e right"] - e))
    family.append(plate.Copy())
print("largest deviation from the rules:", worst)
try:
    plate["height"] = 70
except ValueError as err:
    print(err)
```

```text
largest deviation from the rules: 7.105427357601002e-15
height = 70: height is driven by Expression.1 (height = 0.6*width); remove the expression to set it
```

```python
view = ((-4, 124), (-4, 76))
Row(*((p.Face(), f"width {p['width']:.0f}, holes {p['d']:.2f}", {"view": view}) for p in family),
    caption="One rule set, four widths")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## Equations, not assignments

A rectangular duct must have a cross-section of 600 and, for its pressure drop, a hydraulic diameter 4A/P of 20.
Neither the width nor the height is given. Both sides are reference dimensions, which measure and drive nothing, and
the two rules are plain equations. The solver finds the rectangle, and the closed form is the pair of roots of
t² − (2A/Dh) t + A = 0.

```python
duct = px.Sketch(id="duct")
duct.Move(duct.origin, px.Coincident).Line(40, 0, px.Horizontal, id="floor")
duct.Line(0, 15, px.Perpendicular, id="wall").Line(-40, 0, px.Perpendicular, id="roof")
duct.Close(px.Perpendicular, id="back")
duct.Constrain("floor", px.Distance, id="w", reference=True)
duct.Constrain("back", px.Distance, id="h", reference=True)
duct.Expression("w*h = 600", id="area")
duct.Expression("2*w*h/(w + h) = 20", id="Dh")

A, Dh = 600.0, 20.0
s = 2 * A / Dh
print(duct.status, duct.dof)
print("w", duct["w"], "exact", (s + math.sqrt(s * s - 4 * A)) / 2)
print("h", duct["h"], "exact", (s - math.sqrt(s * s - 4 * A)) / 2)
```

```text
full 0
w 47.32050807568877 exact 47.32050807568878
h 12.679491924311227 exact 12.679491924311225
```

To keep the area but free the shape, the rule for the hydraulic diameter is removed and the floor gets a driving
length. The height then follows the hyperbola h = A/w through a sweep of the width.

```python
duct.RemoveExpression("Dh")
duct.Constrain("floor", px.Distance, duct["w"], id="width")
widths = np.linspace(20, 60, 41)
heights = np.array([duct.Update({"width": w})["h"] for w in widths])
print("largest |h - A/w| over the sweep:", np.max(np.abs(heights - A / widths)))
```

```text
largest |h - A/w| over the sweep: 3.552713678800501e-15
```

```python
Chart("w", "h", lines={"A/w": (list(widths), list(A / widths))},
      dots={"Solved": (list(widths[::4]), list(heights[::4]))},
      title="The height over the width at a constant area of 600")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## Measures of the geometry in a rule

A rule can refer to the solved geometry itself. `brace.length` is the length of the line `brace`, not a dimension of
the sketch. planex2d adds it as a reference dimension, drawn in brackets, and solves it with the rest. In the example,
the sloped edge of a triangular gusset is a quarter longer than its base, so its rise is three quarters of the
base.

```python
gusset = px.Sketch(id="gusset")
gusset.Move(gusset.origin, px.Fix).Line(120, 0, px.Horizontal, id="base")
gusset.Line(-120, 60, id="brace").Close(px.Vertical, id="rise")
gusset.Constrain("base", px.Distance, 120, id="b")
gusset.Expression("brace.length = 1.25*b")
print(gusset.status, gusset.dof, "rise", gusset.Geometry("rise")["length"], "0.75 b =", 0.75 * gusset["b"])
```

```text
full 0 rise 90.0 0.75 b = 90.0
```

```python
Row((gusset, "brace.length = 1.25*b", {"constraints": True}))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## A mechanism from rules

The crank train of an engine follows from three rules. The crank is half the stroke, the connecting rod is three and
a half cranks long, and the piston runs on the cylinder's axis. Only the stroke of 80 and the crank angle `theta` are
numbers. Turning the crank is an `Update` of `theta`, and the piston follows the textbook formula
x(θ) = r cos θ + √(l² − r² sin² θ) at every angle.

```python
engine = px.Sketch(id="engine")
engine.Move((0, -30), px.Fix).Line(80, 0, px.Horizontal, id="gauge", construction=True)
engine.Constrain("gauge", px.Distance, 80, id="stroke")
engine.Move(engine.origin, px.Coincident).Line(30, 20, id="crank").Line(130, -20, id="rod")
engine.Constrain("rod.end", px.H, px.Coincident)
engine.Constrain("crank", px.Distance, 40, id="r")
engine.Constrain("rod", px.Distance, 140, id="l")
engine.Constrain(px.H, "crank", px.Angle, 30, id="theta")
engine.Expression("r = stroke/2")
engine.Expression("l = 3.5*r")

r, l = engine["r"], engine["l"]
angles, piston = [], []
for theta in range(30, 391, 5):
    a = (theta + 180) % 360 - 180
    angles.append(a)
    piston.append(engine.Update({"theta": a}).Location("rod.end")[0])
exact = [r * math.cos(math.radians(a)) + math.sqrt(l**2 - (r * math.sin(math.radians(a))) ** 2) for a in angles]
print(engine.status, "r", r, "l", l, "largest |x - formula|", max(abs(p - e) for p, e in zip(piston, exact)))
```

```text
full r 40.0 l 140.0 largest |x - formula| 5.684341886080802e-14
```

A long-stroke engine is a single number away. With a stroke of 96, the crank and the rod follow their rules, and the
piston's travel between its dead centers is exactly the new stroke.

```python
engine.Update({"stroke": 96, "theta": 0})
top = engine.Location("rod.end")[0]
bottom = engine.Update({"theta": 180}, steps=36).Location("rod.end")[0]
print("r", engine["r"], "l", engine["l"], "travel", abs(top - bottom))
```

```text
r 48.0 l 168.0 travel 96.0
```

```python
order = sorted(range(len(angles)), key=lambda k: angles[k])
Chart("Crank angle θ [°]", "Piston x", lines={"r cos θ + √(l² − r² sin² θ)": ([angles[k] for k in order], [exact[k] for k in order])},
      dots={"The sketch": ([angles[k] for k in order][::3], [piston[k] for k in order][::3])},
      title="The piston over a full turn, stroke 80")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## Guard rails

Rules can repeat each other, misspell a name or ask for the impossible, and the sketch explains the problem in
words.

```python
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    plate.Expression("width = height/0.6")
print(caught[0].message)
plate.RemoveExpression(list(plate.expressions)[-1])
for text in ("height = 0.6*widht", "sqrt(d - width) = 1"):
    try:
        plate.Expression(text)
    except ValueError as err:
        print(err)
```

```text
Expression.6 (width = height/0.6) is redundant (consistent) with Expression.1
Expression 'height = 0.6*widht': unknown id 'widht' (did you mean 'width'?)
Expression 'sqrt(d - width) = 1': sqrt of a negative number (-110)
```

## What an expression can use

| | |
|---|---|
| **Dimensions** | Every dimension by its id, including reference dimensions |
| **Measures** | `line.length`, `line.angle` (its direction in degrees), `arc.r`, `circle.r`, `arc.sweep` (degrees), `point.h`, `point.v` (as in `"rod.end.h"`) |
| **Arithmetic** | `+ - * /`, `^` or `**`, and brackets |
| **Functions** | `sqrt`, `abs`, `min`, `max`, `sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `asin`, `acos`, `atan2`, with angles in degrees |
| **Constants and units** | `pi`, and `mm`, `cm`, `m`, `um`, `inch` and `mil` as the planex2d unit factors, for sketches drawn in meters |

An id cannot contain the operators. `sk.expressions` lists the rules, and `RemoveExpression(id)` removes one. An
expression is read once, in Python, into a small tree that the solver evaluates and differentiates in C++. See
[belt drives solved from the length of their belt](../../examples/belt-drives.md) for what rules can do with the
geometry itself, and [a dipstick for a tank](formulas.md) for a handbook formula without a closed-form inverse, solved
once per mark.

---

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/constraints/formulas.md

# Formulas: a dipstick for a tank

A horizontal cylindrical tank holds 10 % of its volume below a height that no formula gives: the area of a circular
segment of height h is

A(h) = r² acos((r − h)/r) − (r − h) √(2rh − h²),

and it cannot be solved for h, which is why tank makers print tables. In a planex2d sketch, the formula itself is the
rule. A mark is a horizontal chord with both ends on the tank's shell, and one `Expression` states that the segment
below it holds its share of the circle. The solver finds every mark at once, and the dimensions of the tank remain
free to change.

```python
import math
import planex as px
```

## One rule per mark

The tank has a diameter of 2 m and is 5 m long. Its section is sketched in millimeters with the bottom of the shell
at the sketch's origin and the center on the vertical axis, so the height of a mark above the bottom is simply the
v coordinate of its start, `mark1.start.v`. The marks are drawn evenly spaced, by eye, and each gets the formula as its
rule: segment area = k/10 of π r². Expressions take angles in degrees, so `acos` is turned into radians with
`pi/180`.

```python
r, length = 1000, 5000
segment = "r^2*acos((r - {h})/r)*pi/180 - (r - {h})*sqrt(2*r*{h} - {h}^2)"

tank = px.Sketch(id="tank")
tank.Circle(0, r, r, id="shell")
tank.Constrain(tank.origin, "shell", px.Coincident)
tank.Constrain("shell.center", px.V, px.Coincident)
tank.Constrain("shell", px.Radius, r, id="r")
for k in range(1, 10):
    tank.Move((-r, k * r / 5)).Line(2 * r, 0, px.Horizontal, id=f"mark{k}")
    tank.Constrain(f"mark{k}.start", "shell", px.Coincident)
    tank.Constrain(f"mark{k}.end", "shell", px.Coincident)
    tank.Expression(segment.format(h=f"mark{k}.start.v") + f" = {k / 10}*pi*r^2")
print(tank.status, tank.dof)
```

```text
full 0
```

Marks at equal steps of height would be far off, because the bands between them hold from 5.2 % of the volume at
the bottom to 12.6 % in the middle (Figure 1a). The solved marks crowd together where the tank is wide and spread out
near the bottom and the top, and every band holds 10 % (Figure 1b).

```python
view = ((-1.15 * r, 1.15 * r), (-0.08 * r, 2.08 * r))
disc = px.QuickSketch().Circle(0, r, r).Face()
cut = px.Line((-2 * r, r / 5), (2 * r, r / 5))
for k in range(2, 10):
    cut = cut + px.Line((-2 * r, k * r / 5), (2 * r, k * r / 5))
even = sorted(disc.Split(cut), key=lambda b: b.bounding_box[0][1])
labels = [(f"{100 * b.mass / (math.pi * r * r):.1f} %", (0, (k + 0.5) * r / 5))
          for k, b in enumerate(even)]
solved, opt = section(tank, view)
Row((disc, "Marks at equal steps of height",
     {"fills": [(b, SHADES[k % 2]) for k, b in enumerate(even)], "labels": labels,
      "fill": False, "names": False, "view": view}),
    (solved, "The solved marks: 10 % each", opt),
    caption="A tank section with marks at equal steps and at equal volumes")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## Checks

Three checks follow, none of which is part of the rules. Each solved height is compared with a bisection of the
formula in plain Python. The 50 % mark lies on the axis, and the marks are symmetric, so h_k + h_(10−k) = 2r.
Finally, the exact Boolean operations of planex2d measure the result independently of the formula: the disc split by
the nine solved chords gives ten bands, each a tenth of π r².

```python
def area(h, r):
    return r * r * math.acos((r - h) / r) - (r - h) * math.sqrt(2 * r * h - h * h)


def bisect(target, r):
    lo, hi = 0.0, 2.0 * r
    for _ in range(80):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        lo, hi = (mid, hi) if area(mid, r) < target else (lo, mid)
    return (lo + hi) / 2


heights = [tank.Location(f"mark{k}.start")[1] for k in range(1, 10)]
for k, h in enumerate(heights, 1):
    exact = bisect(k / 10 * math.pi * r**2, r)
    print(f"{10 * k:3d} %  h {h:17.12f}, bisection {exact:17.12f}, {h - exact:.1e}")
print("50 % mark - r:", heights[4] - r)
print("symmetry:", max(abs(heights[k] + heights[8 - k] - 2 * r) for k in range(9)))

marks = px.Unify([tank.Edge(f"mark{k}") for k in range(1, 10)])
bands = px.Circle((0, r), r).Face().Split(marks)
share = [b.mass / (math.pi * r**2) for b in bands]
print(len(bands), "bands, largest |share - 0.1|:", max(abs(s - 0.1) for s in share))
```

```text
 10 %  h  312.951173867459, bisection  312.951173867459, -5.7e-14
 20 %  h  508.138167236290, bisection  508.138167236290, 0.0e+00
 30 %  h  680.308490209496, bisection  680.308490209496, -3.4e-13
 40 %  h  842.263806199984, bisection  842.263806199984, -3.4e-13
 50 %  h 1000.000000000000, bisection 1000.000000000000, 1.1e-13
 60 %  h 1157.736193800016, bisection 1157.736193800016, -2.3e-13
 70 %  h 1319.691509790504, bisection 1319.691509790503, 2.3e-13
 80 %  h 1491.861832763710, bisection 1491.861832763710, 0.0e+00
 90 %  h 1687.048826132540, bisection 1687.048826132540, -4.5e-13
50 % mark - r: -1.1368683772161603e-13
symmetry: 9.094947017729282e-13
10 bands, largest |share - 0.1|: 2.498001805406602e-16
```

## The dipstick

The tank is 5 m long, so every band holds a tenth of π r² times the length. The dipstick stands next to the tank at
the same scale, with its foot on the bottom of the shell. It has a long tick at every solved mark, with the volume
below it in liters on one side and its height in millimeters on the other, and a short tick every 100 mm. The chart
shows why the marks cannot be spaced evenly. The fill height over the volume is the handbook formula turned around:
steep at the bottom and the top, and flat in the middle, where a liter adds the least height.

```python
disc, opt = dipstick(tank, length)
Row((disc, "The tank and its dipstick, 10 % between two marks", opt))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

```python
H = [2 * r * j / 400 for j in range(401)]
V = [area(h, r) * length / 1e6 for h in H]
full = math.pi * r * r * length / 1e6
Chart("Volume [L]", "Fill height [mm]",
      lines={"Handbook formula": (V, H), "A box of the same volume": ([0, full], [0, 2 * r])},
      dots={"The solved marks": ([k / 10 * full for k in range(1, 10)], heights)},
      title="The fill height over the volume, tank 2 m by 5 m")
```
