```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

### Thermal: the hottest spot of a cold plate

The example is a cold plate of 120 × 80 with four cooling channels of diameter 10. One channel is drawn at (a, b) and
mirrored about both axes, so that the copies follow it. Under a uniform heat load, a quick proxy for the hottest spot
is the point farthest from every channel, at the end of the longest heat path. `HotSpot` measures that distance on a
grid of n × n points, and with `plot=True` it returns all of them. An odd n puts the corners, the center and the edge
midpoints on the grid, which is where the farthest point of this symmetric layout lies, so here the grid's maximum is
exact.

```python
cp = px.Sketch(id="cold plate")
cp.Move((-60, -40), px.Fix).Rectangle(120, 80, id="outline")
cp.Constrain("outline.Line.1", px.Horizontal)
cp.Constrain("outline.Line.1", px.Distance, 120, id="width")
cp.Constrain("outline.Line.2", px.Distance, 80, id="height")
cp.Circle(20, 12, 5, id="channel", name="channel")
cp.Constrain("channel", px.Diameter, 10)
cp.Constrain("channel.center", px.V, px.Distance, 20, id="a")
cp.Constrain("channel.center", px.H, px.Distance, 12, id="b")
cp.Mirrored(["channel"], px.V)
cp.Mirrored(["channel", "Mirrored.1.channel"], px.H)


def HotSpot(channels="channel", n=41):
    def hot_spot(obj, plot=False, **_):
        part = obj.Face() if isinstance(obj, px.Sketch) else obj
        cooled = px.Compound(px.Wires(part.edges(name=channels)))
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = part.bounding_box
        x, y = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(x0, x1, n), np.linspace(y0, y1, n))
        points = np.column_stack([x.ravel(), y.ravel()])
        points = points[part.Contains(points)]
        values = cooled.Distance(points)
        far = values.argmax()
        if not plot:
            return values[far]
        return {"points": points, "values": values, "value": values[far],
                "label": "distance to a channel", "marks": [(tuple(points[far]), "hot")]}

    return hot_spot


cp.Measure(HotSpot(), id="hot spot")
guess = cp.Face()
exact = max(math.dist(c, (20, 12)) for c in [(0, 0), (60, 0), (0, 40), (60, 40)]) - 5
print("first guess", cp.measures["hot spot"], "exact", exact)
```

```text
first guess 43.826222462934815 exact 43.82622246293481
```

Stored on the sketch, the check serves as an objective for SciPy. The optimizer moves the channels through the
dimensions `a` and `b` and reads the stored measurement after every `Update`. It ends where every channel sits in the
middle of its quarter of the plate, a = 30 and b = 20, the known optimum, and the longest heat path drops by 29 %
(Figure 6).

```python
def objective(ab):
    return cp.Update({"a": ab[0], "b": ab[1]}).measures["hot spot"]


best = minimize(objective, [20, 12], method="Nelder-Mead", options={"xatol": 1e-6, "fatol": 1e-9})
optimum = math.hypot(30, 20) - 5
print("a", best.x[0], "b", best.x[1], "after", best.nfev, "evaluations")
print("hot spot", best.fun, "exact", optimum, "shorter by", round(100 * (1 - best.fun / exact)), "%")
```

```text
a 30.000000016029325 b 20.000000000498638 after 149 evaluations
hot spot 31.055512768253692 exact 31.055512754639892 shorter by 29 %
```

```python
heat = {"field": HotSpot(n=81), "cmap": MAP.reversed()}
Row((guess, f"First guess: {exact:.1f} to the farthest point", heat),
    (cp.Face(), f"Optimized by scipy: {optimum:.1f}", heat),
    caption="The distance to the nearest channel, before and after the optimization")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The checks need no registration and no plug-in interface. Put them in a module and give them parameters, as
`HotSpot` has, and they work everywhere the built-in ones do: stored on sketches, in sweeps, in optimizers and as
maps. A check can also call a field solver. The [field solvers page](../../integrations/netgen/field-solvers.md) has
netgen mesh the plate and NGSolve compute its temperature and the stress at a hole by finite elements. The
[SciPy page](../../integrations/scipy.md) optimizes a plate with two power modules on it, fits a sketch to measured
points and solves for the dimension that meets a requirement.

## Sections in torsion and flow

`pm.TorsionConstant()` has NGSolve solve for the warping function of a cross-section, holes included, and integrates
the torsion constant J. The example is a tube with an outer radius of 25 and a wall of 3. For a tube, J is the polar
moment π/2 (R⁴ − r⁴) (Figure 7a). Slit lengthwise by a cut 2 wide (Figure 7b), the tube keeps almost all of its area
but loses almost all of its torsional stiffness: J drops to that of a thin open section, about s t³/3 for the length
s of its midline and the wall t. `pm.HydraulicDiameter()` is 4A/P, which for an annular gap is exactly the outer minus
the inner diameter.

```python
tube = px.Circle((0, 0), 25).Face() - px.Circle((0, 0), 22).Face()
slit = tube - px.QuickSketch((21, -1)).Rectangle(5, 2).Face()

J = tube.Measure(pm.TorsionConstant())
J_slit = slit.Measure(pm.TorsionConstant())
s, t = math.pi * (25 + 22) - 2, 3
print("tube: J", J, "exact", math.pi / 2 * (25**4 - 22**4))
print("slit: J", J_slit, "thin-walled", s * t**3 / 3)
print("the slit keeps", slit.mass / tube.mass, "of the area and", J_slit / J, "of J")
print("hydraulic diameter", tube.Measure(pm.HydraulicDiameter()), "exact", 50 - 44)
```

```text
tube: J 245623.84396350075 exact 245623.85082459118
slit: J 1294.4559949603376 thin-walled 1310.8936924684826
the slit keeps 0.9864507905037337 of the area and 0.005270074655914478 of J
hydraulic diameter 6.000000000000003 exact 6
```

```python
Row((tube, "A tube: J = π/2 (R⁴ − r⁴)"),
    (slit, f"Slit: 1/{J / J_slit:.0f} of the tube's J"), caption="A tube and a slit tube in torsion")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## How far apart two curves are

The Hausdorff distance is the largest distance from a point of one curve to the other, in either direction. It shows
how far a polygon, a fit or a tool path strays from the exact curve. The first example is a circle of radius 30 and
the regular 64-gon that a CAM system might cut instead. They differ by the sagitta R (1 − cos(π/64)), in the middle of
each side (Figure 8a). The second is a free-form cam and the polyline through its `Polylines(0.05)` points, which
stays within the requested 0.05 (Figure 8b). The lenses magnify the largest gap.

```python
circle = px.Circle((0, 0), 30)
turns = [2 * math.pi * k / 64 for k in range(64)]
polygon = px.FromPolyline([(30 * math.cos(a), 30 * math.sin(a)) for a in turns], closed=True)
print("circle to 64-gon", circle.Hausdorff(polygon), "exact", 30 * (1 - math.cos(math.pi / 64)))

cam = px.Spline([(30, 0), (12, 24), (-14, 22), (-26, 2), (-12, -22), (14, -20)], periodic=True)
path = px.FromPolyline(cam.Polylines(0.05)[0], closed=True)
print("cam to its", len(path.edges), "segments", cam.Hausdorff(path))
```

```text
circle to 64-gon 0.03613631384483469 exact 0.03613631384482785
cam to its 164 segments 0.013402827710692363
```

```python
def widest(curve, other):
    samples = curve.Polylines(1e-4)[0]
    return tuple(samples[other.Distance(samples).argmax()])


def lens(spot, at, R_lens, half, other):
    near = other.ClosestPoint(spot)
    return {"spot": spot, "r": 2.2, "at": at, "R": R_lens, "half": half,
            "points": [spot, (near[0], near[1])]}


gap = widest(circle, polygon)
worst = widest(cam, path)
Row((polygon, "A circle and the 64-gon",
     {"fill": False, "highlight": circle.edges,
      "zoom": lens(gap, (-4, 0), 17, 0.12, polygon)}),
    (path, f"A cam and its {len(path.edges)} segments",
     {"fill": False, "highlight": cam.edges,
      "zoom": lens(worst, (-2, 2), 14, 0.05, path)}),
    caption="Hausdorff distances: a circle and a polygon, a cam and its polyline")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **A measurement** | `f(obj, **params)` returns a value; a drawable one returns `{"points", "values", "label", "value", "marks"}` for `f(obj, plot=True)` |
| **Using it** | `obj.Measure(f)`; stored with `sketch.Measure(f, id=...)`, read with `sketch.measures`, removed with `RemoveMeasure(id)`; drawn with `px.PlotField(f, obj, samples=n)`, or on the edges with `on="edges"` |
| **planex.measurements** | `MinThickness`, `MaxThickness` (`method="ball"` or `"ray"`, `samples`, `ignore_corners`), `Clearance(a, b)`, `Hausdorff(a, b)`, `HydraulicDiameter`, `TorsionConstant(order, maxh)` |
| **Ids** | `obj.id`, and the `id` of every element, vertex and face; `id=` on the calls that create objects; `px.Find(id)`, `px.Plot(id)` |
| **Selecting** | `obj(...)`, `sketch(...)`, `obj.edges(...)`, `.faces(...)`, `.vertices(...)` by ids, `name=`, `kind=` and `near=`; conditions such as `[(px.x > 0) & (px.v < 5)]`; `Min`, `Max`, `Sorted`; `.faces`, `.edges`, `.outline`; points such as `"Arc.5.center"`, `.start`, `.end`, `.mid` |
| **Corners** | `vertex.angle` (inside the face, up to 360°), `vertex.radius` (of the smallest arc ending there) |

See the [KiCad page](../../integrations/kicad.md) for a check of the copper clearance of a whole board, net by net.

---

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/files.md

# Files

planex2d reads and writes KiCad boards and gmsh `.geo` files itself, and the other formats go through a package of
their own. Each section names the package it needs. A function whose package is missing says so when it is called,
so planex2d itself installs without any of them.

| Format | Read | Write | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| DXF | `px.FromDXF` | `WriteDXF` | `ezdxf` |
| STEP, BREP (IGES: read) | `px.FromOCC(path)` | `WriteStep`, `WriteBrep` | OpenCASCADE through `netgen.occ` (`netgen-mesher`, which brings `netgen-occt`) |
| SVG | | `ToSVG` (the picture as text) | Nothing |
| shapely geometry | `px.FromShapely` | `px.ToShapely` | `shapely` |
| KiCad boards | `px.FromKiCad` | `px.WriteKiCad` | Nothing for `.kicad_pcb`; KiCad 10 (`kicad-cli`) for boards of other programs |
| gmsh `.geo` | | `WriteGeo` | Nothing to write it; gmsh to mesh it |

```python
import math
import planex as px
```

## DXF

DXF needs `ezdxf` (`pip install ezdxf`). The lines, arcs, circles, polylines with bulges, splines and ellipses of a
CAD drawing become planex2d edges, and a full circle becomes one circle edge. The layer becomes the edge name, and the
layer color becomes its `col`. `FromDXF` returns a list of wires, one per chain, and `px.Face` builds the face from
them.

The example is a cover plate of 120 × 80 with a window slot of 50 × 30 and four screw holes of diameter 5.5, drawn in
one sketch with its edges named. Written to DXF and read back, it keeps its geometry and its edge names, which travel
as layers (Figure 1).

```python
import ezdxf

s = px.QuickSketch().RectangleC(120, 80, name="outline")
s.Move((-25, 0)).Slot(50, 30, name="window")
for x in (-52, 52):
    for y in (-32, 32):
        s.Circle(x, y, 2.75, name="screw hole")
face = s.Face()
face.WriteDXF("cover.dxf")
back = px.Face(px.FromDXF("cover.dxf"))
print("area difference", back.mass - face.mass)
print(sorted({e.name for e in back.edges}))
```

```text
area difference 0.0
['outline', 'screw hole', 'window']
```

```python
Row((face, "Written"), (back, "Read back: the edges named window in cyan", {"highlight": list(back.edges(name="window"))}),
    caption="A cover plate written to DXF and read back")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

### A gasket drawing

The example is a gasket drawing made with ezdxf, as another CAD program would write it: an outer diameter of 120 and
a bore of 60 on a blue layer, six holes of diameter 9 on a red one, and the bolt circle of diameter 95 on a green
center line layer that is not part of the part.

```python
doc = ezdxf.new()
doc.layers.add("outline", color=5)
doc.layers.add("holes", color=1)
doc.layers.add("centerlines", color=3)
msp = doc.modelspace()
msp.add_circle((0, 0), 60, dxfattribs={"layer": "outline"})
msp.add_circle((0, 0), 30, dxfattribs={"layer": "outline"})
msp.add_circle((0, 0), 47.5, dxfattribs={"layer": "centerlines"})
for k in range(6):
    a = 2 * math.pi * k / 6
    msp.add_circle((47.5 * math.cos(a), 47.5 * math.sin(a)), 4.5, dxfattribs={"layer": "holes"})
doc.saveas("gasket.dxf")
```

`layers` reads only the outline and the holes. Each edge takes its layer's color, and the bolt circle, which is left
out, is shown dashed (Figure 2).

```python
gasket = px.Face(px.FromDXF("gasket.dxf", layers=["outline", "holes"]))
print(sorted({e.name for e in gasket.edges}))
```

```text
['holes', 'outline']
```

```python
left_out = px.Circle((0, 0), 47.5)
Row((gasket, "Outline and holes, in their layers' colors", {"colors": True, "dashed": [left_out]}),
    caption="A gasket read from two of its three layers")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

```python
print("area", gasket.mass, "exact", math.pi / 4 * (120**2 - 60**2 - 6 * 9**2))
```

```text
area 8100.596657281283 exact 8100.596657281281
```

### Polylines with arcs

DXF draws arcs in polylines as bulges. The example is a slot of width 10 along a spine of 40, drawn as one closed
polyline, where a bulge of 1 is a half circle (Figure 3).

```python
doc = ezdxf.new()
points = [(0, 0, 0), (40, 0, 1), (40, 10, 0), (0, 10, 1)]
doc.modelspace().add_lwpolyline(points, format="xyb", close=True)
doc.saveas("slot.dxf")
slot = px.Face(px.FromDXF("slot.dxf"))
```

```python
Row((slot, "A slot from one polyline", {"marks": Vertices(slot)}), caption="A polyline with bulges")
```

```python
print("area", slot.mass, "exact", 40 * 10 + math.pi * 25)
```

### Units

planex2d has no unit of its own (see [Units](basics/units.md)), and `FromDXF` returns meters. It reads the unit of
the drawing from its header (`$INSUNITS`) and converts to meters. A drawing that names no unit is read as meters, with
a warning, and `unit` sets the unit instead. The gasket above uses millimeters, but ezdxf writes meters into the
header of a new drawing unless told otherwise:

```python
print(px.Compound(px.FromDXF("gasket.dxf", layers=["outline"], unit=px.mm)).bounding_box)
```

```text
((-0.06, -0.06), (0.06, 0.06))
```

### Gaps

Drawings often have ends that miss each other slightly. The example is a rectangle of 50 × 30 whose last line stops
10⁻⁵ short of its start, so it stays open. `tol` joins end points that are closer than the given value:

```python
doc = ezdxf.new()
msp = doc.modelspace()
corners = [(0, 0), (50, 0), (50, 30), (0, 30), (0, 1e-5)]
for a, b in zip(corners, corners[1:]):
    msp.add_line(a, b)
doc.saveas("gap.dxf")

print([w.IsClosed() for w in px.FromDXF("gap.dxf")], [w.IsClosed() for w in px.FromDXF("gap.dxf", tol=1e-4)])
```

```text
[False] [True]
```

## STEP and BREP

STEP and BREP need OpenCASCADE through `netgen.occ` (`pip install netgen-mesher`, which brings OpenCASCADE as
`netgen-occt`). `WriteStep` and `WriteBrep` write the export described in
[To OCC shapes](../integrations/occ/export.md), with its options. `px.FromOCC` reads a planar STEP, BREP or IGES file
back as a planex2d shape, with its names.

```python
face.WriteStep("cover.step")
face.WriteBrep("cover.brep")
again = px.FromOCC("cover.step")
print("area", again.mass, "written", face.mass)
```

```text
area 7298.108475171204 written 7298.108475171204
```

## SVG

SVG needs no extra package. `ToSVG` returns the picture that a notebook shows as text, for a file or a web page. See
[SVG](plotting/svg.md) for details.

```python
with open("cover.svg", "w") as f:
    f.write(face.ToSVG())
```

## shapely

shapely geometry needs `shapely`. `px.FromShapely` turns polygons and line strings into faces and wires, and
`px.ToShapely` converts the other way. See [shapely](../integrations/shapely.md) for details.

## KiCad

planex2d reads and writes `.kicad_pcb` boards itself. A board from another program, such as Altium or Eagle, is first
converted by KiCad 10's `kicad-cli`, which then has to be installed. See [KiCad](../integrations/kicad.md) for
details.

## gmsh

`WriteGeo` writes a gmsh `.geo` file, with the names as physical groups, and gmsh is needed to mesh it. See
[gmsh and FEniCSx](../integrations/fenicsx.md) for details.

# Defeaturing and simplification

- [Small gaps](gaps.md)
- [Small edges](small-edges.md)
- [Collinear lines](collinear.md)
- [Fitting arcs](arcs.md)
- [Fitting splines](splines.md)


[![A tessellated outline before and after fitting: two lines, one arc and one spline](index_files/index_1.svg)<span>Short segments turned back into lines, an arc and a spline</span>](../../core/defeaturing/arcs.md)
[![A level-set cell of a shape optimization, sampled and fitted with splines](index_files/index_2.png)<span>A shape optimization result, fitted with splines</span>](../../integrations/netgen/levelset.md)


Imported and computed geometry often contains details that a mesher cannot use: ends that miss each other by a hair,
edges far shorter than the part, straight runs in many pieces, and arcs or free-form curves tessellated into short
segments. `Simplify` cleans these up in place, `Simplified` returns a cleaned copy, and the exports to OpenCASCADE and
netgen run the same steps. Gaps, small edges and collinear pieces are handled below 10⁻⁷ by default, the resolution
of OpenCASCADE and netgen. Fitting arcs and splines is switched on when needed, and every fit is checked against the
edges it replaces and rejected if it strays further than its tolerance.

<p class="px-label">In this section</p>


[![Small gaps](index_files/index_3.png)<b>Small gaps</b><span>Ends that miss each other, joined within a tolerance.</span>](gaps.md)
[![Small edges](index_files/index_4.png)<b>Small edges</b><span>Edges shorter than a tolerance, removed with their ends merged.</span>](small-edges.md)
[![Collinear lines](index_files/index_5.png)<b>Collinear lines</b><span>Straight runs in several pieces, joined into one line.</span>](collinear.md)
[![Fitting arcs](index_files/index_6.png)<b>Fitting arcs</b><span>A measured bore turned back into three arcs, with the tolerance and the checks.</span>](arcs.md)
[![Fitting splines](index_files/index_7.png)<b>Fitting splines</b><span>A tessellated ellipse turned back into two B-splines.</span>](splines.md)


## The steps, in order

| Step | Option | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Close small gaps | `close_gaps_smaller` | `1e-7` |
| Merge collinear lines | `merge_collinear_closer` | `1e-7` |
| Fit arcs | `fit_arcs`: `True`, or a dict of `tol`, `max_edge_length`, `max_edge_angle`, `ignore_edges_smaller` | Off |
| Fit splines | `fit_splines`: `True`, or a dict of the same options | Off |
| Remove small edges | `remove_edges_smaller` | `1e-7` |
| Remove free edges (touching no other edge at either end) | `remove_free_edges` | On for faces, off for wires |
| Remove small faces | `remove_faces_smaller`, `merge_small_faces_instead` | `0` (none) |

The defaults are stored in `px.config` and can be changed for the whole session. A dict for a fit changes the options
it names and switches the fit on:

```python
import planex as px

px.config.fit_arcs = dict(tol=1e-4)
print(px.config.fit_arcs)
```

```text
{'enabled': True, 'tol': 0.0001, 'max_edge_length': 0.0001, 'max_edge_angle': 30.0, 'ignore_edges_smaller': 1e-05}
```

---

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/defeaturing/gaps.md

# Small gaps

Ends that should meet but miss each other by a small distance keep a wire open. `CloseGaps(tol)` moves them
together.

```python
import planex as px
```

## A square that does not close

The example is a unit square whose right side starts 10⁻⁴ above the end of the bottom (Figure 1a). Magnified at that
corner, the two open ends are marked (Figure 1b). `Wire.Add` refuses an edge that misses the wire's end, so the four
loose edges go through `px.Wires`, which chains them into one open wire.

```python
corners = [((0, 0), (1, 0)), ((1, 1e-4), (1, 1)), ((1, 1), (0, 1)), ((0, 1), (0, 0))]
(w,) = px.Wires([px.Line(a, b) for a, b in corners])
print(w.IsClosed(), w.OpenEnds())
```

```text
False [(0, False), (3, True)]
```

```python
Row((w, "The wire", {"fill": False}),
    (w, "Magnified at (1, 0)", {"fill": False, "marks": [(1, 0), (1, 1e-4)], "view": ((1 - 3e-4, 1 + 3e-4), (-2e-4, 3e-4))}),
    caption="A square whose ends miss by 10⁻⁴")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

Closed with a tolerance of 10⁻³, the two ends meet in one vertex, marked in the same magnified view, and the wire
bounds a face (Figure 2). The ends meet halfway, at (1, 5·10⁻⁵), so the area is 1 − 5·10⁻⁵.

```python
w.CloseGaps(1e-3)
square = w.Face()
print(w.IsClosed(), square.mass)
```

```text
True 0.99995
```

```python
Row((square, "The face"),
    (w, "Magnified at (1, 0)", {"fill": False, "marks": Vertices(w), "view": ((1 - 3e-4, 1 + 3e-4), (-2e-4, 3e-4))}),
    caption="Closed with a tolerance of 10⁻³")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

# Small edges

Edges shorter than a tolerance are removed, and their two ends meet in the middle. Splines are kept.

```python
import planex as px
```

## A step of 10⁻⁵

The example is an outline 2 × 1 with a step of 10⁻⁵ in its bottom (Figure 1a). Magnified there, the tiny edge runs
between the two marked vertices (Figure 1b). `SmallEdges` lists the edges shorter than a given length:

```python
outline = [(0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1e-5), (2, 1e-5), (2, 1), (0, 1)]
face = px.Face([px.FromPolyline(outline, closed=True)])
print(face.SmallEdges(1e-4))
```

```text
[1]
```

```python
Row((face, "The outline"), (face, "Magnified at (1, 0)", {"marks": [(1, 0), (1, 1e-5)], "view": ((1 - 3e-5, 1 + 3e-5), (-1.5e-5, 2.5e-5))}),
    caption="A step of 10⁻⁵")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

Once the step is removed, its two ends meet in one vertex, marked in the same view (Figure 2):

```python
face.RemoveSmallEdges(1e-4)
```

# Collinear lines

Straight runs often come in many pieces. Sketches and Boolean operations already merge pieces that lie exactly on one
line, and `MergeCollinearEdges` also merges nearly collinear ones, as they occur in imported data. Two lines meeting at
a vertex become one if the vertex lies within the tolerance of the line through their far ends.

```python
import planex as px
```

## A bottom in four pieces

The example is a rectangle 4 × 1 whose bottom is drawn as four lines, with the vertex at x = 3 lifted by 10⁻⁶.
`FromPolyline` already joins the two exactly collinear pieces, so the face has six edges, and the default tolerance of
10⁻⁷ changes nothing (Figure 1a). A tolerance of 10⁻⁵ makes the whole bottom one line (Figure 1b). The vertices are
marked.

```python
face = px.Face([px.FromPolyline([(0, 0), (1, 0), (2, 0), (3, 1e-6), (4, 0), (4, 1), (0, 1)], closed=True)])
merged = face.Copy().MergeCollinearEdges()
straight = face.Copy().MergeCollinearEdges(1e-5)
print(len(face.edges), len(merged.edges), len(straight.edges))
```

```text
6 6 4
```

```python
Row((merged, "Default tolerance", {"marks": Vertices(merged)}),
    (straight, "Tolerance 10⁻⁵", {"marks": Vertices(straight)}), caption="Nearly collinear lines merged")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

---

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/defeaturing/arcs.md

# Fitting arcs

Chains of short edges are replaced by arcs, or by lines where they are straight, as a tessellated or measured outline
needs before it is exported or meshed. The points do not have to lie exactly on a circle: an arc runs through the two
ends of the chain it replaces, and its center is computed from the points between them by least squares. Every fit
is then checked against the edges it replaces:

- each point has to lie within the tolerance of the arc;
- the edges have to stay within the tolerance of it, plus an allowance where the chain bends at a vertex, because the
  chords of a tessellated circle lie inside it.

A fit that deviates more is rejected, and the edges stay as they are.

```python
import math
import random
import planex as px
```

## A measured bore

The example is a bore of radius 10, measured at 256 points that each lie up to 0.03 off the circle at random, as a
scan or a coordinate measuring machine delivers them, and joined by lines with `px.FromPolyline` (Figure 1a). Fitted
with a tolerance of 0.1, it becomes three arcs with radii within 0.07 of 10 (Figure 1b). The magnified view shows the
measured points in gray around the fitted arc, which runs between them, not through them.

```python
random.seed(1)
pts = []
for k in range(256):
    t = 2 * math.pi * k / 256
    r = 10 + random.uniform(-0.03, 0.03)
    pts.append((r * math.cos(t), r * math.sin(t)))
bore = px.Face([px.FromPolyline(pts, closed=True)])
fitted = bore.Copy().FitArcs(tol=0.1, max_edge_length=0.5)
```

```python
spot = (10 * math.cos(math.radians(30)), 10 * math.sin(math.radians(30)))
lens = {"spot": spot, "r": 0.7, "at": (-0.5, -1.5), "R": 7.0, "half": 0.45, "points": pts}
Row((bore, f"{len(bore.edges)} measured points joined"),
    (fitted, f"Fitted: {len(fitted.edges)} arcs", {"zoom": lens}),
    caption="A measured bore fitted with arcs, tolerance 0.1")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

```python
print("radii", [round(e.edge.radius, 4) for e in fitted.edges])
print("area", fitted.mass, "circle", math.pi * 100)
```

```text
radii [10.0066, 10.0603, 9.9984]
area 314.21891028047474 circle 314.1592653589793
```

## Tolerance

A fit needs a tolerance above the noise of its points. The example is a unit circle of 64 points with their
coordinates rounded to three digits. Below the rounding, the fits deviate from the edges by more than allowed and are
rejected, so the 64 edges remain. Just above it, only some chains fit, and well above it, the circle becomes two arcs.

```python
rounded = [(round(math.cos(2 * math.pi * k / 64), 3), round(math.sin(2 * math.pi * k / 64), 3)) for k in range(64)]
circle = px.Face([px.FromPolyline(rounded, closed=True)])
for tol in (1e-5, 1e-4, 1e-3):
    f = circle.Copy().FitArcs(tol=tol, max_edge_length=0.2)
    radii = [e.edge.radius for e in f.edges if hasattr(e.edge, "radius")]
    error = max(abs(r - 1) for r in radii) if radii else "none, no arcs fitted"
    print("tol", tol, ":", len(f.edges), "edges, largest radius error", error)
```

```text
tol 1e-05 : 64 edges, largest radius error none, no arcs fitted
tol 0.0001 : 40 edges, largest radius error 0.01307012691401388
tol 0.001 : 2 edges, largest radius error 2.294391787671657e-09
```

## On export

The exports take the same options, and the exported face of the rounded circle has 2 edges instead of 64:

```python
exported = circle.ToOCCShape(fit_arcs=dict(max_edge_length=0.2, tol=1e-3))
print(len(exported.edges), "edges")
```

```text
2 edges
```

---

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/defeaturing/splines.md

# Fitting splines

Chains of short edges that are not arcs, such as tessellated ellipses or free-form outlines, become B-splines. The
fit is an approximation by least squares, not an interpolation. The B-spline runs through the two ends of the chain
but does not have to pass through the points between them, so it smooths over the small kinks at the vertices instead
of bending sharply at each of them. As with arcs, every fit is checked against the edges it replaces. It is rejected
if it strays from them by more than the tolerance, plus the allowance at bends, or if it leaves or arrives in a
different direction than the chain. Fitted splines are meant for export, so run Boolean operations first and simplify
last.

```python
import math
import random
import planex as px
```

## An ellipse from 128 segments

The example is an ellipse with half axes 2 and 1, tessellated into 128 lines, with its vertices moved off it by up to
2·10⁻⁵ at random (Figure 1a). It becomes B-splines, whose ends are marked (Figure 1b).

```python
random.seed(1)
pts = []
for k in range(128):
    t = 2 * math.pi * k / 128
    s = 1 + random.uniform(-2e-5, 2e-5)
    pts.append((s * 2 * math.cos(t), s * math.sin(t)))
ellipse = px.Face([px.FromPolyline(pts, closed=True)])
smooth = ellipse.Simplified(fit_splines=dict(max_edge_length=0.2, tol=1e-4))
print([type(e.edge).__name__ for e in smooth.edges])
```

```text
['SplineEdge', 'SplineEdge']
```

```python
Row((ellipse, f"{len(ellipse.edges)} edges"),
    (smooth, f"{len(smooth.edges)} splines", {"marks": Vertices(smooth)}),
    caption="A tessellated ellipse fitted with B-splines")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

planex2d measures a fitted spline on the chain it replaced, so its area does not change. The exported B-spline is the
smooth curve and comes closer to the ellipse's area π a b:

```python
exact = 2 * math.pi
for name, area in {"segments": ellipse.mass, "splines": smooth.mass, "exported": smooth.ToOCCFace().mass}.items():
    print(name, "relative area error", (area - exact) / exact)
```

```text
segments relative area error -0.000401521475626761
splines relative area error -0.0004015214756269024
exported relative area error -1.7651805034993964e-06
```

## Arcs first

With both fits enabled, arcs are fitted first, and splines take what is left:

```python
options = dict(max_edge_length=0.2, tol=1e-4)
both = ellipse.Simplified(fit_splines=options, fit_arcs=options)
print(sorted({type(e.edge).__name__ for e in both.edges}), len(both.edges))
```

```text
['ArcEdge', 'LineEdge', 'SplineEdge'] 32
```

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/core/comparison/index.md

# Comparison with other libraries

These pages run the same tasks in planex2d, in OpenCASCADE (the netgen-occt build, used through `netgen.occ`) and in
four polygon libraries: shapely (GEOS), pyclipper (Clipper), gdstk and manifold3d (Clipper2). OpenCASCADE is the
kernel that planex2d passes its results to, and both keep lines, arcs and splines exact. The polygon libraries work
with straight edges only, so round shapes reach them as polygons. The method:

- the polygons are shapely buffers, tessellated finely enough that the area agrees with the exact planex2d area to
  about 10⁻⁷, and all four polygon libraries get the same polygons;
- the polygons are converted for each library before the clock starts, and only the Boolean operation is timed;
- the times are the best of three runs, and for OpenCASCADE of one run;
- as on the landing page, the three libraries built on Clipper share one bar, which shows the fastest of them;
- the code is `comparison_libraries.py` in the docs folder.

The timings are measured every time the documentation is built, on the machine that builds it:

```python
import platform
print(platform.processor() or platform.machine(), "Python", platform.python_version())
```

```text
x86_64 Python 3.12.15
```

- [Union of traces](traces.md)
- [Merging split edges](merge.md)
- [Nearly coincident edges](accuracy.md)
- [Gluing many faces](glue.md)

# Union of many discs

500 random discs of radius 0.3 to 1.2 in a square of 30 are united: in planex2d with `Unify`, in OpenCASCADE with
`Fuse` and `UnifySameDomain`, and in the polygon libraries as polygons of 2048 segments per quarter circle. Figure 1
shows the union from planex2d and from OpenCASCADE, and Figure 2 the times.

```python
import random
import netgen.occ as occ
import shapely
import planex as px
from comparison_libraries import best, chart, union
```

```python
random.seed(1)
n = 500
data = []
for _ in range(n):
    x, y = random.uniform(0, 30), random.uniform(0, 30)
    data.append((x, y, random.uniform(0.3, 1.2)))
px_discs = [px.QuickSketch().Circle(x, y, r).Face() for x, y, r in data]
occ_discs = [occ.WorkPlane().Circle(x, y, r).Face() for x, y, r in data]
polygons = [shapely.Point(x, y).buffer(r, quad_segs=2048) for x, y, r in data]
```

```python
t_px, a = best(lambda: px.Unify(px_discs))
t_occ, b = best(lambda: occ.Fuse(occ_discs).UnifySameDomain(), repeats=1)
others = union(polygons)

print(f"planex2d   {t_px:.4f} s, area {a.mass:.6f}, {len(a.edges)} edges")
occ_area = sum(f.mass for f in b.faces)
print(f"OCC        {t_occ:.4f} s, area {occ_area:.6f}, {len(b.edges)} edges")
for name, (t, area) in others.items():
    relative = (area - a.mass) / a.mass
    print(f"{name:10} {t:.4f} s, area {area:.6f}, relative to planex2d {relative:+.0e}")
```

```text
planex2d   0.0024 s, area 612.803230, 640 edges
OCC        9.5292 s, area 612.803230, 640 edges
shapely    1.0983 s, area 612.803194, relative to planex2d -6e-08
pyclipper  1.6787 s, area 612.803194, relative to planex2d -6e-08
gdstk      1.4541 s, area 612.803194, relative to planex2d -6e-08
manifold3d 1.2514 s, area 612.803194, relative to planex2d -6e-08
```

```python
Row((a, "planex2d", {"fill": False}), (b, "OpenCASCADE"), caption="The union of 500 discs")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

```python
Times(chart(t_px, others, t_occ), title="Uniting 500 discs", note=POLYGONS)
```

# Union of traces

500 random strokes, 2 long and 0.2 wide with round ends, lie in a square of 30. OpenCASCADE gets the faces as
exported by planex2d, and the polygon libraries get the strokes buffered with 512 segments per quarter circle.
Figure 1 shows the union from planex2d and from OpenCASCADE, and Figure 2 the times.

```python
import math
import random
import netgen.occ as occ
import shapely
import planex as px
from comparison_libraries import best, chart, union
```

```python
random.seed(2)
strokes = []
for _ in range(500):
    x, y = random.uniform(0, 30), random.uniform(0, 30)
    strokes.append((x, y, random.uniform(0, 360)))
px_traces = [px.QuickSketch((x, y)).Turn(a).Line(2).Wire().Offset(0.1)
             for x, y, a in strokes]
occ_traces = [t.ToOCCShape() for t in px_traces]
polygons = []
for x, y, a in strokes:
    end = (x + 2 * math.cos(math.radians(a)), y + 2 * math.sin(math.radians(a)))
    polygons.append(shapely.LineString([(x, y), end]).buffer(0.1, quad_segs=512))
```

```python
t_px, a = best(lambda: px.Unify(px_traces))
t_occ, b = best(lambda: occ.Fuse(occ_traces).UnifySameDomain(), repeats=1)
others = union(polygons)

print(f"planex2d   {t_px:.4f} s, area {a.mass:.6f}, {len(a.edges)} edges")
occ_area = sum(f.mass for f in b.faces)
print(f"OCC        {t_occ:.4f} s, area {occ_area:.6f}, {len(b.edges)} edges")
for name, (t, area) in others.items():
    relative = (area - a.mass) / a.mass
    print(f"{name:10} {t:.4f} s, area {area:.6f}, relative to planex2d {relative:+.0e}")
```

```text
planex2d   0.0059 s, area 191.735856, 3023 edges
```

```text
OCC        11.2101 s, area 191.735856, 3023 edges
shapely    0.7236 s, area 191.735837, relative to planex2d -1e-07
pyclipper  0.5965 s, area 191.735837, relative to planex2d -1e-07
gdstk      0.4969 s, area 191.735837, relative to planex2d -1e-07
manifold3d 0.4980 s, area 191.735837, relative to planex2d -1e-07
```

```python
Row((a, "planex2d", {"fill": False}), (b, "OpenCASCADE"), caption="The union of 500 traces")
```

# Merging split edges

The task is the union of a grid of 20 × 20 unit squares. The planex2d union merges the pieces of each side into one
edge by itself. OpenCASCADE's `Fuse` leaves them split until `UnifySameDomain` runs, and after that, both have the four
edges of the outline. The squares have no arcs, so the polygon libraries get them exactly. Figure 1 shows the squares
and the unions from planex2d and from OpenCASCADE, with their vertices marked, and Figure 2 shows the times.

```python
import netgen.occ as occ
import shapely
import planex as px
from comparison_libraries import best, chart, union
```

```python
n = 20
cells = [(i, j) for i in range(n) for j in range(n)]
px_squares = [px.QuickSketch((i, j)).Rectangle(1, 1).Face() for i, j in cells]
occ_squares = [occ.WorkPlane().MoveTo(i, j).Rectangle(1, 1).Face() for i, j in cells]
polygons = [shapely.box(i, j, i + 1, j + 1) for i, j in cells]
```

```python
t_px, a = best(lambda: px.Unify(px_squares))
t_occ, b = best(lambda: occ.Fuse(occ_squares).UnifySameDomain(), repeats=1)
others = union(polygons)

print(f"planex2d   {t_px:.4f} s, {len(a.edges)} edges")
print(f"OCC        {t_occ:.4f} s, {len(b.edges)} edges")
for name, (t, area) in others.items():
    print(f"{name:10} {t:.4f} s, area {area:.6f}")
```

```text
planex2d   0.0010 s, 4 edges
OCC        1.7253 s, 4 edges
shapely    0.0057 s, area 400.000000
pyclipper  0.0006 s, area 400.000000
gdstk      0.0006 s, area 400.000000
manifold3d 0.0004 s, area 400.000000
```

```python
Row((px.Compound(px_squares), f"{len(px_squares)} unit squares", {"fill": False}),
    (a, f"planex2d: {len(a.edges)} edges", {"fill": False, "marks": Vertices(a)}),
    (b, f"OpenCASCADE: {len(b.edges)} edges", {"marks": Vertices(b)}),
    caption="The union of a grid of unit squares")
```

# Nearly coincident edges

The task is the union of two unit squares, the second shifted by `d` along x. The exact area of the union is 1 + d,
and the output lists the errors of both kernels for d from 10⁻⁴ down to 10⁻¹⁰:

```python
import netgen.occ as occ
import planex as px
```

```python
ds = [1e-4, 1e-6, 1e-8, 1e-10]
for d in ds:
    square = px.QuickSketch().Rectangle(1, 1).Face()
    moved = px.QuickSketch((d, 0)).Rectangle(1, 1).Face()
    a = square + moved
    first = occ.WorkPlane().Rectangle(1, 1).Face()
    second = occ.WorkPlane().MoveTo(d, 0).Rectangle(1, 1).Face()
    b = (first + second).UnifySameDomain()
    err_px = a.mass - (1 + d)
    err_occ = sum(f.mass for f in b.faces) - (1 + d)
    print(f"d = {d:.0e}   planex2d error {err_px:+.1e}   OCC error {err_occ:+.1e}")
```

```text
d = 1e-04   planex2d error +0.0e+00   OCC error +2.2e-16
d = 1e-06   planex2d error +0.0e+00   OCC error +2.2e-16
d = 1e-08   planex2d error +0.0e+00   OCC error -1.0e-08
d = 1e-10   planex2d error +0.0e+00   OCC error -1.0e-10
```

Figure 1 shows the last case, d = 10⁻¹⁰. At this scale, the two squares look like one square, so a lens magnifies
the lower right corner, where their right sides run 10⁻¹⁰ apart. Next to them are the unions from planex2d and from
OpenCASCADE, with their vertices marked.

```python
lens = {"spot": (1, 0), "r": 0.07, "at": (0.48, 0.5), "R": 0.36, "half": 3e-10}
Row((px.Compound([square, moved]), "two squares 10⁻¹⁰ apart", {"fill": False, "zoom": lens}),
    (a, f"planex2d: {len(a.edges)} edges", {"fill": False, "marks": Vertices(a)}),
    (b, f"OpenCASCADE: {len(b.edges)} edges", {"marks": Vertices(b)}),
    caption="The union of two unit squares 10⁻¹⁰ apart")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

# Gluing many faces

The task is a fiber composite cross-section: 200 fibers of radius 0.6 glued into a matrix 30 × 30, so that every
fiber and the matrix share the fiber's outline. The fibers are named `fiber` and the matrix `matrix`. For the polygon
libraries, the task is to cut the fibers, as polygons of 2048 segments per quarter circle, out of the matrix, which
gives the face of the matrix. Figure 1 shows the result of `Glue` in planex2d and in OpenCASCADE, and
Figure 2 the times.

```python
import math
import random
import netgen.occ as occ
import shapely
import planex as px
from comparison_libraries import best, chart, difference
```

```python
random.seed(2)
L, r, n = 30.0, 0.6, 200
centers = []
while len(centers) < n:
    p = (random.uniform(r, L - r), random.uniform(r, L - r))
    if all(math.dist(p, q) > 2.2 * r for q in centers):
        centers.append(p)

matrix = px.QuickSketch().Rectangle(L, L).Face()
matrix.name = "matrix"
px_fibers = [px.QuickSketch().Circle(x, y, r).Face() for x, y in centers]
for fiber in px_fibers:
    fiber.name = "fiber"
occ_matrix = occ.WorkPlane().Rectangle(L, L).Face()
occ_fibers = [occ.WorkPlane().Circle(x, y, r).Face() for x, y in centers]
polygons = [shapely.Point(x, y).buffer(r, quad_segs=2048) for x, y in centers]
```

```python
t_px, a = best(lambda: px.Glue([matrix, *px_fibers]))
t_occ, b = best(lambda: occ.Glue([occ_matrix, *occ_fibers]), repeats=1)
others = difference([(0, 0), (L, 0), (L, L), (0, L)], polygons)

matrix_area = sum(f.mass for f in a.faces(name="matrix"))
occ_area = sum(f.mass for f in b.faces)
print(f"planex2d   {t_px:.4f} s, {len(a.faces)} faces, matrix {matrix_area:.6f}")
print(f"OCC        {t_occ:.4f} s, {len(b.faces)} faces, area {occ_area:.6f}")
for name, (t, area) in others.items():
    relative = (area - matrix_area) / matrix_area
    print(f"{name:10} {t:.4f} s, matrix {area:.6f}, relative to planex2d {relative:+.0e}")
```

```text
planex2d   0.0009 s, 201 faces, matrix 673.805329
OCC        0.0152 s, 201 faces, area 900.000000
shapely    0.8803 s, matrix 673.805351, relative to planex2d +3e-08
pyclipper  0.5844 s, matrix 673.805351, relative to planex2d +3e-08
gdstk      0.6872 s, matrix 673.805351, relative to planex2d +3e-08
manifold3d 0.6687 s, matrix 673.805351, relative to planex2d +3e-08
```

```python
Row((a, "planex2d", {"fill": False}), (b, "OpenCASCADE"), caption="200 fibers glued into a matrix")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

```python
Times(chart(t_px, others, t_occ), title="Gluing 200 fibers into a matrix", note=POLYGONS)
```


# OpenCASCADE


[![NACA sections drawn by planex2d on planes along the span of a wing, before the loft](index_files/index_1.png)<span>Airfoil sections on their planes in space</span>](../../integrations/occ/loft.md)
[![The wing with winglets lofted through the planex2d sections in OpenCASCADE, mirrored](index_files/index_2.png)<span>The wing lofted through them</span>](../../integrations/occ/loft.md)
[![A C-clamp frame extruded from a planex2d sketch, with its screw hole and anvil pad](index_files/index_3.png)<span>A C-clamp from one sketch</span>](../../integrations/occ/clamp.md)
[![A unit cube with a square tunnel along (2, 1, 2), wide enough for a cube of side 1.04](index_files/index_4.png)<span><em class="px-tag">Example</em> Prince Rupert&#x27;s cube: a cube through a cube</span>](../../examples/prince-ruperts-cube.md)


A planex2d object lies on a plane in 3D, so its faces and wires become OpenCASCADE shapes as they are: exact lines,
arcs, full circles and B-splines with shared vertices. They can be extruded, revolved and lofted into solids or cut
from solids, and a sketch can be drawn on the face of a solid with the solid's edges projected into it. Names, colors
and mesh sizes travel with the edges and faces into the solid, where netgen reads them as boundaries, materials and
mesh sizes. The export can clean up the geometry on the way out, fit splines, and write arcs for tools that accept
nothing else. It needs netgen's OpenCASCADE (`pip install netgen-mesher`). Planes are `px.Plane` objects on these
pages; every plane argument also takes netgen's `occ.Axes`, so existing netgen code can pass its axes unchanged (see
[API conventions](../../core/conventions.md)).

## Everything at a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| **Export** | `ToOCCShape()`, `ToOCCFace()`, `ToOCCWire()`, `ToOCCWires()`, with the cleanup options of `Simplify` (see [Export options](export-options.md)) |
| **Solids** | `px.Pad(profile, length)` and `px.Pocket(target, profile, length)`, with `length2`, `dir`, `reverse` and `until`; OpenCASCADE's own operations on the exported shapes, such as `Extrude` and `occ.ThruSections` |
| **Sketching on solids** | `px.QuickSketch(face)` and `px.Sketch(face)` on a planar face, `sk.Project(edge)` for its edges as references (see [Placing a sketch](../../core/sketch/placement.md)) |
| **Back into planex2d** | `px.FromOCC(shape or file)`, `px.Project(shape, plane)`, `px.Intersect3d(plane, shape)` |
| **Drawing** | `px.Plot3d(objects)` in 3D, `px.Plot(shape, plane)` for a section |
| **Meshing** | `px.OCCGeometry(face)` for netgen (see [netgen and NGSolve](../netgen/index.md)) |

# To OCC shapes

Faces, wires and sketches become OpenCASCADE shapes with exact lines, arcs, full circles and B-splines, shared
vertices, names and colors. The export needs OpenCASCADE through `netgen.occ` (`pip install netgen-mesher`, which
brings OpenCASCADE as `netgen-occt`). On the way out, the export can apply everything that `Simplify` does. See
[Defeaturing](../../core/defeaturing/index.md) for details.

![A model rocket exported to OpenCASCADE](export_files/export_1.png){.preview}

The [rocket example](../../examples/rocket.md) is revolved, lofted and extruded from planex2d sketches.

The example is a plate 4 × 2 with a bore of radius 0.5, with its outline and bore named (Figure 1):

```python
import planex as px

plate = px.QuickSketch((-2, -1)).Rectangle(4, 2, name="outline").Face()
part = plate - px.QuickSketch().Circle(0.5, name="bore").Face()
shape = part.ToOCCShape()
print(len(shape.edges), "edges:", sorted({e.name for e in shape.edges}))
```

```text
5 edges: ['bore', 'outline']
```

```python
Row((part, "The plate, its bore highlighted", {"highlight": list(part.edges(name="bore"))}),
    caption="A plate with a named bore")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## Faces and wires

A face, its wires, or a wire on its own can each be exported as OpenCASCADE objects. The example exports the
plate as a face and as its wires, and a slot of width 1 along a spine of 3 as one wire:

```python
face = part.ToOCCFace()
wires = part.ToOCCWires()
slot = px.QuickSketch().Slot(3, 1).Wire().ToOCCWire()
print(type(face).__name__, len(wires.edges), len(slot.edges))
```

```text
Face 5 4
```

## Everything at a glance

| Object | `ToOCCShape()` gives | Also |
|---|---|---|
| Face | The face | `ToOCCFace`, `ToOCCWire`, `ToOCCWires` |
| Wire | Its wires | `ToOCCWire`, `ToOCCWires`, `ToOCCFace` |
| Sketch | The face of everything drawn | `ToOCCFace`, `ToOCCWire`, `ToOCCWires` |
| Compound | Faces and wires glued together | |

---

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/integrations/occ/export-options.md

# Export options

Every export can apply everything that `Simplify` does (see [Defeaturing](../../core/defeaturing/index.md)). The face
itself is not changed, because the cleanup runs on a copy on the way out. The examples on this page use an ellipse
with half axes 1 and 0.5, tessellated into 64 lines.

```python
import math
import planex as px

turns = [2 * math.pi * k / 64 for k in range(64)]
outline = px.Face([px.FromPolyline([(math.cos(t), 0.5 * math.sin(t)) for t in turns], closed=True)])
```

## Splines on the way out

The example exports the ellipse once as it is and once with `fit_splines`, as B-splines, which is the same cleanup
that `Simplified` does. The ends of the edges are marked (Figure 1), and the face itself keeps its 64 edges.

```python
options = {"fit_splines": dict(max_edge_length=0.1, tol=1e-4)}
exported, fitted = outline.ToOCCShape(), outline.ToOCCShape(**options)
print(len(exported.edges), len(fitted.edges), len(outline.edges))
```

```text
64 2 64
```

```python
smooth = outline.Simplified(**options)
Row((outline, f"{len(outline.edges)} edges", {"marks": Vertices(outline)}),
    (smooth, f"With fit_splines: {len(smooth.edges)} edges", {"marks": Vertices(smooth)}),
    caption="An ellipse of 64 lines exported as it is and with fitted splines")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## Defaults for the session

Options that are not given take their value from `px.config`. A dict for a fit changes the options it names and
switches the fit on:

```python
px.config.fit_splines = dict(max_edge_length=0.1, tol=1e-4)
print(len(outline.ToOCCShape().edges))
px.config.fit_splines = False
```

```text
2
```

## Open wires

`remove_free_edges` removes the edges that touch no other edge at either end, with a warning. It is on by default for
faces and off by default for wires, which use it only when it is passed. A chain is never cut, so an open path keeps
its open ends. The example is a path of two lines, exported as it is and with `remove_free_edges=True`. It keeps both
its edges:

```python
path = px.Line((0, 0), (1, 0)) + px.Line((1, 0), (1, 1))
print(len(path.ToOCCWires().edges), len(path.ToOCCWires(remove_free_edges=True).edges))
```

```text
2 2
```

---

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/integrations/occ/splines-as-arcs.md

# Splines as arcs

planex2d computes with splines through a chain of arcs, with lines where the curve is straight.
`approximation=True` exports that chain instead of the B-spline, for tools that accept only lines and arcs. Figure 1
shows a spline through four marked points and a magnified piece of it with the joints of the chain that planex2d
computes with:

```python
import planex as px

curve = px.Spline([(0, 0), (1, 0.6), (2, 0), (3, 0.8)])
chain = curve.edges[0].edge.approximation
print(len(curve.ToOCCWire().edges), "edge,", len(curve.ToOCCWire(approximation=True).edges), "with approximation=True")
```

```text
1 edge, 142 with approximation=True
```

```python
joints = [(a.start.h, a.start.v) for a in chain] + [(chain[-1].end.h, chain[-1].end.v)]
p = curve.edges[0].PointAt(0.15)
view = ((p.h - 0.12, p.h + 0.12), (p.v - 0.09, p.v + 0.09))
Row((curve, "A spline", {"fill": False, "marks": [(0, 0), (1, 0.6), (2, 0), (3, 0.8)]}),
    (curve, f"Magnified: joints of its {len(chain)} pieces", {"fill": False, "marks": joints, "view": view}),
    caption="A spline and the chain of arcs it is computed with")
```


```python
print(sorted({type(e).__name__ for e in chain}), len(chain), "pieces")
```

# A C-clamp, step by step

Five numbers drive the frame of a C-clamp: the throat depth of 60, the jaw gap of 40, the wall thickness t = 12, the
fillet radius r = 6 and the frame thickness b = 16. The profile is drawn with the pen, with every side a length along
it and every corner a turn or an arc. All of them are computed from the five numbers, so changing a number changes the
whole part. The profile is then extruded into the frame, drilled for the screw and given an anvil pad, with
OpenCASCADE doing the 3D operations.

```python
import math
import netgen.occ as occ
from ngsolve_webgpu.jupyter import Draw
import planex as px
```

## The profile

The sketch lies in the xz plane, with h along x and v along z, so its normal points along −y. W = t + depth is the
width of the profile and H = gap + 2t its height. The pen starts at the end of the lower bend, heading
along x, and runs once around counterclockwise. It draws the bottom, the lower tip, the lower jaw, the inner fillet of
radius `r` into the throat and out of it, the upper jaw and tip, the top, and the outer bends of radius `r + t` around
the same centers, so that the wall keeps its thickness around the bend. `Turn(90)` turns the pen left for a square
corner, and `Arc(r, -90)` is a fillet that turns it right, into the mouth. Every edge carries a `name`, which the faces
of the solid take over below (Figure 1).

```python
depth, gap, t, r, b = 60, 40, 12, 6, 16
W, H = t + depth, gap + 2 * t

side = px.QuickSketch(px.Plane(normal=(0, -1, 0), axis=(1, 0, 0)))
side.Move((r + t, 0), dir=(1, 0))
side.Line(W - r - t, name="bottom").Turn(90).Line(t, name="lower tip").Turn(90)
side.Line(W - t - r, name="lower jaw").Arc(r, -90, name="lower fillet")
side.Line(gap - 2 * r, name="throat").Arc(r, -90, name="upper fillet")
side.Line(W - t - r, name="upper jaw").Turn(90).Line(t, name="upper tip").Turn(90)
side.Line(W - r - t, name="top").Arc(r + t, 90, name="upper bend")
side.Line(H - 2 * (r + t), name="rear").Arc(r + t, 90, name="lower bend")
face = side.Face()
print("the pen ends at", side.pen.position, "where it started")
```

```text
the pen ends at (18.0, 0.0) where it started
```

```python
shift = {"rear": -9, "throat": 10}
names = [(e.name, (e.PointAt(0.5).h + shift.get(e.name, 0), e.PointAt(0.5).v)) for e in face.edges
         if "tip" not in e.name]
Row((side, "The profile drawn with the pen", {"fill": False, "marks": Vertices(face)}),
    (face, "The face, its edges named", {"labels": names}), caption="The C-clamp profile")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## Check

The area is that of the outer rectangle with two rounded corners minus the mouth with two rounded corners:

```python
print("area", face.mass, "exact", area)
```

`px.Pad` extrudes the profile along its normal by b into an OpenCASCADE solid:

## The screw hole

The screw hole, of diameter 10, is sketched on the top face of the frame, 20 from its tip. `px.QuickSketch(face)` puts
the sketch on the face's plane with its outward normal and projects the origin and the x axis onto it, so here h = x
and v = y. `px.Pocket` cuts the hole from there down through the upper jaw.


The anvil pad, of diameter 14 and 3 high, is sketched on the face of the lower jaw, which is the face nearest to the
screw axis at jaw height. `px.Pad` extrudes it out of that face, and the union adds it to the frame.

```python
jaw = px.QuickSketch(frame.faces.Nearest(occ.Pnt(W - 20, -b / 2, t)))
frame = frame + px.Pad(jaw.Circle(W - 20, -b / 2, 7), 3)
Draw(frame)
```

# Sketching on and projecting 3D geometry

`px.Project(shape, plane)` lays an OpenCASCADE shape flat onto a plane and returns its edges as a list of clean
wires. Lines stay lines, circles and arcs parallel to the plane stay circles and arcs, and all other curves become exact
splines. Edges that fall onto each other are kept once, with the name of the one nearest to the viewer. In a sketch,
`Project` adds the result as construction elements to draw against.

```python
import math
import netgen.occ as occ
from ngsolve_webgpu.jupyter import Draw
import planex as px
```

The examples use the C-clamp frame with its screw hole from [A C-clamp, step by step](clamp.md), with the throat
depth of 60, the jaw gap of 40, the wall thickness t = 12, the fillet radius r = 6 and the frame thickness b = 16:

```python
depth, gap, t, r, b = 60, 40, 12, 6, 16
W, H = t + depth, gap + 2 * t

side = px.QuickSketch(px.Plane(normal=(0, -1, 0), axis=(1, 0, 0)))
side.Move((r + t, 0), dir=(1, 0))
side.Line(W - r - t, name="bottom").Turn(90).Line(t, name="lower tip").Turn(90)
side.Line(W - t - r, name="lower jaw").Arc(r, -90, name="lower fillet")
side.Line(gap - 2 * r, name="throat").Arc(r, -90, name="upper fillet")
side.Line(W - t - r, name="upper jaw").Turn(90).Line(t, name="upper tip").Turn(90)
side.Line(W - r - t, name="top").Arc(r + t, 90, name="upper bend")
side.Line(H - 2 * (r + t), name="rear").Arc(r + t, 90, name="lower bend")

frame = px.Pad(side.Face(), b)
top = px.QuickSketch(frame.faces.Max(occ.Z))
frame = px.Pocket(frame, top.Circle(W - 20, -b / 2, 5), 2 * t)
Draw(frame)
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## Edges as targets: a marking groove

Edges of the solid can be targets in a sketch, so lines can start and end on them or run parallel to them. They are
projected into the sketch plane on the way and never become part of the sketch. The example is a marking groove on
the roof of the frame, parallel to its front edge and 2 in from it, running from the seam where the bend begins to the
tip. The groove is the line offset by 0.5, pocketed 0.5 deep.

```python
roof = frame.faces.Max(occ.Z)
front = roof.edges.Max(occ.Y)
tip = roof.edges.Max(occ.X)
seam = roof.edges.Min(occ.X)

top = px.QuickSketch(roof)
top.Line(seam, tip, parallel=front, through=(0, -2), name="groove")
Draw(px.Pocket(frame, top.Wire().Offset(0.5), 0.5))
```

## Inclined circles

A round port on a face inclined at 60° looks like an ellipse from above. The example is a circle of radius 10 tilted
by 60°, whose projection has the area π 10² cos 60°. The projection keeps it as an exact spline.
The planex2d area comes from the spline's arc approximation, while the exported OpenCASCADE face uses the exact
curve.

```python
tilt = math.radians(60)
port = occ.Circle(occ.Pnt(0, 0, 0), occ.Dir(0, math.sin(tilt), math.cos(tilt)), 10)
ellipse = px.Face(px.Project(port))
exact = math.pi * 10**2 * math.cos(tilt)
occ_area = sum(f.mass for f in ellipse.ToOCCFace().faces)
print([type(e.edge).__name__ for e in ellipse.edges])
print("planex2d", ellipse.mass, "OCC", occ_area, "exact", exact)
```

```text
['SplineEdge', 'SplineEdge']
planex2d 157.0796805204156 OCC 157.07963267948975 exact 157.0796326794897
```

## In a sketch

`sketch.Project(shape, id=...)` adds construction edges, or drawn edges with `construction=False`, and `name` names
them all. The projected elements get ids under the projection's id, using the same edge numbers that netgen's webgui
shows on a click. Here, `pin.Edge.0` is the pin's circle, one edge, and `pin.Center.1` is its center. An edge seen
end-on becomes a point. In the example, a dowel pin standing on the roof is projected into a sketch on the roof and
places the clearance hole for the mating part concentric with it (Figure 3):

```python
pin = occ.Cylinder(occ.Pnt(30, -b / 2, H), occ.Z, 3, 10)
deck = px.QuickSketch(roof)
deck.Project(roof, id="roof")
deck.Project(pin, id="pin")
print(sorted(deck.elements["Circle"]))
deck.Circle(3.4, concentric="pin.Edge.0", id="clearance")
print(deck.Measure("clearance")["center"], "exact", (30.0, -b / 2, H))
```

```text

(30.0, -8.0, 64.0) exact (30.0, -8.0, 64)
```

OpenCASCADE shapes are also targets of `Line`, `Arc` and `Circle` (as shown above) and cutters of `Split` and `Trim`

# Lofting sections

A loft builds a solid through planar sections. Every section is a planex2d face on its own plane in 3D, and
`occ.ThruSections` lofts their outlines. The example is a wing half with NACA 2412 sections. It tapers from a chord of
100 to 50 over 300, with 3° dihedral and 3° washout, and then bends with a radius of 20 into a winglet canted at 75°,
60 long, swept back by 30° and tapered to a chord of 25.

When the sections change quickly, a loft between them can overshoot. See [lofts with guide curves](guided-loft.md)
for how to steer it.

```python
import math
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import netgen.occ as occ
from ngsolve_webgpu.jupyter import Draw
import planex as px
```

The numbers of the wing: the root chord `c_root` tapers to `c_tip` over the span `b`, with `washout` and `dihedral` in
degrees. The bend has the radius `R` and turns up to the winglet's `cant`, and the winglet is `hw` long, with the tip
chord `c_winglet` and the `sweep` angle.

```python
c_root, c_tip, b, washout, dihedral = 100, 50, 300, 3, 3
R, cant, hw, c_winglet, sweep = 20, 75, 60, 25, 30
```

## The profile

`px.FromNACA` returns the airfoil as a face, here with 2 % camber at 40 % of the chord, 12 % thickness and a sharp
trailing edge. The leading edge sits at the origin of its plane, with the chord along h, and `angle` turns the profile
nose up about the quarter chord point (`pivot`).

```python
root = px.FromNACA("2412", chord=c_root)
```

```python
Row((root, "NACA 2412, chord 100"))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The plane of each section is perpendicular to the span line, with its origin a quarter chord ahead of it, so the
quarter chord points lie on the span line and the twist turns about them. The cambered upper side points away from
the bend, so on the winglet it faces inboard. Washout lowers the nose, which is a negative angle.

```python
def section(q, phi, c, twist):
    f = math.radians(phi)
    plane = px.Plane(origin=(q[0] - c / 4, q[1], q[2]), normal=(0, -math.cos(f), -math.sin(f)), axis=(1, 0, 0))
    return px.FromNACA("2412", chord=c, angle=-twist, plane=plane)
```

## Along the span

The span line rises at the dihedral angle, bends with radius R up to the cant angle and continues straight into the
winglet, and s is the distance along it. The loft interpolates smoothly between the sections, so they are placed
evenly along the span line, about every 10.

```python
g, k = math.radians(dihedral), math.radians(cant)
bend = R * (k - g)
center = (0, b * math.cos(g) - R * math.sin(g), b * math.sin(g) + R * math.cos(g))

def station(s):
    if s <= b:
        return section((0, s * math.cos(g), s * math.sin(g)), dihedral, c_root + (c_tip - c_root) * s / b,
                       washout * s / b)
    if s <= b + bend:
        f = g + (s - b) / R
        return section((0, center[1] + R * math.sin(f), center[2] - R * math.cos(f)), math.degrees(f), c_tip,
                       washout)
    h = s - b - bend
    y0, z0 = center[1] + R * math.sin(k), center[2] - R * math.cos(k)
    return section((h * math.tan(math.radians(sweep)), y0 + h * math.cos(k), z0 + h * math.sin(k)), cant,
                   c_tip + (c_winglet - c_tip) * h / hw, washout)

length = b + bend + hw
count = round(length / 10)
sections = [station(length * i / count) for i in range(count + 1)]
px.Plot3d(sections)
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## The loft

```python
wing = occ.ThruSections([s.outer.ToOCCWire() for s in sections], solid=True)
px.Plot3d(wing)
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The wing is shown from the front and from above, with the sections in black and the edges of the loft in red.

```python
def views(axes, edges, **style):
    for e in edges:
        t0, t1 = e.parameter_interval
        pts = [e.Value(t0 + (t1 - t0) * j / 100) for j in range(101)]
        axes[0].plot([q.y for q in pts], [q.z for q in pts], **style)
        axes[1].plot([q.y for q in pts], [q.x for q in pts], **style)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(12, 8))
views(axes, [e for s in sections for e in s.outer.ToOCCWire().edges], color="black", lw=0.5)
views(axes, wing.edges, color="tab:red", lw=0.8)
for ax, title in zip(axes, ("front", "top")):
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_title(title)
plt.show()
```

Both halves, with the second one mirrored about the plane of symmetry:

```python
px.Plot3d([wing, wing.Mirror(occ.Axes((0, 0, 0), n=occ.Y, h=occ.X))])
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## Check

The end caps of the solid are the root and tip sections, with the same area and the same centroid.

```python
for name, cap, s in (("root", wing.faces.Min(occ.Y), sections[0]), ("tip", wing.faces.Max(occ.Z), sections[-1])):
    f = s.ToOCCFace()
    print(name, "cap", cap.mass, "section", f.mass, "centroids", (cap.center - f.center).Norm(), "apart")
```

```text
root cap 817.7744876597249 section 817.7744876597251 centroids 4.080187622190639e-15 apart
tip cap 51.110905478732974 section 51.110905478732704 centroids 1.154495294690031e-13 apart
```

The straight parts are frusta of similar sections. The bend is the tip section turned about the bend axis, so by
Pappus's theorem its volume is the area times the path of the section's centroid, which camber and washout move
slightly off the radius R. The smooth loft rounds the corners where the parts meet, so the sum agrees closely but not
exactly:

```python
unit = sections[0].ToOCCFace().mass / c_root**2

def frustum(c1, c2, L):
    return unit * L * (c1**2 + c1 * c2 + c2**2) / 3

centroid = station(b + bend / 2).ToOCCFace().center
arm = math.hypot(centroid.y - center[1], centroid.z - center[2])
parts = frustum(c_root, c_tip, b) + unit * c_tip**2 * arm * (k - g) + frustum(c_tip, c_winglet, hw)
print("centroid", arm, "from the bend axis, R =", R)
print("volume", wing.mass, "parts", parts, "relative difference", (wing.mass - parts) / parts)
```

```text
centroid 18.78062133328242 from the bend axis, R = 20
volume 155091.44574105335 parts 155091.01843317546 relative difference 2.755207117796072e-06
```

Source: https://planex2d.org/docs/integrations/occ/guided-loft.md

# Lofts with guide curves

A loft through a few sections is smooth, but between the sections it goes wherever its splines take it. When the
sections change quickly, its walls overshoot, and a passage can pinch shut where it should stay open. Guide curves
steer a loft. In planex2d, the guides go through the named corners of the sections, they are cut every few
millimeters, and every cut becomes a section of its own, so `occ.ThruSections` has no room left between the sections.
The construction is the same as for the [3D duct](../pytorch-duct.md), here on a simpler part.

A blower nozzle takes air from a hose fitting, a rounded square of 40 × 40, and blows it out of a flat slot of
120 × 8 at 100 along the axis. It flattens early, to a neck of 60 × 10 at 30, and then fans out to the slot.

```python
import math
import netgen.occ as occ
import numpy as np
import planex as px
```

## The sections

Each section is a rounded rectangle in a constraint sketch on its own plane, the xy plane lifted to its height with
`px.XY.Offset(z)`. It is made of four lines and four arcs that are tangent all around, centered on the axis, with the
dimensions `w`, `h` and `r`. Figure 1 shows the three sketched sections at one scale. The dots are the eight named
corners of each section, `bottom.start`, `bottom.end`, `right.start` and so on, through which the guides will pass.

```python
def section(w, h, r, z, id="section"):
    sk = px.Sketch(px.XY.Offset(z), id=id)
    sk.Move((-w / 2 + r, -h / 2)).Line(w - 2 * r, 0, px.Horizontal, id="bottom")
    sk.Arc(r, 90, px.Tangent, id="a1")
    sk.Line(0, h - 2 * r, px.Vertical, px.Tangent, id="right")
    sk.Arc(r, 90, px.Tangent, id="a2")
    sk.Line(-(w - 2 * r), 0, px.Horizontal, px.Tangent, id="top")
    sk.Arc(r, 90, px.Tangent, id="a3")
    sk.Line(0, -(h - 2 * r), px.Vertical, px.Tangent, id="left")
    sk.Arc(r, 90, px.Tangent, id="a4")
    sk.Constrain("a4.end", "bottom.start", px.Coincident)
    sk.Constrain("a4", "bottom", px.Tangent)
    sk.Constrain("a1", px.Radius, r, id="r")
    for arc in ("a2", "a3", "a4"):
        sk.Constrain("a1", arc, px.Equal)
    sk.Constrain("left", "right", px.Distance, w, id="w")
    sk.Constrain("bottom", "top", px.Distance, h, id="h")
    sk.Constrain("bottom.mid", px.V, px.Coincident)
    sk.Constrain("left.mid", px.H, px.Coincident)
    return sk


inlet = section(40, 40, 14, 0, "inlet")
neck = section(60, 10, 3, 30, "neck")
slot = section(120, 8, 3, 100, "slot")
sketched = [inlet, neck, slot]
CORNERS = [f"{edge}.{end}" for edge in ("bottom", "right", "top", "left")
           for end in ("start", "end")]
```

```python
def flat(s, caption):
    corners = [s(c).center[:2] for c in CORNERS]
    axes = [px.FromPolyline([(-61, 0), (61, 0)]), px.FromPolyline([(0, -21), (0, 21)])]
    return (s.Face(), caption, {"view": ((-62, 62), (-22, 22)), "dashed": axes,
                                "dots": corners, "dot": GUIDE})


Row(*(flat(s, f"{s.id}, {s['w']:g} × {s['h']:g}, z {s.ToXYZ((0, 0))[2]:g}") for s in sketched),
    caption="The three sketched sections and their named corners")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## The plain loft

`occ.ThruSections` through the three sketches gives a smooth solid. The height of its passage along the axis, read
from the loft's long edges (the top ones are the highest points of each cross-section), shows the problem. After the
neck, the walls swing past the slot's height, and the passage closes almost completely before it opens up to the slot
again.

```python
plain = occ.ThruSections([s.ToOCCWire() for s in sketched], solid=True)


def points(edge, n=200):
    t0, t1 = edge.parameter_interval
    return [edge.Value(t0 + (t1 - t0) * k / n) for k in range(n + 1)]


def passage(solid, z):
    top = np.full(len(z), -np.inf)
    for e in solid.edges:
        q = sorted(points(e), key=lambda p: p.z)
        if q[-1].z - q[0].z > 99:
            top = np.maximum(top, np.interp(z, [p.z for p in q], [p.y for p in q]))
    return 2 * top


z = np.linspace(0, 100, 201)
print("plain loft: smallest height", passage(plain, z).min(), "slot", slot["h"])
```

```text
plain loft: smallest height 0.40861213982749645 slot 8.0
```

## Guides

Two interpolated sections in each gap, at a third and at two thirds of the way, with width, height and corner radius
interpolated linearly between their neighbors, make seven sections. A spline through each named corner of all seven,
leaving the inlet and reaching the slot along the axis, is a guide (Figure 2a).

```python
def z_of(sk):
    return sk.ToXYZ((0, 0))[2]


def size(sk):
    x, y, _ = sk("right.start").center
    bottom = sk("bottom.start").center[1]
    return 2 * x, -2 * bottom, y - bottom


def between(a, b, t):
    w, h, r = (p + t * (q - p) for p, q in zip(size(a), size(b)))
    return section(w, h, r, z_of(a) + t * (z_of(b) - z_of(a)), "interpolated")


sections = [inlet]
for a, b in zip(sketched, sketched[1:]):
    sections += [between(a, b, 1 / 3), between(a, b, 2 / 3), b]
axial = {0: occ.Z, len(sections) - 1: occ.Z}
guides = []
for c in CORNERS:
    corners = [occ.Pnt(*s.ToXYZ(tuple(s(c).center[:2]))) for s in sections]
    guides.append(occ.SplineInterpolation(corners, tangents=axial))
```

## Sections cut from the guides

Every 2.5 along the axis, the eight guides are cut, and their points give a new section, with the sides through the
outermost corners and the corner radius from the corners between them. These sections cost little and hold the loft
to the guides between the sketches (Figure 2b). One `occ.ThruSections` through all of them gives the nozzle.

```python
def meet(guide, z):
    a, b = guide.parameter_interval
    for _ in range(50):
        m = (a + b) / 2
        a, b = (m, b) if guide.Value(m).z < z else (a, m)
    return guide.Value(a)


def from_corners(points, z):
    x, y = np.array([(p.x, p.y) for p in points]).T
    left, right = x[6:].mean(), x[2:4].mean()
    bottom, top = y[:2].mean(), y[4:6].mean()
    r = np.mean([right - x[1], y[2] - bottom, top - y[3], right - x[4],
                 x[5] - left, top - y[6], y[7] - bottom, x[0] - left])
    return section(right - left, top - bottom, r, z, "cut")


step = 2.5
known = [z_of(s) for s in sections]
cuts = [from_corners([meet(g, at) for g in guides], at)
        for at in np.arange(step, z_of(slot), step)
        if min(abs(at - k) for k in known) > 1e-6]
everything = sorted(sections + cuts, key=z_of)
nozzle = occ.ThruSections([s.ToOCCWire() for s in everything], solid=True)
print(len(sketched), "sketched,", len(sections) - len(sketched), "interpolated,",
      len(cuts), "cut sections")
```

```text
3 sketched, 4 interpolated, 36 cut sections
```

```python
VIEW = (20, 50, 0)
KEY = {"ink": "sketched", "accent": "interpolated", "light": "cut from the guides", "guide": "guides"}
ink = [(s.ToOCCWire(), "ink") for s in sketched]
interpolated = [(s.ToOCCWire(), "accent") for s in sections if s.id == "interpolated"]
lines = [(g, "guide") for g in guides]
cut = [(s.ToOCCWire(), "light") for s in cuts]
Views(("The seven sections and the guides", ink + interpolated + lines),
      ("all sections of the loft", cut + ink + interpolated + lines), angles=VIEW, key=KEY,
      caption="The sections and the guide curves")
```


## Checks

The end caps of the loft are the sketched inlet and slot. Its long edges, which leave the planes of the sections and
run through their corners, lie on the guides up to the distance printed below. Its volume agrees with the areas of
the sections summed along the axis by the trapezoidal rule, which is close because the sections are dense. Finally,
the passage stays open, as its smallest height compared with that of the plain loft shows.

```python
for s, cap in ((inlet, nozzle.faces.Min(occ.Z)), (slot, nozzle.faces.Max(occ.Z))):
    print(s.id, "cap", cap.mass, "sketch", s.Face().mass)

tracks = []
for g in guides:
    q = points(g, 4000)
    tracks.append(np.array([(p.z, p.x, p.y) for p in q]).T)
worst = 0.0
for e in nozzle.edges:
    q = points(e, 20)
    if max(p.z for p in q) - min(p.z for p in q) < 1e-6:
        continue
    for p in q:
        off = [math.hypot(p.x - np.interp(p.z, gz, gx), p.y - np.interp(p.z, gz, gy)) for gz, gx, gy in tracks]
        worst = max(worst, min(off))
print("long edges off the guides: at most", worst)

areas = np.array([s.Face().mass for s in everything])
zs = np.array([z_of(s) for s in everything])
summed = np.sum(np.diff(zs) * (areas[1:] + areas[:-1]) / 2)
print("volume", nozzle.mass, "sections summed", summed, "relative", (nozzle.mass - summed) / summed)
print("smallest height: guided", passage(nozzle, z).min(), "plain", passage(plain, z).min())
```

```text
inlet cap 1431.7521598176133 sketch 1431.7521601035994
slot cap 952.2743338691761 sketch 952.274333882308
long edges off the guides: at most 0.3344470312668278
```

```text
volume 88110.88359715887 sections summed 88102.51107996187 relative 9.503153876512192e-05
smallest height: guided 7.57039630381177 plain 0.40861213982749645
```

# netgen and NGSolve


[![The potential flow around a cylinder in a channel, solved with NGSolve on the mesh of a planex2d face](index_files/index_1.png)<span>A potential flow on the mesh of a planex2d face</span>](../../integrations/netgen/meshing.md)
[![The temperature of a cold plate with four bores, a planex2d measurement solved by NGSolve](index_files/index_2.png)<span>A cold plate&#x27;s temperature as a measurement</span>](../../integrations/netgen/field-solvers.md)
[![An auxetic lattice tiled from a level set unit cell, extruded and loaded, its displacement in color](index_files/index_3.png)<span>An auxetic lattice from a level set, loaded</span>](../../integrations/netgen/levelset.md)


planex2d faces and shapes become netgen geometries in one call. The geometry reaches netgen through OpenCASCADE, in the
build that netgen ships as `netgen-occt`, so everything on the [OpenCASCADE](../occ/index.md) pages applies here too,
and every plane argument takes netgen's `occ.Axes` besides a `px.Plane`. Face names turn into materials, edge names into
boundary conditions, and vertex names into point names. `maxh` and `hpref` on faces, edges and vertices set the mesh
size and refine towards corners. Faces glued into a shape share their edges, so the regions of the mesh fit together
without gaps. Results come back onto the geometry: `px.PlotField` draws NGSolve and FEniCSx fields on the exact planex2d
geometry, also in cuts through 3D parts. A measurement can pass the part to netgen for meshing and to NGSolve for
solving, and `px.FromLevelSet` turns a level set function into a planex2d shape.

# Coming from netgen's WorkPlane

Drawing code written for `netgen.occ.WorkPlane` keeps working. `px.WorkPlane` takes the same drawing calls (`MoveTo`,
`LineTo`, `Line`, `Arc`, `ArcTo`, `Circle`, `Rectangle`, `RectangleC`, `Spline`, `Rotate`, `Direction`, `Close` and
the others) and returns planex2d objects: `Face()` gives a face, `Wire()` and `Wires()` give wires. These are faces and
shapes with exact Boolean operations, passed back to OpenCASCADE only when requested (`ToOCCFace`, `ToOCCShape`).
Faces that netgen has already drawn come over with `px.FromOCC`. The example is a re-entrant honeycomb, a metamaterial
with a negative Poisson's ratio, originally drawn for netgen.

## The minimal example

The minimal example draws an L-shaped plate with one function, once on netgen's work plane and once on planex2d's.
The netgen face is also taken over with `px.FromOCC`:

```python
import netgen.occ as occ
import planex as px

def plate(wp):
    return wp.MoveTo(0, 0).LineTo(4, 0).LineTo(4, 1) \
        .LineTo(1, 1).LineTo(1, 3).LineTo(0, 3).Close().Face()

netgen_face = plate(occ.WorkPlane())
face = plate(px.WorkPlane())
taken_over = px.FromOCC(netgen_face)
print(isinstance(face, px.Face), netgen_face.mass, face.mass, taken_over.mass)
```

```text
True 6.0 6.0 6.0
```

The area is 4 · 1 + 1 · 2 = 6 in all three cases. The rest of the page uses a larger part.

```python
import math
import time
import warnings
from ngsolve_webgpu.jupyter import Draw
```

## One cell

The cell has a strut thickness of 0.5, a width of 3.5, a height of 6 and a re-entrant angle of 30°. The function
draws it on whichever work plane it is given, netgen's or planex2d's:

```python
t, w, h, phi = 0.5, 3.5, 6.0, 30.0
d = t / math.sin(math.radians(90 - phi))
a = w / math.tan(math.radians(90 - phi))

def cell(wp):
    return (wp.MoveTo(w - t / 2, a + d / 2).LineTo(t / 2, d / 2) \
            .LineTo(t / 2, h - d / 2).LineTo(w - t / 2, h - a - d / 2) \
            .LineTo(w - t / 2, h - a + d / 2).LineTo(t / 2, h + d / 2) \
            .LineTo(-t / 2, h + d / 2).LineTo(-t / 2, -d / 2) \
            .LineTo(t / 2, -d / 2).LineTo(w - t / 2, a - d / 2).Close().Face())

netgen_cell = cell(occ.WorkPlane())
planex_cell = cell(px.WorkPlane())
print(f"netgen {netgen_cell.mass:.15f}")
print(f"planex {planex_cell.mass:.15f}, difference {planex_cell.mass - netgen_cell.mass:.1e}")
```

```text
netgen 6.752776749732569
planex 6.752776749732570, difference 8.9e-16
```

```python
Row((planex_cell, "One cell, from px.WorkPlane"), caption="A re-entrant honeycomb cell drawn with WorkPlane calls")
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

## The sheet

netgen moves faces with `Move` and adds them one by one, while planex2d moves them with `Translated` and unites them
all at once with `px.Unify`. The frame cuts the sheet to a window. netgen needs the inner rectangle reversed to make
it a hole. In planex2d, a loop inside another is a hole by nesting, so `px.WorkPlane` draws the frame without
`Reverse()`. It still accepts `Reverse()`, so netgen code runs unchanged, and without it, a `PlanexWarning` says that
the inner wire is taken as a hole.

```python
nx, ny = 9, 7
offsets = [((2 * i + k) * w, (2 * j + k) * (h - a)) \
           for j in range(ny) for k in (0, 1) for i in range(nx)]

start = time.perf_counter()
netgen_sheet = sum(netgen_cell.Move((dx, dy, 0)) for dx, dy in offsets)
netgen_frame = occ.WorkPlane().MoveTo(3.255, 3.5) \
    .Rectangle(49.490, 43).Reverse() \
    .MoveTo(-10, -10).Rectangle(100, 100).Face()
netgen_geo = netgen_sheet - netgen_frame
netgen_time = time.perf_counter() - start

start = time.perf_counter()
planex_sheet = px.Unify([planex_cell.Translated(o) for o in offsets])
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore", px.PlanexWarning)
    planex_frame = px.WorkPlane().MoveTo(3.255, 3.5).Rectangle(49.490, 43) \
        .MoveTo(-10, -10).Rectangle(100, 100).Face()
planex_geo = planex_sheet - planex_frame
planex_time = time.perf_counter() - start

print(f"netgen {netgen_time:.3f} s, area " \
      f"{sum(f.mass for f in netgen_geo.faces):.9f}")
print(f"planex {planex_time:.3f} s, area {planex_geo.mass:.9f}")
```

```text
netgen 4.627 s, area 534.854430306
planex 0.005 s, area 534.854430306
```

```python
Row((planex_geo, "The sheet cut to its window"))
```

```text
<IPython.core.display.HTML object>
```

The cells only touch, so the sheet holds exactly 126 cells of material, and every pocket between them remains a
hole:

```python
print(f"sheet {planex_sheet.mass:.12f}, " \
      f"{len(offsets)} cells {len(offsets) * planex_cell.mass:.12f}, " \
      f"{len(planex_sheet.Face().inner)} holes")
```

```text
sheet 850.849870466301, 126 cells 850.849870466304, 96 holes
```
